domains.title: Blood flow, vessels and blood
domains.overview: The most consistent vascular findings in ME/CFS concern circulation when upright: cerebral blood flow falls much more than normal on tilt, stroke volume is low, red-cell and blood volume are below predicted in a large minority to about half, and during exercise the heart is under-filled (preload failure). These are reported by several groups, though the cerebral blood flow and invasive exercise data each come mostly from one centre, and a 2026 study found blood volume did not predict who has orthostatic abnormalities. Reduced endothelial function (FMD, PORH) has been found in three independent cohorts, and newer work shows fewer muscle capillaries than bed rest would explain and narrowed retinal vessels in post-COVID ME/CFS. Complement activation is replicated in long COVID but inconsistent in ME/CFS. Microclots remain contested on method, and pooled blood proteomics do not show raised coagulation, platelet or endothelial-activation proteins.

findings.finding: Red cell volume and total blood volume are below predicted in a large minority to about half of ME/CFS patients measured by isotope or CO-rebreathing methods.
findings.plain: Many patients have less blood than expected for their size, mainly because they have fewer red cells. Less blood means less returns to the heart when upright.
findings.detail: Hurwitz 2009 (Clin Sci): total blood volume -15%, plasma volume -13%, red cell volume -19% in CFS, and the blood-volume deficit explained 91-94% of group differences in cardiac volume indices. Newton 2016 linked lower plasma volume to smaller cardiac MRI volumes and to fatigue severity but not to illness duration (argues against pure deconditioning). Five independent groups report a red-cell-volume deficit (Streeten 2000, Hurwitz, Newton, van Campen 2018, Yamazaki 2026). Measurement methods differ (I-131 albumin, Cr-51, CO-rebreathing) and predicted values depend on body-size formulas, so prevalence figures are not comparable across studies.

studies.result: TBV -15.4%, PV -13.2%, RBCV -19.1%; deficit explained most of the lower stroke index

studies.n: CFS vs controls (cardiac MRI + red cell mass)
studies.result: Lower cardiac volumes tracked plasma and red cell volume; PV correlated with fatigue severity; no link to illness duration
RBC volume deficient in 49%; TBV hypovolaemic 35%, normal 43%, hypervolaemic 22%

studies.cite: Streeten & Bell 2000, Am J Med Sci
studies.design: case series, Cr-51 red cell mass
studies.result: Low red cell mass in most patients; orthostatic symptoms

contradicting.result: Blood-volume category did not predict any lean-test abnormality (POTS, hypocapnia, hypotension); 22% were hypervolaemic

open_questions: Why does red cell mass fall: reduced marrow output (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of FinnGen labs found lower reticulocytes and soluble transferrin receptor with normal iron), inactivity, or altered EPO signalling?
Does blood volume change with severity or after crashes?
If low blood volume does not predict orthostatic intolerance (Yamazaki 2026), how much of the symptom burden does it explain?
findings.test_available: Haemoglobin mass by CO-rebreathing (some sports-science and research labs); isotope blood volume (Daxor BVA-100, a few US centres). Reticulocytes, ferritin, transferrin saturation are routine.

findings.finding: The hormones that should rise to restore blood volume (renin, aldosterone, EPO) are not raised in ME/CFS or POTS despite low volume, and blood proteomics shows no consistent change in them.
findings.plain: If blood volume is low the body should release hormones to retain salt and water. In many patients these hormones stay normal or low, which suggests the volume set-point itself is off.
findings.detail: In POTS, low aldosterone and an inappropriately low renin for the plasma-volume deficit (the renin-aldosterone paradox) were described by Raj et al. 2005; adrenal responsiveness to ACTH is intact (Laurin 2023), so the defect sits upstream. Older ME/CFS work reported low renin in tilt-positive patients and normal EPO. A Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of SomaScan and UK Biobank Olink data (about 150 patients plus UKB) found renin, ACE, BNP, EPO and hepcidin flat across cohorts.

studies.result: Plasma volume deficit with low renin and aldosterone for the degree of hypovolaemia
Adrenal aldosterone and cortisol responses to ACTH intact in POTS

studies.n: Hoel, Germain, Walitt SomaScan + UKB Olink
studies.result: RAAS/natriuretic, EPO, hepcidin sets null (q>0.7)

open_questions: Is the low-renin pattern present in ME/CFS without POTS?
Does ADH/copeptin respond normally to upright posture?
findings.test_available: Supine and upright renin/aldosterone; copeptin. Routine labs, but interpretation needs posture and salt-intake control.

findings.finding: Left-ventricular volumes and stroke volume are smaller in ME/CFS at rest and fall more than normal on tilt, largely in proportion to low blood volume rather than to weak heart muscle.
findings.plain: The heart is not damaged, but it is under-filled, so each beat pumps less blood, especially when upright.
findings.detail: Hurwitz 2009: severe CFS had about 10% lower stroke index and end-diastolic volume; adjusting for blood volume removed most of the difference. Hollingsworth 2012 (cardiac MRI) reported markedly lower end-diastolic volume and stroke volume. Miwa reports a 'small heart' (cardiothoracic ratio <0.42) subgroup with orthostatic intolerance. van Campen 2024 (233 POTS, many more normal HR-BP response) showed larger stroke-volume-index falls on tilt in all ME/CFS groups than in controls, with two patterns: venous pooling (HR rise 30-39) and a hyperadrenergic pattern (HR rise >=40) with relatively preserved SVI.

studies.n: 233 ME/CFS with POTS + normal-response patients vs HC
studies.result: SVI fall larger than HC in all groups; two POTS haemodynamic profiles
Lower LV end-diastolic volume and stroke volume
Small heart and downregulated renin-aldosterone/ADH systems in OI subgroup

contradicting.result: Cardiac dimensions within normal range after indexing in a referral cohort

open_questions: Do stroke-volume deficits normalise after volume loading, and does that predict symptomatic benefit?
How much of the van Campen echo data has been reproduced in another centre with blinded readers?
findings.test_available: Echocardiogram (routine, but usually reported normal at rest); tilt with stroke-volume monitoring (Finapres/bioimpedance at autonomic units).

findings.finding: During upright invasive exercise testing most ME/CFS patients have abnormally low right-atrial filling pressure (preload failure), and a high-flow subgroup shows poor systemic oxygen extraction.
findings.plain: When patients exercise, too little blood returns to the heart. In some, blood also bypasses the muscles, so oxygen goes unused.
findings.detail: Joseph/Systrom 2021 (Chest): of 1,516 iCPETs, 160 met ME/CFS criteria with RAP <6.5 mmHg; peak RAP 1.9 vs 8.3 mmHg, peak VO2 80% vs 101% predicted. Low-flow tertile had lower peak cardiac output; high-flow tertile had lower systemic O2 extraction (0.74 vs 0.86-0.88). Selection by low RAP is built into the cohort, so the prevalence of preload failure in ME/CFS generally is not established. Novak 2026 reports preload failure in 92% of the 66 ME/CFS patients who had iCPET (same Harvard group). Long COVID iCPET shows the same pattern (Singh 2022; Joseph 2023 review). Independent replication outside the Systrom network is lacking.

studies.result: Peak RAP 1.9 vs 8.3 mmHg; impaired O2 extraction in high-flow tertile; SFN in 31%
Preload failure 92% ME/CFS (of 66 tested), 96% LC (of 25)
Pyridostigmine improved peak VO2 vs placebo via higher cardiac output (acute effect)

open_questions: What is the preload-failure prevalence in an unselected ME/CFS cohort?
Can non-invasive tests (pulse pressure narrowing on stand, Day 2023; CO-rebreathing cardiac output) stand in for iCPET?
Does preload failure precede or follow illness onset?
findings.test_available: Invasive CPET at a few US centres (Brigham, Yale, Mount Sinai); not routine. Two-day CPET is non-invasive but does not measure preload.

findings.finding: A subset of patients with unexplained exertional intolerance cannot extract oxygen normally from blood during exercise, associated with hypocapnia and possible arteriovenous shunting.
findings.plain: Blood arrives at the muscles but leaves with too much oxygen still in it, so the muscles get less than they need.
findings.detail: Melamed 2019 (Systrom group) described a poor-extraction phenotype with relative hypocapnia (PaCO2 29.9 vs 37.5 mmHg) and high mixed-venous O2 saturation at peak (44% vs 31%). Proposed causes: microvascular shunting from small-fibre neuropathy, mitochondrial limitation, or a left-shifted oxyhaemoglobin curve from hyperventilation. Muscle-oxygenation work by the Wüst group (NIRS post-occlusion) points in the same direction. All iCPET data come from one network.

studies.result: Poor systemic O2 extraction with hypocapnia; high peak SvO2
High-flow tertile extraction 0.74 vs 0.86-0.88
impaired extraction
75% impaired extraction
reduced extraction

open_questions: Which contributes most: shunting, mitochondria, or CO2-related Bohr shift?
Is impaired extraction present at rest or only at peak?
findings.test_available: Research only (iCPET); muscle NIRS in research labs.

findings.finding: Cerebral blood flow falls about 26% during head-up tilt in ME/CFS versus 7% in controls, including in patients with normal heart rate and blood pressure responses.
findings.plain: Standing up reduces blood flow to the brain far more than normal, even when pulse and blood pressure look fine, and the drop tracks orthostatic symptoms.
findings.detail: van Campen 2020 (429 patients, 44 HC, extracranial carotid+vertebral Doppler): 82% of normal-response, 98% of delayed-OH and 100% of POTS patients exceeded the control lower limit (13%). Flow recovery after tilt is incomplete and slowest in severe patients (van Campen 2021). The CO-CBF relation is roughly 1:1 in most patients, unlike the 3:1 seen in health (van Campen 2024, 2025). Transcranial Doppler work from other groups (Medow/Stewart; Novak 2026: reduced orthostatic CBF velocity in 88% ME/CFS) agrees. Caveats: most volume-flow data come from one Dutch clinic, operators are not blinded to diagnosis, controls are few relative to patients, and the 2025 POTS paper found CBF reduction did not differ between its two haemodynamic subgroups.

studies.result: End-tilt CBF -26% vs -7%; ~90% abnormal
CBF reduced after tilt, slowest recovery in most severe
Reduced orthostatic CBFv in 88% ME/CFS, 92% LC
Two-thirds ~1:1 CO-CBF reduction; one-third limited CO fall with high HR (hyperadrenergic)

open_questions: Independent replication of extracranial volume-flow method with blinded readers
Does CBF reduction predict response to fluids, compression, or vasoconstrictors?
What happens to CBF in sitting (the posture patients actually spend time in)?
findings.test_available: Extracranial Doppler on tilt (Stichting CardioZorg, Netherlands); transcranial Doppler on tilt at some autonomic labs.

findings.finding: Many ME/CFS patients over-breathe when upright (orthostatic hypocapnia), and during exercise hyperventilation and dysfunctional breathing are common.
findings.plain: When standing, some patients breathe off too much CO2. Low CO2 narrows brain arteries, which can add to dizziness and brain fog.
findings.detail: End-tidal CO2 falls on tilt in several groups (Naschitz 2000, Razumovsky 2003, Natelson 2007, Medow 2014, Novak's 'hypocapnic cerebral hypoperfusion'). Yamazaki 2026: postural orthostatic syndrome of hypocapnia (POSH) in 41% of 49 on a lean test. Mancini 2025: hyperventilation and/or dysfunctional breathing during CPET common, with VE/VCO2 34.7 vs 28.1 in hyperventilators. But van Campen 2023 found CO2 reactivity normal and the PETCO2 fall explained only a modest share of the CBF fall, so hypocapnia is probably a contributor, not the main driver. Whether over-breathing is primary (chemoreflex/autonomic) or compensatory (e.g. to aid venous return via thoracic pump) is unresolved.

studies.result: Upright hyperventilation and CBFv fall; phenylephrine restored n-back performance
POSH 40.8%, most common orthostatic abnormality
18 hyperventilators; elevated VE/VCO2 or dysfunctional breathing in 83% of them

contradicting.result: CO2 reactivity normal; PETCO2 explains only a modest part of CBF fall

open_questions: Is upright hypocapnia a cause, a compensation, or a marker of sympathetic activation?
Does breathing retraining or added CO2 change orthostatic symptoms?
findings.test_available: Capnography during a 10-minute stand or tilt (cheap; available in some respiratory/autonomic labs); CPET with breathing-pattern analysis.

findings.finding: Raising blood pressure with phenylephrine during tilt blocked hyperventilation, restored cerebral blood velocity and improved working memory in ME/CFS, whereas CO2 or acetazolamide alone did not.
findings.plain: In a lab test, a drug that tightens blood vessels improved both brain blood flow and thinking speed when patients were upright.
findings.detail: Medow 2014 and Medow & Stewart 2024 (same New York group) used acute infusions with n-back testing; numbers are small (single-digit to low teens per condition). These are mechanistic studies, not treatment trials. Compression of legs and abdomen reduced cardiac output fall (-15% vs -27%) and CBF fall (-14% vs -25%) on tilt in van Campen 2021 (n=16).

studies.cite: Medow & Stewart 2024, Am J Physiol Regul
studies.result: Only phenylephrine improved upright n-back and phase synchronisation
Compression reduced CO and CBF falls

open_questions: Do oral analogues (midodrine) reproduce the cognitive effect in daily life?
Placebo-controlled trials of compression garments in ME/CFS
findings.test_available: Research only; midodrine and compression are used clinically for orthostatic intolerance.

findings.finding: Large-artery flow-mediated dilation and microvascular post-occlusive reactive hyperaemia are reduced in ME/CFS in two independent Norwegian cohorts and by peripheral arterial tonometry in Berlin.
findings.plain: The lining of blood vessels does not widen properly when it should. This has been found in several groups with different methods.
findings.detail: Sandvik 2023 (RituxME substudy, 39 patients): FMD 5.1% vs 8.2% (p<0.0001, adjusted for diameter and sex), PORH 1354 vs 2208 PU; rituximab had no effect; PORH but not FMD improved over 18 months and PORH correlated with daily steps. Sørland 2021 (cyclophosphamide cohort, 35 patients): FMD 5.9% vs 7.7%, PORH 1331 vs 1886 PU. Scherbakov 2020 (EndoPAT): endothelial dysfunction (RHI <=1.81) in 51% of 35 vs 20% of 20 controls, linked to severity. Haffke 2022: reduced RHI in 5/14 post-COVID ME/CFS. Caveats: inactivity lowers FMD, controls were mostly not activity-matched, and FMD and PORH did not correlate with each other.

studies.result: FMD 5.1% vs 8.2%; PORH 1354 vs 2208 PU
FMD 5.9% vs 7.7%; PORH lower; no change with clinical response
ED in 51% vs 20%; associated with severity
ED in 5/14 and 5/16, none of HC; ET-1 raised
endothelial dysfunction
endothelial dysfunction
impaired vascular function

contradicting.result: no dysfunction
normal

open_questions: Is endothelial dysfunction cause, consequence of inactivity, or a marker of an immune/serum factor?
Does it track PEM or orthostatic severity over time?
Activity-matched control studies
findings.test_available: FMD ultrasound and EndoPAT in vascular research labs; not standard clinical tests.

findings.finding: Plasma or purified IgG from ME/CFS patients alters cultured endothelial cells: lower nitric oxide production, more mitochondrial fragmentation, and anti-endothelial antibody binding.
findings.plain: Something in patients' blood seems to make lab-grown vessel-lining cells work less well. This has been seen by three labs using different tests, none yet repeated by another lab using the same test.
findings.detail: Bertinat 2022: HUVECs exposed to ME/CFS plasma (11 vs 12) produced less NO with higher inhibitory eNOS Thr495 phosphorylation. Flaskamp 2022 (Charité): more anti-endothelial antibody binding in post-COVID ME/CFS, and sera lacked the pro-angiogenic effect seen in non-ME post-COVID sera. Prusty 2026 (BBIH): purified IgG from 39 ME/CFS and 15 post-COVID ME/CFS fragmented endothelial mitochondria versus MS and healthy IgG; single lab, nominal p-values over many readouts (summarised in Solving ME/CFS serum-factors review). No lab has reproduced another's assay.

studies.result: Lower NO production, higher eNOS Thr495 phosphorylation
Higher AECA binding in PCS/CFS; no pro-angiogenic effect
Endothelial mitochondrial fragmentation with ME IgG, not MS or HC IgG

open_questions: Blinded multi-lab exchange of the same coded sera
What is the antigen, and is the effect IgG-dependent in every assay?

findings.finding: Retinal imaging shows narrower arterioles, lower arteriolar-to-venular ratio, reduced flicker-induced venular dilation and lower capillary vessel density in post-COVID patients, most pronounced in those meeting ME/CFS criteria.
findings.plain: The tiny vessels at the back of the eye, which can be photographed without needles, look narrower and respond less in post-COVID ME/CFS.
findings.detail: Wallraven 2026 (BMC Med, 'All Eyes on PCS'): 102 PCS (62 with ME/CFS) vs 102 recovered and 96 never-infected; CRAE 178 vs 186 um, AVR 0.83 vs 0.87, venular flicker dilation 3.7% vs 4.8%; ME/CFS subgroup most affected (AUC 0.79); robust to CV-risk adjustment except AVR attenuated. Schlick 2022 (Erlangen, OCT-A): lower vessel density in superficial and intermediate capillary plexus in PCS, lower still with chronic fatigue. Data are almost entirely post-COVID; pre-2020 ME/CFS cohorts have not been imaged with these methods.

studies.result: Narrower arterioles, lower AVR and flicker dilation; ME/CFS most affected; AVR tied to IL-6, ICAM-1, VCAM-1
Lower retinal capillary vessel density; worse with chronic fatigue

open_questions: Is the same seen in pre-pandemic, non-COVID ME/CFS?
Do retinal measures change with PEM or with treatment?
findings.test_available: OCT-A at ophthalmology clinics (widely available, though reference values for vessel density vary by device); dynamic vessel analysis research only.

findings.finding: Sublingual video-microscopy shows reduced perfused capillary density and glycocalyx changes in long COVID, persisting many months after infection.
findings.plain: Under the tongue, fewer small vessels carry blood in long COVID patients.
findings.detail: Osiaevi/Rovas/Kümpers (Münster) used sideStream dark-field microscopy with automated analysis (GlycoCheck) and reported persistent capillary rarefaction in long COVID (Nephrol Dial Transplant 2024; Angiogenesis 2023). No ME/CFS-specific cohort has been published with this method; whether rarefaction correlates with ME/CFS-defined PEM is unknown.

studies.result: Capillary rarefaction proposed as possible cause of long COVID

open_questions: Apply sublingual microscopy to pre-pandemic ME/CFS
Does capillary density recover over time?

findings.finding: Muscle biopsies show fewer capillaries per fibre in ME/CFS and less capillary supply per fibre size in both ME/CFS and long COVID, unlike the pattern after 60 days of bed rest; thickened capillary basement membrane has been reported but is not yet peer-reviewed.
findings.plain: Muscles of patients have fewer and possibly thicker-walled small blood vessels, and this is different from what happens to healthy people kept in bed.
findings.detail: Charlton 2026 (Nat Commun, Wüst group): ME/CFS (n=23-24) had lower capillary-to-fibre ratio than controls (p<0.001, n=30) and long COVID; both patient groups had lower capillary density and lower capillary supply for a given fibre area; healthy bed rest (n=17-24) instead raised capillary density because fibres shrank. This argues against inactivity as the full explanation. Slaghekke 2025 (conference poster, electron microscopy, about 11 patients per group) reported basement membrane thickening (p<0.0001) and smaller capillary lumens in ME/CFS and post-COVID; the composite CF x collagen IV measure that correlated with CPET has been questioned. Appelman 2024 found amyloid-containing deposits in long COVID muscle that increased after induced PEM.

studies.design: case-control + bed-rest comparison, vastus lateralis biopsy
studies.result: ME/CFS lower capillary-to-fibre ratio and density; patterns differ from bed rest
Thicker capillary basement membrane, smaller lumen
Amyloid-containing deposits and myopathy worse after PEM
capillary basement-membrane thickening, microvascular changes
lower capillary/fibre ratio

open_questions: Independent replication of basement membrane thickening with blinded EM
Is thickening caused by repeated ischaemia, immune deposition, or pericyte loss?
Severe and housebound patients have not been biopsied
findings.test_available: Research only (needle biopsy at a research centre).

findings.finding: Pericytes and vascular smooth-muscle cells have not been examined directly in ME/CFS tissue, but blood proteins from mural cells and vessel matrix (NOTCH3, ITGAV, TGF-beta set, LUM) are lower across several ME/CFS cohorts and in long COVID.
findings.plain: Pericytes are the cells wrapped around capillaries that control their width. Nobody has looked at them in ME/CFS tissue yet; indirect blood clues suggest they may be fewer or less active.
findings.detail: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of SomaScan (Hoel, Germain, Walitt) and UK Biobank Olink data: ITGAV d -0.34 (UKB q=0.002), NOTCH3 -0.32, THBS1 -0.50, LUM -0.92; vascular smooth-muscle tissue score d -0.48 (p=0.001) but flat in UKB competitive tests. The long COVID UK Explore set also showed lower endothelial/TGF-beta proteins (ANGPT2 -0.84, EDN1 -0.65). Lower circulating NOTCH3 could reflect less shedding rather than fewer cells. The basement-membrane thickening reported in muscle (where pericytes help build the membrane) is a possible link.

studies.n: 3 SomaScan cohorts + UKB Olink + LC UK
studies.result: Lower mural/ECM proteins in 3-4 cohorts and long COVID

contradicting.result: Vascular smooth-muscle set flat in UKB

open_questions: Stain pericyte markers (PDGFRB, NG2, alpha-SMA) in existing muscle and skin biopsies
Relate NOTCH3/ITGAV levels to orthostatic stroke volume

findings.finding: Proteomic panels do not show a consistent rise in classic endothelial-activation or vasoactive proteins in ME/CFS; most named candidates are null and the endothelial-activation set trends down.
findings.plain: Blood tests for vessel damage markers mostly come back normal in ME/CFS when large datasets are pooled, which differs from what small studies suggested.
findings.detail: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: VWF, SELP, SELE, VCAM1, ANGPT1/2, VEGFA, EDN1, ADM, ACE, REN, NPPB null; ICAM1 +0.20 (driven by UKB), ACE2 +0.21, NPPC +0.23; endothelial-activation set d -0.30 (q=0.09, down). By contrast, smaller ELISA studies report raised endothelin-1 (Haffke 2022) and Wallraven 2026 found raised IL-6, ICAM-1, VCAM-1 in PCS and ME/CFS. Post-COVID ME/CFS may differ from pre-pandemic cohorts.

studies.result: ET-1 raised in both patient groups
IL-6, ICAM-1, VCAM-1 raised
Immune cells show low ATP/ADP ratio (energy stress); skewed T, NK and dendritic subsets; raised plasma proteins for thrombus formation and vascular reactivity

contradicting.result: Named endothelial/vasoactive proteins null; activation set lower
sVCAM and sICAM did not differ between patients with and without ED

open_questions: Are post-COVID cohorts more inflammatory/endothelial than pre-pandemic ME/CFS?
Do any of these markers change after exertion?
findings.test_available: Endothelin-1, ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 are available from some specialist labs but not validated for ME/CFS.

findings.finding: VEGF-A has been reported lower, not higher, in ME/CFS plasma, and proteomic re-analysis finds no consistent change; long COVID cohorts more often report raised VEGF.
findings.plain: VEGF is a signal that makes new small vessels. Results in ME/CFS are inconsistent, and they differ from long COVID.
findings.detail: Landi 2016 reported clustered reductions of IL-7, IL-16 and VEGF-A in ME/CFS that were not seen in liver-disease fatigue controls. Large cytokine panels (e.g. Montoya 2017) did not find VEGF among robust differences; the Solving ME/CFS proteome re-analysis found VEGFA null. In long COVID several cohorts report raised VEGF (e.g. Patel 2022). Flaskamp 2022 found post-COVID non-ME sera pro-angiogenic but post-COVID ME/CFS sera not, consistent with a missing compensatory angiogenic response in ME/CFS.

studies.n: ME/CFS vs controls and liver-disease controls
studies.result: Lower VEGF-A, IL-7, IL-16

studies.n: PCS-ME/CFS vs PCS vs HC sera
studies.result: PCS sera pro-angiogenic; PCS-ME/CFS sera not

contradicting.result: VEGFA null

open_questions: Is there a tissue-level angiogenic deficit (e.g. muscle capillary rarefaction) that blood VEGF misses?

findings.finding: Red blood cells from ME/CFS patients were stiffer in one microfluidic study, and real-time deformability cytometry found altered red-cell deformation persisting after COVID-19.
findings.plain: Red cells need to bend to squeeze through capillaries. In a small study, patients' red cells were stiffer.
findings.detail: Saha 2019 (Stanford/OMF, custom microfluidic channels, small paired sample, about 12-14 patients) reported slower entry and reduced elongation of ME/CFS red cells. Kubánková 2021 (Biophys J, real-time deformability cytometry) found altered erythrocyte deformation and size heterogeneity persisting months after COVID-19. No independent ME/CFS replication; older reports of abnormal red-cell shape (stomatocytes) are from the 1990s and used subjective scoring.

studies.n: small ME/CFS vs age-matched HC sample
studies.result: ME/CFS RBCs significantly stiffer
Erythrocyte deformation changes persisted after recovery

open_questions: Replication with RT-DC or ektacytometry in a larger ME/CFS cohort
Is stiffness linked to oxidative stress or membrane lipids?
findings.test_available: Research only (ektacytometry exists in some haematology labs).

findings.finding: Fibrinaloid microclots (thioflavin-T-positive amyloid fibrin deposits) are reported to be increased in platelet-poor plasma in ME/CFS and long COVID, but the method is not standardised and haemostasis experts dispute the inference that they cause symptoms.
findings.plain: One research network sees tiny clot-like particles in patients' plasma. Other experts say the method is unreliable and the particles may not exist in circulating blood. Anticoagulant treatment based on them is not supported.
findings.detail: Nunes 2022 (25 ME/CFS vs 15 HC): microclot image area commonly >10-fold higher, platelet spreading score 2.72 vs 1.00, hypercoagulable TEG; load lower than in long COVID. Kruger 2022 found entrapped inflammatory proteins in long COVID microclots. Dalton 2024 (Sheffield, independent group, semi-automated counting) found higher counts in long COVID as a cohort, with wide overlap and high counts also after recent COVID. Critiques: visual scoring, uncertain blinding, ex vivo artefact possible, no in vivo demonstration; Hunt 2024 (RPTH) concluded the hypothesis is not evidence-based and unlicensed antithrombotics or apheresis are not justified outside trials; Kell 2024 rebutted. Solving ME/CFS proteome re-analysis found a platelet/microclot protein set slightly lower, not higher.

studies.result: Microclot area >10x; platelet hyperactivation
Higher counts in LC as a group, broad overlap
Entrapped inflammatory molecules, alpha-2 antiplasmin
microclots

contradicting.result: Microclot inferences not evidence-based; antithrombotics not justified
Platelet/microclot protein set d -0.33 (down)

open_questions: Blinded, multi-lab, standardised counting in ME/CFS with disease controls
Do microclots exist in vivo (e.g. capillaroscopy, biopsy)?
Any controlled trial of antithrombotic therapy
findings.test_available: Not reliably: some private labs offer microclot imaging; no validated clinical test.

findings.finding: Platelet activation findings in ME/CFS are inconsistent: one network reports hyperactivated platelets, while an earlier controlled study found no platelet activation or hypercoagulability.
findings.plain: Whether platelets are overactive in ME/CFS depends on who measured and how.
findings.detail: Nunes 2022 reported PAC-1 and CD62P staining and spreading consistent with activation. Kennedy 2006 (Dundee) measured platelet aggregation, P-selectin and coagulation markers and found no evidence of activation or hypercoagulability, explicitly arguing against antiplatelet therapy. In long COVID, Cervia-Hasler 2024 found monocyte-platelet aggregates and platelet-activation markers raised. No ME/CFS-specific flow cytometry replication.

studies.result: Platelet hyperactivation by microscopy
Platelet activation and monocyte-platelet aggregates in active LC
platelet hyperactivation

contradicting.result: No platelet activation or hypercoagulable state

open_questions: Standardised whole-blood flow cytometry in ME/CFS with exercise challenge

findings.finding: Routine coagulation markers (D-dimer, fibrinogen, PT/APTT) are generally normal in ME/CFS; claims of hypercoagulability rest on small 1990s studies and on thromboelastography from one network.
findings.plain: Standard clotting blood tests are usually normal in ME/CFS.
findings.detail: Berg 1999 reported a 'hypercoagulable state' (soluble fibrin monomer, thrombin-antithrombin) in a small sample; Kennedy 2006 found no coagulation differences. Proteomic re-analysis found the coagulation set null. Thromboelastography abnormalities (Nunes 2022; Saleem 2026 review) are not validated as ME/CFS markers.

studies.result: Reported hypercoagulable markers
raised VWF/FVIII-type markers

contradicting.result: No coagulation differences
Coagulation set null

open_questions: Do markers change transiently after exertion?
findings.test_available: D-dimer, fibrinogen, PT/APTT are routine; expected normal.

findings.finding: Active long COVID shows persistent complement dysregulation (terminal complex, alternative and classical pathway activation) with thromboinflammation markers, replicated across several cohorts.
findings.plain: Complement is part of the innate immune system. In long COVID it stays switched on months after infection, together with signs of platelet and vessel injury.
findings.detail: Cervia-Hasler 2024 (Science): >6,500 proteins in 268 longitudinal samples; terminal complement dysregulation, classical activation linked to herpesvirus antibody titres, raised haemolysis, tissue-injury and platelet markers. Baillie 2024 (Med, 166 LC vs 79): iC3b, TCC, Ba and C5a predicted LC (AUC 0.785). Further partial replication in Klein 2023 and Barratt-Due 2024; one adjusted null (Farztdinov preprint). Long COVID only; ME/CFS evidence is separate.

studies.result: Terminal and alternative/classical complement activation; thromboinflammation
Complement activation fragments raised; 4-marker AUC 0.785

contradicting.result: Complement differences not significant after age/BMI adjustment

open_questions: Does complement activation persist in long-duration LC that meets ME/CFS criteria?
Trials of complement inhibitors (none completed in LC or ME/CFS as of late 2026 to our knowledge)
findings.test_available: C3, C4, CH50, sC5b-9 available in some immunology labs; not validated for long COVID or ME/CFS.

findings.finding: In ME/CFS, complement findings are heterogeneous: an exercise-induced C4a rise, a genetically defined alternative-pathway subgroup, and proteomic signals that point in different directions across cohorts.
findings.plain: Complement may be abnormal in some ME/CFS patients, but studies disagree on which part and in which direction.
findings.detail: Sorensen 2003/2009 (CDC): C4a rose after exercise in CFS, with lectin-pathway MASP2 transcript differences. Maya 2026 (IJMS, CDC; 50 ME/CFS vs 121 controls from population sample): complement pQTL carriers showed alternative-pathway dysregulation (high C3/low Bb), six pQTLs linked to fatigue phenotypes in UK Biobank; SC5b-9 association possibly genetic. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: alternative/terminal complement up in Hoel and UKB, null in Germain, down in Walitt (I2 0.7-0.9); CSF complement/coagulation sets lower in ME/CFS with POTS (Bragée 2026, 10 vs 21, exploratory).

studies.result: Lectin-pathway changes underlying post-exercise C4a rise
Alternative-pathway subgroup (high C3/low Bb) linked to pQTLs

contradicting.result: Complement direction inconsistent between cohorts

open_questions: Measure activation fragments (C5a, sC5b-9, Ba) with careful pre-analytics before and after exertion
Is the long COVID complement signal present in pre-pandemic ME/CFS?
findings.test_available: Research only for activation products; C3/C4 routine but non-specific.

findings.finding: POTS is present in roughly a fifth of ME/CFS patients on formal testing (prevalence varies 6-43%), but cerebral hypoperfusion and preload failure are found in most patients regardless of whether they meet POTS heart-rate criteria.
findings.plain: POTS is a fast heart rate on standing. Only some ME/CFS patients have it, but most have reduced brain blood flow when upright anyway.
findings.detail: Novak 2026: POTS 19% ME/CFS and 22% long COVID, but reduced orthostatic CBFv 88-92%. van Campen 2020: CBF abnormal in 82% of patients with normal HR/BP response. van Campen 2024/2025 split ME/CFS-POTS into a venous-pooling profile and a hyperadrenergic profile (HR rise >=40) with different CO-CBF relations, which may have different treatment implications. Yamazaki 2026: hypocapnia more common than POTS on a lean test. Low plasma volume and the renin-aldosterone paradox are well described in POTS itself.

studies.result: POTS 19%/22%; orthostatic CBFv reduction 88%/92%
Two haemodynamic POTS profiles

open_questions: Prospective trial stratified by POTS profile (venous pooling vs hyperadrenergic)
Standardised orthostatic testing duration and posture across studies
findings.test_available: Tilt table or 10-minute NASA lean test (widely available); add capnography and stroke-volume monitoring where possible.

findings.finding: Coronary microvascular dysfunction (ANOCA) and ME/CFS overlap: about 18% of ANOCA patients meet ME/CFS criteria and most ME/CFS patients undergoing iCPET had ANOCA physiology.
findings.plain: Small heart blood-vessel problems seem to overlap with ME/CFS in one centre.

studies.result: 18% of ANOCA had ME/CFS; 24/27 ME/CFS had ANOCA; impaired extraction

hypotheses_notes.for: Red-cell volume deficits in 5 groups; small, under-filled heart explained by volume; preload failure on iCPET in most tested; CBF falls on tilt in about 90%; compression and vasoconstrictors reduce CBF falls.
hypotheses_notes.against: Blood-volume category did not predict orthostatic abnormalities (Yamazaki 2026); iCPET cohorts pre-selected for low RAP; one Dutch clinic supplies most CBF data; volume-regulating hormones not consistently abnormal.

hypotheses_notes.for: FMD/PORH/EndoPAT reduced in 3 independent cohorts; patient plasma/IgG impairs endothelial cells in vitro in 3 labs; retinal vessel narrowing in post-COVID ME/CFS.
hypotheses_notes.against: Inactivity alone lowers FMD; blood endothelial-activation proteins are not raised in pooled proteomics; no in vitro assay replicated across labs.

hypotheses_notes.for: Lower muscle capillarisation unlike bed rest (Charlton 2026); basement membrane thickening (poster); retinal and sublingual capillary loss in long COVID; poor O2 extraction subgroup.
hypotheses_notes.against: Mostly long COVID or small samples; basement-membrane data not peer-reviewed; no severe patients biopsied.

hypotheses_notes.for: Pretorius/Kell network reports raised microclot load in ME/CFS and LC; Dalton 2024 independent count in LC higher on average.
hypotheses_notes.against: Method unstandardised and visually scored; wide overlap with controls; no in vivo proof; haemostasis critiques (Hunt 2024); platelet/coagulation proteins not raised in pooled proteomics; Kennedy 2006 no platelet activation.

hypotheses_notes.for: Replicated complement activation in active long COVID; exercise C4a rise and genetic alternative-pathway subgroup in ME/CFS.
hypotheses_notes.against: ME/CFS proteomic complement direction inconsistent across cohorts; no complement-inhibitor trial.

hypotheses_notes.for: SFN in about a third to half of iCPET/autonomic cohorts; shunting proposed to explain poor extraction; hyperadrenergic POTS profile.
hypotheses_notes.against: Denervation severity did not correlate with exertional measures (Joseph 2021).

hypotheses_notes.for: Patient plasma lowers endothelial NO; IgG fragments endothelial mitochondria (MS-controlled).
hypotheses_notes.against: Single-lab assays, no cross-lab replication.

glossary.plain: How much blood fills the heart before each beat. Low preload means each beat pumps less.
An exercise test with catheters in the heart and an artery, measuring filling pressures and oxygen use directly.
Ultrasound measure of how much an arm artery widens after a cuff is released; a test of the vessel lining.
Post-occlusive reactive hyperaemia: the skin blood-flow surge after a cuff is released, a test of small vessels.
Low carbon dioxide in the blood, usually from over-breathing; it narrows brain arteries.
A thin protein layer around each capillary; thickening can slow oxygen passing to tissue.
A cell wrapped around capillaries that controls their width and helps keep their walls intact.
About 30 blood proteins in the innate immune system that tag and punch holes in targets; terminal complex (sC5b-9) marks full activation.
A clot-like particle of misfolded fibrin seen under a microscope with an amyloid dye; its significance is disputed.
The total amount of red blood cells in the body, measured with tracer methods, not by a standard blood count.
Optical coherence tomography angiography: a non-invasive scan of the tiny vessels in the retina.

key_reviews.why: Defines preload failure and impaired extraction phenotypes in the largest iCPET series.
Largest cerebral blood flow on tilt study (429 patients).

key_reviews.cite: Nunes, Kell, Slaghekke, Wüst 2026, Cell Death Dis
key_reviews.why: Recent synthesis proposing endothelial senescence as a unifying model (hypothesis paper, not evidence).
Haemostasis-expert critique of the microclot hypothesis.
Shared autonomic/cerebrovascular phenotype of long COVID and ME/CFS in 313 patients.
Cardiometabolic and vascular perspective on PEM.

gaps: No blinded, multi-centre replication of the van Campen cerebral blood flow method.
Preload failure prevalence in unselected ME/CFS (iCPET cohorts are pre-selected).
No placebo-controlled trials of volume expansion (saline, desmopressin, fludrocortisone) targeting measured low blood volume in ME/CFS.
Microclots: no standardised blinded multi-lab assay and no in vivo demonstration.
Retinal, sublingual and muscle capillary studies are almost all post-COVID; pre-pandemic ME/CFS is rarely studied.
Severe and very severe patients are almost absent from vascular studies.
Pericyte markers have never been stained in ME/CFS tissue.
Complement activation fragments have not been measured with modern pre-analytics before and after exertion in ME/CFS.
Whether endothelial dysfunction exceeds what activity-matched inactive controls show.
Mechanism of low red-cell mass (marrow output vs destruction vs EPO signalling) is unstudied.

domains.title: Muscle, exertion and energy
domains.overview: People with ME/CFS reliably have lower aerobic capacity and a low peak heart rate on exercise testing, and they report delayed, prolonged PEM that took about two weeks to resolve after a 2-day test. Whether performance measurably drops on a second test 24 hours later is now contested: several linked groups and two meta-analyses say yes, mainly at the ventilatory threshold, while a 2026 replication found no change. Invasive testing points to poor cardiac filling and poor oxygen extraction, and newer biopsy work from one Amsterdam group finds fewer oxidative fibres, fewer capillaries and lower mitochondrial capacity in ME/CFS that bed rest does not reproduce, plus post-exertion muscle damage and amyloid-containing deposits in long COVID. Mitochondrial studies in blood cells disagree in direction, and the idea that patient serum alters muscle-cell mitochondria failed a large pre-registered replication (Ryback 2026). Post-exertion omics (metabolomics, proteomics, EVs) show resting differences and recovery-phase changes, but within-person exercise effects are modest and mostly unreplicated.

findings.finding: PEM is usually delayed by hours to a day, lasts days to weeks, and after a 2-day CPET took ME/CFS patients a mean of about 13 days to recover versus about 2 days in sedentary controls.
findings.plain: After overdoing it, people with ME/CFS often feel worse later rather than at once, and the crash can last much longer than ordinary tiredness after exercise.
findings.detail: Chu 2018 (n=150 survey): 84% reported PEM lasting 24 h or more; onset varied, and only 11% had a consistent delay of at least 24 h. Moore 2023 (80 vs 64, Ithaca 2-day CPET): judged recovery 12.7 ± 1.2 d vs 2.1 ± 0.2 d, range 1-64 d; one patient had not recovered at one year. NIH qualitative work (Stussman 2024, 10 vs 9) found every patient's PEM had a different onset, trajectory and worst symptom, and VAS scales missed changes that interviews caught. Self-report designs and one centre for the recovery data are the main limits.

studies.result: 90% PEM with physical, cognitive and emotional triggers; 84% PEM >=24 h; 11% consistent >=24 h delay

studies.design: prospective symptom tracking for 10 days after 2-day CPET
studies.result: Recovery 12.7 d vs 2.1 d (p<0.0001); <10% of patients took >3 weeks

studies.design: mixed-methods (VAS + qualitative interviews) over 72 h after CPET
studies.result: Each patient had a unique PEM course; no controls had PEM; interviews outperformed VAS at peak PEM

contradicting.n: 34 long COVID exercise cohort, 9 ME/CFS, 9 controls; 244 questionnaire cohort
contradicting.design: CPET with serial VAS and interviews over 72 h
contradicting.result: Self-reported PEM 67% in long COVID questionnaires, but only 2 of 34 long COVID patients showed observable PEM after CPET; ME/CFS PEM was more severe and prolonged

open_questions: Is there an objective marker that tracks PEM onset and recovery within a person?
Why does self-reported PEM in long COVID often not reproduce after a laboratory stressor?
Do cognitive and orthostatic triggers produce the same biology as physical exertion?
findings.test_available: Clinical history and symptom diaries (DSQ-PEM questionnaire); no objective clinical test

findings.finding: On a single maximal exercise test, ME/CFS patients have lower peak oxygen uptake (pooled about 5 ml/kg/min below controls) with a low peak heart rate (chronotropic incompetence).
findings.plain: Patients can take in and use less oxygen at maximal effort than healthy people, and their heart rate does not rise as high.
findings.detail: Large clinical series (VanNess 2003, n=189) and case-control studies (Keller 2024, Walitt 2024 NIH, Charlton 2026) agree. Effort criteria (RER, perceived exertion) are usually met, which argues against low effort. The main confounder is deconditioning; Keller 2024 used VO2-matched pairs and Charlton 2026 compared with 60-day bed rest, and both found patterns that inactivity did not reproduce. A single CPET's peak VO2 overlaps heavily with sedentary controls, so it is not diagnostic on its own.

studies.result: Peak VO2 below predicted in all impairment groups; peak HR and SBP lower in more impaired groups
Pooled VO2peak 5.2 (95% CI 3.8-6.6) ml/kg/min lower in ME/CFS vs controls
Peak VO2 lower (p=0.004), peak HR lower (p=0.07), about 3.3 METs difference; patients performed at a lower % of predicted

studies.n: 84 ME/CFS vs 71 sedentary controls (55 VO2-matched pairs)
studies.result: ME/CFS failed to reproduce day-1 values: e.g. ~6% fall in peak VO2/kg and 6.7% fall in VO2 at ventilatory threshold in matched pairs; controls stable; both groups met maximal-effort criteria

studies.n: 19-23 ME/CFS, 24-25 long COVID, 29-30 matched controls, 24 healthy people after 60-day bed rest
studies.result: ME/CFS: lower type I fibre proportion and type I-specific atrophy, lower SDH activity, lower OXPHOS capacity, lower capillary-to-fibre ratio; bed rest caused atrophy but no fibre-type shift; OXPHOS tracked VO2max only after bed rest

open_questions: How much of low VO2 is preload/venous return versus muscle oxygen use?
Does peak VO2 track severity in severe and housebound patients, who are rarely tested?
findings.test_available: Cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) at cardiology/sports-medicine labs; carries PEM risk

findings.finding: ME/CFS patients perform worse on a second maximal exercise test 24 h after the first, most clearly in workload and VO2 at the ventilatory threshold, but two independent groups (Lien 2019; Mancini and Natelson 2026) did not reproduce the VO2 effect.
findings.plain: Several labs found that patients cannot repeat their performance a day after a hard test, while healthy people can. A 2026 study using the same design found no drop, so the test's reliability as a PEM marker is in doubt.
findings.detail: Positive studies: Snell 2013 (51 vs 10 women; 95% classification), van Campen 2020/2021 (82 women by severity; idiopathic chronic fatigue improved on day 2 while ME/CFS declined), Keller 2024 (84 vs 71; declines of ~5-7% in peak VO2 and VO2 at threshold), Hodges 2018 (MS controls improved), Davenport 2026 preprint (84 ME/CFS, 79 long COVID, 71 controls). Meta-analyses: Lim 2020 (workload at VT difference -10.8 day 1 vs -33.0 day 2) and Franklin & Graham 2022 (work at anaerobic threshold -21 W, 78% predictive probability of exceeding a 10 W MCID). Most positive data come from the Workwell/Pacific/Ithaca network and the van Campen clinic, so they are not fully independent. Mancini/Natelson 2026 (58 vs 25) and Lien 2019 (VO2peak day-2 fall not different between groups) did not reproduce the VO2 effect. Effect sizes are small relative to test-retest noise, and threshold detection is operator-dependent.

studies.result: No difference on test 1; on test 2 lower VO2 and workload at peak and threshold; 95.1% classification

studies.n: 84 ME/CFS vs 71 sedentary controls (55 VO2-matched pairs)
studies.result: ME/CFS failed to reproduce day-1 values: e.g. ~6% fall in peak VO2/kg and 6.7% fall in VO2 at ventilatory threshold in matched pairs; controls stable; both groups met maximal-effort criteria
All four parameters fell on day 2 (p 0.003 to <0.0001); peak workload fall largest in severe (-19%)

studies.n: 50 ME/CFS vs 51 idiopathic chronic fatigue (women); 26 vs 25 (men)
studies.result: ME/CFS worsened on day 2; idiopathic chronic fatigue improved
CFS workload fell on day 2; MS and controls improved
All parameters fell on day 2 in ME/CFS, rose in controls; workload at VT difference grew from -10.8 to -33.0

studies.cite: Franklin & Graham 2022, Fatigue: Biomed Health Behav
studies.result: Day-2 drop in peak work -8.55 W and in work at anaerobic threshold -21 W vs controls
Both patient groups had reduced VO2 and workload at threshold, larger in women; groups similar
day-2 decline in LC

contradicting.result: No day-2 change in peak VO2 (22.3 to 22.5 ml/kg/min) or VO2 at threshold in either group; patients had lower peak HR and higher perceived exertion; authors say 2-day CPET should not be used to define PEM
VO2peak fell on day 2 in patients, but the change did not differ significantly between groups
no day-2 decline

open_questions: Why did Mancini 2026 find no day-2 effect: cohort selection, threshold method, or sample from a different clinic?
What is the test-retest variability of workload at VT in sedentary people, and does the day-2 effect exceed it?
Can a gentler, submaximal provocation give the same information with less harm (Moore 2023: about two weeks to recover)?
findings.test_available: Offered by a few specialist labs (e.g. Workwell-linked) mainly for disability documentation; provokes PEM and is not advised for moderate-severe patients

findings.finding: Some patients produce more lactate for a given workload, and this worsens on a repeat test, but plasma studies after one maximal test show a smaller total lactate rise that mainly reflects lower achieved workloads.
findings.plain: Muscles in some patients seem to lean on the quick, lactate-producing fuel route earlier than expected, especially the day after hard effort.
findings.detail: Lien 2019 (18 vs 15 women): arterial lactate per power output was higher in patients on both tests and rose on day 2 while it fell in controls (interaction p<0.001). Lane 1998: about a third of patients had an abnormal lactate rise on a sub-anaerobic-threshold test, and this subgroup had fewer type 1 fibres (n=105 biopsies). Wong 1992 (31P-MRS) inferred accelerated glycolysis. The Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Germain 2022 found the post-exercise lactate rise was smaller in patients (log2 +1.02 vs +1.40), which disappears as a signal once effort is considered. Lactate per watt, not peak lactate, is the informative measure.

studies.design: 2-day CPET with arterial lactate every 30 s
studies.result: Higher lactate per power output in patients; lactate increased on day 2 in patients and fell in controls

studies.design: biopsy plus sub-anaerobic threshold exercise test
studies.result: Abnormal lactate responders had fewer type 1 fibres; no ultrastructural abnormality
Similar pH/PCr patterns but faster changes and lower ATP at exhaustion in CFS; authors infer accelerated glycolysis

contradicting.cite: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Germain 2022 data
contradicting.design: within-person change scores, mixed models, permutation
contradicting.result: Resting differences real (~150 of 780 metabolites at p<0.05 vs ~35 expected, perm p=0.002); exercise-response differences at chance (perm p=0.12-0.61); survivors: smaller lactate rise (explained by effort), blunted post-exercise glucose rise, rise in oxidised cys-gly

open_questions: Is early lactate due to poor oxygen delivery, fibre-type shift, or a mitochondrial/PDH block?
Does lactate per watt separate ME/CFS from deconditioned controls prospectively?
findings.test_available: Research only (lactate measured during CPET in some labs)

findings.finding: Invasive exercise testing shows two peripheral limits in ME/CFS: low cardiac filling (preload failure) and, in a high-flow subgroup, poor systemic oxygen extraction by tissue.
findings.plain: During exercise, either not enough blood returns to the heart, or the blood that reaches muscle passes through without giving up enough oxygen.
findings.detail: Joseph 2021 (Systrom lab, 160 ME/CFS vs 36 controls from 1,516 iCPETs): right atrial pressure 1.9 vs 8.3 mmHg, peak VO2 80% vs 101% predicted; the high-flow tertile had impaired extraction (0.74 vs 0.86-0.88), consistent with peripheral shunting; 31% had small-fibre neuropathy on skin biopsy. Melamed 2019: impaired extraction was the sole limit in 12.5% of unexplained exertional intolerance. Vermeulen 2014 (non-invasive, 178 CFS women) estimated lower peak extraction and a steep cardiac output/VO2 slope. McCully 1999 (NIRS) found slower muscle oxygen delivery. Invasive data come largely from one centre; capillary rarefaction in Charlton 2026 offers a structural explanation for low extraction.

studies.design: invasive CPET plus skin biopsy, retrospective
studies.result: Low RAP (preload failure); impaired O2 extraction in high-flow tertile; 31% SFN
Impaired systemic O2 extraction sole limit in 12.5%; higher mixed-venous saturation at peak

studies.n: 178 CFS women, 172 idiopathic fatigue, 11 healthy women (plus men)
studies.result: Peak extraction 10.8 vs 13.5 ml/100 ml in women; dQ/dVO2 >6 L/L in 70% of patients
Slower post-exercise and post-ischaemia muscle oxygen resaturation in CFS
Muscle deoxygenation responses lower in long COVID

open_questions: Is poor extraction due to microvascular shunting, capillary loss, or mitochondria that cannot use oxygen?
Independent invasive replication outside the Systrom lab is lacking.
Do extraction subgroups predict response to pyridostigmine or volume expansion?
findings.test_available: Invasive CPET (a few centres, e.g. Brigham/Harvard); NIRS research only

findings.finding: 31P-MRS studies from Newcastle found exaggerated muscle acidosis and up to ~4-fold slower pH recovery after repeated exercise in a subset of patients, but other MRS studies found no consistent group abnormality.
findings.plain: Magnetic scans of calf muscle during exercise suggest that some patients' muscles become more acidic and clear acid slowly, but not all studies see this.
findings.detail: Jones 2010 (16 vs 8): proton efflux immediately post-exercise 1.1 vs 3.6 mmol/L/min, time to maximal efflux 25.6 vs 3.8 s, and the normal link between efflux and pH nadir was lost, possibly via autonomic dysfunction. Jones 2012 (18 vs 12): 10 of 18 had low PCr depletion; the other 8 showed more acidosis over three bouts, no adaptation and about 4-fold longer pH recovery. Lane 1998 found lower end-exercise pH and slower ATP synthesis only in the lactate-responder subgroup. Barnes 1993 (46 patients) found no consistent abnormality overall, with 12 outliers; Wong 1992 found similar end-points; a 2025 7 T study found no resting muscle differences. Small samples, subgroup analyses and heterogeneous criteria dominate.

studies.design: 31P-MRS plantar flexion at 35% MVC plus HRV
studies.result: Suppressed proton efflux and delayed peak efflux; correlation with pH nadir lost in CFS
Subgroup with normal PCr depletion had more acidosis, no adaptation, ~4-fold slower pH recovery
Lower end-exercise pH and slower ATP resynthesis in lactate-responder subgroup only

contradicting.n: 46 CFS vs controls and mitochondrial myopathy
contradicting.result: No consistent abnormality of glycolysis, mitochondrial metabolism or pH regulation; 12 of 46 outside normal range
No group differences in pH, PCr or Pi at rest, exhaustion or recovery; lower ATP at exhaustion

contradicting.design: 7 T MRS brain and calf muscle at rest
contradicting.result: Resting muscle metabolites did not differ (brain lactate raised in ME/CFS)

open_questions: Would a pre-registered, larger repeat-bout 31P-MRS study with matched activity levels reproduce the Newcastle subgroup?
Is slow pH recovery a perfusion problem or a muscle-intrinsic one?
Does the MRS phenotype change during PEM?

findings.finding: 23Na-MRI in 6 women with ME/CFS and 6 controls found higher resting muscle sodium in all lower-leg compartments and a larger sodium rise after exercise, inversely related to grip strength.
findings.plain: A special MRI scan found more salt inside leg muscles of patients, which in theory could disturb muscle energy and calcium handling. The study was very small.
findings.detail: Petter 2022: anterior compartment 12.20 ± 1.66 vs 9.38 ± 0.71 mM (p=0.0034); medial gastrocnemius rose 30% vs 17% at 12 min after plantar flexion. Sodium correlated with lower handgrip strength (R2=0.38). This fits the Wirth/Scheibenbogen model in which hypoperfusion overloads the Na+/H+ exchanger, then Na+/Ca2+ exchange, loading muscle with calcium and damaging mitochondria. No independent replication; n=12 total.

studies.design: 23Na-MRI lower leg before and after plantar flexion
studies.result: Higher baseline sodium in all compartments; larger exercise rise; correlates with weaker grip

open_questions: Replication in a larger, sex-balanced cohort with deconditioned and disease controls.
Does muscle sodium change during PEM or with treatments that improve perfusion?

findings.finding: Older ME/CFS muscle biopsy studies mostly found normal or nonspecific histology, without the fibre atrophy and type 2 shift expected from inactivity, with abnormalities confined to subgroups.
findings.plain: Muscle samples taken in the 1990s mostly looked normal or only mildly abnormal under the microscope.
findings.detail: Lane 1998 (105 quadriceps biopsies): type 1 predominance (23%) was more common than type 2 predominance (3%); atrophy in 10%; no ultrastructural abnormality in 41 EM samples; the abnormal-lactate subgroup had fewer type 1 fibres. Grau 1992 (n=20): only minor nonspecific changes in 9. Wassif 1994 (n=10): normal ischaemic lactate responses. Behan 1991 reported mitochondrial structural changes and Bowles 1993 enteroviral RNA in muscle (41/158 postviral fatigue vs 2/152 controls), neither reproduced with modern methods. Criteria, techniques and selection varied widely.

studies.result: Changes not those of inactivity; no ultrastructural abnormality; lactate responders fewer type 1 fibres
Minor nonspecific changes in 9/20
Enterovirus RNA in 41/158 vs 2/152; histology otherwise normal
Mitochondrial structural abnormalities reported

contradicting.design: ischaemic lactate/ammonia test and biopsy histomorphometry
contradicting.result: No distinctive CFS abnormality

open_questions: Re-examine archived biopsies with modern immunostaining (capillaries, immune cells, amyloid).
findings.test_available: Diagnostic muscle biopsy (neuromuscular clinics) mainly to exclude myopathy

findings.finding: In long COVID with PEM, muscle biopsies taken one day after a maximal exercise test showed lower mitochondrial enzyme activity, more fibre necrosis, more T-cell infiltration and more amyloid-containing deposits than before exercise and than in controls.
findings.plain: When patients with long COVID were biopsied before and after a hard exercise test, their muscle looked more damaged and inflamed afterwards, and had more abnormal protein clumps.
findings.detail: Appelman 2024 (25 vs 21, Amsterdam): lower VO2max and gas exchange threshold; more glycolytic fibres; SDH activity fell after exercise in patients; large necrotic areas in 36% of patients after exercise (group p=0.09, so not firmly significant); CD3+ T cells present in patients but absent in controls; CD68 macrophages higher. Biopsies were scored as present/absent because sizes varied, and a first biopsy can itself cause regeneration at the second site. It is long COVID, not ME/CFS, and the amyloid-deposit finding has not been reproduced by another lab. The study prompted published criticism and replies in Nat Commun 2025.

studies.design: longitudinal case-control; vastus lateralis biopsies before and 1 day after a maximal CPET
studies.result: Lower exercise capacity; after exercise, lower SDH activity, more atrophic fibres and focal necrosis, more T-cell infiltration, more amyloid-containing deposits in patients

studies.design: opinion article from the same group
studies.result: Argue for intrinsic mitochondrial dysfunction, endothelial abnormalities and glycolytic fibre shift as drivers; PEM trigger unknown

open_questions: Does the same post-exertion pathology occur in ME/CFS (registered study NCT05225688 includes ME/CFS)?
Are the amyloid-containing deposits fibrin(ogen)-derived and do they occlude capillaries?
Is necrosis specific to PEM or a nonspecific response to unaccustomed maximal effort?

findings.finding: ME/CFS muscle has a lower proportion of type I (oxidative) fibres, type I-specific atrophy, lower mitochondrial capacity and fewer capillaries per fibre, a pattern that 60 days of strict bed rest in healthy people did not reproduce.
findings.plain: Patients' muscles have fewer endurance-type fibres and fewer tiny blood vessels. Healthy volunteers kept in bed for two months did not develop the same pattern, so lack of activity alone does not seem to explain it.
findings.detail: Charlton 2026 (Amsterdam group; 19-23 ME/CFS, 24-25 long COVID, 29-30 controls, 24 bed rest): type I proportion lower (p<0.001), type IIa/IIx higher; ME/CFS-only lower SDH; both patient groups lower OXPHOS; capillary-to-fibre ratio lower in ME/CFS than in long COVID and controls (p<0.001), whereas bed rest caused atrophy with unchanged capillary-to-fibre ratio and fibre type. OXPHOS correlated with VO2max in controls and after bed rest but not in patients. Same lab as Appelman; bed-rest cohort was a different (younger, male) population studied separately. Lane 1998 reported type 1 predominance more often than type 2 in older ME/CFS biopsies, which does not fit; differences in criteria and methods may explain this.

studies.n: 19-23 ME/CFS, 24-25 long COVID, 29-30 matched controls, 24 healthy people after 60-day bed rest
studies.result: ME/CFS: lower type I fibre proportion and type I-specific atrophy, lower SDH activity, lower OXPHOS capacity, lower capillary-to-fibre ratio; bed rest caused atrophy but no fibre-type shift; OXPHOS tracked VO2max only after bed rest

studies.design: longitudinal case-control; vastus lateralis biopsies before and 1 day after a maximal CPET
studies.result: Lower exercise capacity; after exercise, lower SDH activity, more atrophic fibres and focal necrosis, more T-cell infiltration, more amyloid-containing deposits in patients

studies.n: small CFS, post-COVID and control groups
studies.design: high-resolution respirometry and EM of muscle
studies.result: Complex I OXPHOS lower in post-COVID vs controls; CFS showed more advanced mitochondrial structural changes than post-COVID

contradicting.result: Type 1 predominance (23%) more common than type 2 predominance (3%)

open_questions: Independent replication of capillary rarefaction in ME/CFS muscle.
Is the glycolytic shift a cause of exercise intolerance or an adaptation to poor oxygen delivery?
Do severe, bedbound patients show the same profile?

findings.finding: WASF3 protein is raised in ME/CFS muscle, and in cells and mice it disrupts respiratory supercomplex assembly and lowers exercise capacity via ER stress.
findings.plain: One protein, WASF3, was found at high levels in patients' muscle; in experiments it jammed the parts of mitochondria that make energy.
findings.detail: Wang/Hwang 2023 (NIH): started from one patient with high WASF3; transgenic mice overexpressing WASF3 ran less, with lower complex IV; endotoxin-induced ER stress raised WASF3; the ER-stress inhibitor 4-PBA lowered WASF3 and improved the patient's cell respiration. A cohort of ME/CFS muscle biopsies showed raised WASF3 and ER stress markers (small cohort; group n not given in abstract). Glass 2025 also found ER-stress proteins in post-exercise EVs tracking PEM severity. No independent replication of the WASF3 biopsy finding.

studies.n: index patient; transgenic mice; small ME/CFS biopsy cohort
studies.design: mechanistic case study plus cohort biopsies
studies.result: WASF3 disrupts supercomplexes; raised WASF3 and ER stress in ME/CFS muscle

open_questions: Replication of raised muscle WASF3 in a larger, activity-matched cohort.
Does patient serum induce WASF3 in healthy muscle cells?
Would ER-stress modulators help in a trial?

findings.finding: Muscle cells grown from ME/CFS patients failed to activate AMPK and raise glucose uptake after electrical pulse stimulation, and secreted less IL-6, suggesting a defect that persists outside the body.
findings.plain: Patients' muscle cells grown in a dish did not respond to simulated exercise the normal way, which hints at a built-in problem rather than one caused only by something in the blood.
findings.detail: Brown 2015 (Newcastle): control cultures increased AMPK phosphorylation and glucose uptake after 16 h EPS; CFS cultures did not, though insulin-stimulated uptake was preserved; IL-6 secretion lower. Sample sizes small. Tomas 2019 (same group) found no differences in individual complex activity in patient myotubes (n=6), so the defect, if real, is in signalling rather than respiratory chain capacity.

studies.design: in vitro EPS of cultured myotubes
studies.result: No AMPK activation or glucose uptake rise after EPS; lower IL-6

contradicting.n: myotubes n=6; PBMC 13 CFS vs 6 controls
contradicting.result: No differences in complex I, II, IV activity or FAO/glutaminolysis-supported respiration

open_questions: Replication with more donors and blinded processing.
Is the defect epigenetic or genetic?

findings.finding: Mitochondrial function in patients' blood cells has been reported as lower (PBMC maximal respiration, T-cell glycolysis), higher (lymphoblast maximal respiration with Complex V inefficiency) or normal, depending on lab and cell type.
findings.plain: Studies of energy production in white blood cells disagree with each other, so it is unclear whether blood cells show an energy defect.
findings.detail: Tomas 2017: lower PBMC maximal respiration (p<=0.003), but control groups were small (fresh n=3, frozen n=12, vs 25 and 38 patients). Mandarano 2020 (53 vs 45, Hanson lab): reduced glycolysis in CD4 and CD8 T cells at rest and reduced CD8 membrane potential, with normal mitochondrial respiration in most measures. Missailidis 2020/2021 (51 CCC patients; immortalised lymphoblasts): higher maximal respiration and spare capacity but lower ATP synthesis fraction (Complex V inefficiency), with TCA, PPP and beta-oxidation enzymes up; claimed high discrimination, unreplicated. Vermeulen 2010 and Tomas 2019 found normal PBMC OXPHOS or complex activity. Directions conflict between studies, freezing affects results, and blood cells may not reflect muscle.

studies.result: Lower maximal respiration and other OXPHOS parameters

studies.design: Seahorse on isolated CD4/CD8 T cells
studies.result: Reduced T-cell glycolysis; reduced CD8 membrane potential

studies.n: 51 ME/CFS lymphoblast lines vs matched controls
studies.result: Complex V inefficiency; elevated maximal OCR and spare capacity; mTORC1 hyperactivation
Elevated TCA, PPP, FAO enzymes: dysregulated substrate supply
Immune cells show low ATP/ADP ratio (energy stress); skewed T, NK and dendritic subsets; raised plasma proteins for thrombus formation and vascular reactivity
PBMC Seahorse, 27 LC vs 16 controls: higher baseline oxygen use and abnormal ATP-synthase behaviour; correlated with autonomic scores
mitochondrial dysfunction
IDO/kynurenine; immune metabolism

contradicting.result: PBMC oxidative phosphorylation normal despite worse day-2 performance
No complex activity differences
Exploratory; small

open_questions: A multi-lab, blinded, pre-registered PBMC Seahorse study with fresh cells and adequate controls.
Do blood-cell findings correlate with muscle mitochondrial measures in the same people?
findings.test_available: Research only; commercial 'mitochondrial function' blood tests are not validated

findings.finding: Fluge 2016 proposed impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) function from low TCA-fuelling amino acids and raised PDK mRNA in blood cells; this has not been independently confirmed.
findings.plain: One group suggested that the step that lets sugar enter mitochondria to be burned cleanly is partly blocked, pushing cells toward lactate. Others have not yet confirmed it.
findings.detail: Fluge 2016 (200 vs 102): lower serum amino acids feeding the TCA cycle (mainly women), raised 3-methylhistidine in men, PDK1/2/4, SIRT4 and PPARdelta mRNA up in PBMC. Mughal 2025 found PDK3/PDK4 up in 3D muscle exposed to patient serum (n=4 ME/CFS). The serum-transfer part of Fluge 2016 failed replication (Ryback 2026). Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of resting plasma metabolomics found low acylcarnitines and fatty acids (lower fat-fuel supply) rather than a pile-up pattern, and a 5-cohort aromatic-lactate deficit, which point to related but different steps. No study has measured PDH activity directly in ME/CFS muscle.

studies.n: 200 ME/CFS vs 102 controls (serum amino acids); 12 vs 12 (myoblast serum assay)
studies.design: case-control metabolomics, PBMC qPCR, serum-transfer cell assay
studies.result: Lower TCA-fuelling amino acids (mainly women); PDK1/2/4, SIRT4, PPARdelta mRNA up in PBMC; severe-patient serum raised myoblast respiration and lactate secretion
PDK3/PDK4 up by qPCR; glycolysis/TCA genes up

contradicting.cite: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis (resting metabolomics, several cohorts)
contradicting.n: Germain 2022 60 vs 45 plus 5 cohorts for aromatic lactates
contradicting.result: Resting pattern fits low fat-derived fuel supply, not a PDH/fat-oxidation block with acylcarnitine build-up; aromatic lactates -0.53 SD

open_questions: Direct PDH activity and phosphorylation in muscle biopsies.
Replication of the amino-acid pattern in an independent cohort with diet control.

findings.finding: The claim that ME/CFS serum changes healthy myoblast mitochondrial respiration failed a pre-registered replication of 67 patients vs 53 controls, though a small 3D engineered-muscle study reported weaker contraction with patient serum.
findings.plain: An influential idea was that something in patients' blood harms muscle cells' energy production. A large, careful repeat of the original experiment found no difference.
findings.detail: Ryback 2026: blinded, randomised, 1,926 wells, primary maximal OCR +2.50 pmol/min (95% CI -1.62 to 6.62); recomputed participant-level d=0.14 (CI -0.22 to 0.50), excluding the original d=1.32. Limits: mostly mild-moderate (only 6 severe), resting samples, batch partly collinear with group, one myoblast donor, single readout. Mughal 2025 (4/5/4 donors, IBEC) found reduced contractile force at 48 h and mitochondrial fragmentation later, with pseudoreplication risk. Prusty 2026 found patient IgG fragments endothelial (not muscle) mitochondria, with MS controls. The refutation applies to the 2D myoblast respiration readout, not to all serum-factor ideas.

studies.result: Higher respiration and lactate secretion with patient serum

studies.design: 3D muscle tissue force under electrical stimulation
studies.result: Lower force after 48 h patient serum; fragmented mitochondria by 96-144 h

contradicting.design: pre-registered, blinded replication of Fluge 2016; healthy myoblasts in 20% serum 6 days, Seahorse
contradicting.result: No difference in maximal respiration (+2.50 pmol/min, 95% CI -1.62 to 6.62, p=0.23) or any secondary measure; powered for d=0.52 vs original d=1.32

contradicting.cite: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Ryback 2026 supplementary data
contradicting.result: d=0.14 overall; severe subgroup (n=6) d=0.002

open_questions: Do sera drawn during PEM or from severe patients behave differently?
Would differentiated myotubes, force readouts or IgG fractions show an effect that whole serum in 2D did not?
Can a blinded two-lab sample exchange reproduce the 3D force result?

findings.finding: After moderate exercise, leukocyte mRNA for metabolite-detecting (ASIC3, P2X4/5, TRPV1), adrenergic and immune genes rose for up to 48 h in most CFS patients but not in controls or MS patients.
findings.plain: In one lab's studies, a 25-minute bout of moderate exercise switched on 'muscle-fatigue sensing' genes in patients' white blood cells for two days, and this tracked how tired and sore they felt.
findings.detail: Light 2012 (48 CFS, 18 FM, 49 controls; 25 min at 70% age-predicted HR, blood at 0.5, 8, 24, 48 h, blinded qPCR of 13 genes): 71% of CFS had increases correlating with fatigue and pain; the other 29% showed decreased alpha-2A receptor mRNA and more orthostatic intolerance. White 2012 (22 CFS, 20 MS, 23 controls) added a disease control. All from the Utah Light lab with a small targeted gene panel; no independent replication. Vu 2024 single-cell RNA-seq after exercise found minimal immune changes other than platelets.

studies.result: Post-exercise rise in sensory/adrenergic/cytokine gene mRNA for 48 h in 71% of CFS; none in controls
Larger rises in P2X4, TRPV1, CD14 and adrenergic receptors in CFS than controls; MS differed
First report of post-exercise gene rises
sensory/adrenergic receptor mRNA rise

contradicting.n: ME/CFS vs controls, before and after exercise
contradicting.result: Minimal post-exercise changes outside platelets (improper platelet activation)

open_questions: Independent replication with a pre-registered gene panel.
Do leukocyte receptor transcripts reflect muscle afferent signalling at all?

findings.finding: Plasma metabolomics across a 2-day CPET shows clear resting differences in ME/CFS, but once each person is compared with themselves the exercise response differs little from controls.
findings.plain: Blood chemistry differs between patients and healthy people even at rest. Whether hard exercise changes it in a disease-specific way is less clear.
findings.detail: Germain 2022 reported growing patient-control divergence (women: 6 to 54 metabolites at q<0.05 across four timepoints) and glutamate/TCA-linked recovery pathways. The Solving ME/CFS re-analysis reproduced those counts but found day-1 and day-2 differences correlate at 0.85 and the within-person response is at chance; alpha-ketoglutarate did not reproduce. Surviving modest signals: blunted post-exercise glucose rise (p=0.018, survives lactate adjustment), oxidised cys-gly rise in patients (q=0.033), lower day-2 N-acetylarginine and C6-DC acylcarnitine. Che 2025 (56 vs 52, Lipkin) reported TCA, beta-oxidation and urea-cycle abnormalities worse 24 h after exercise, but with only pre/24 h timepoints. Five of the most impaired male patients lacked post-exercise samples in Germain 2022.

studies.result: Reported growing patient-control disparity over the two days, with lipid, energy and glutamate-linked pathways in recovery

studies.design: plasma metabolomics/proteomics and stimulated immune responses before and 24 h after exercise
studies.result: Exaggerated innate responses; impaired energy pathways; many abnormalities worse after exercise and correlated with symptoms

contradicting.cite: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Germain 2022 data
contradicting.design: within-person change scores, mixed models, permutation
contradicting.result: Resting differences real (~150 of 780 metabolites at p<0.05 vs ~35 expected, perm p=0.002); exercise-response differences at chance (perm p=0.12-0.61); survivors: smaller lactate rise (explained by effort), blunted post-exercise glucose rise, rise in oxidised cys-gly

open_questions: Does a within-person analysis of Che 2025 hold up?
Plasma may be the wrong compartment; paired muscle microdialysis or biopsy metabolomics are lacking.

findings.finding: Plasma proteomics of 79 ME/CFS and 53 sedentary controls across a 2-day CPET found the largest patient-specific changes in the 24 h recovery phase, with suppressed T/B-cell and IL-17 signalling and raised glycolysis proteins.
findings.plain: The biggest differences in blood proteins appeared during the recovery day, when PEM begins, rather than straight after exercise.
findings.detail: Germain 2025 (SomaScan 7K, 6,361 proteins; 96 F, 36 M): persistent dysregulation of immune, metabolic and neuromuscular pathways; protein-VO2max/AT relationships present in controls were disrupted in patients; sex-specific responses. Che 2025 proteomics added complement activation and extracellular-matrix ligands after exercise. The Solving ME/CFS proteome re-analysis found resting muscle-derived proteins lower in 3 SomaScan cohorts (including Germain) and UK Biobank (d -0.50). Pathway enrichment across thousands of aptamers is vulnerable to multiplicity; no independent post-exertion proteomics cohort yet.

studies.result: Recovery-phase maladaptation; suppressed lymphocyte and IL-17 signalling; glycolysis up; links to muscle pain and sore throat
Complement activation, ECM disruption, redox imbalance worse post-exercise

contradicting.result: 0 proteins with a patient-specific exercise response at FDR; pathway claims not reproduced per person

open_questions: Replication of recovery-phase protein changes in an independent cohort.
Which changes are effort-dependent (adjust for achieved workload)?

findings.finding: Extracellular-vesicle protein cargo responds to maximal exercise differently in ME/CFS (blunted in women; TCA proteins down and complement up in men), and recovery-phase changes correlate with PEM severity.
findings.plain: Tiny packages that cells release into the blood carry different proteins after exercise in patients than in healthy people.
findings.detail: Giloteaux 2024 (18 vs 17 women; pre, 15 min, 24 h; TMT proteomics): patients' EV changes differed and correlated with symptom severity, involving coagulation, muscle contraction, cytoskeleton, immune and brain proteins. Glass 2025 (10 vs 12 men): TCA-cycle proteins down and complement up at 15 min; ER-stress and protein-folding changes in recovery correlated with PEM; EV-VO2 correlations seen in controls were absent in patients. Both from the Hanson lab, small, many comparisons; no transfer experiment shows patient EVs act on cells.

studies.design: EV proteomics pre/15 min/24 h post CPET
studies.result: Different EV response in patients; correlates with severity

studies.design: EV proteomics pre/15 min/24 h post CPET
studies.result: TCA down, complement up post-exercise; ER-stress changes track PEM

open_questions: Independent replication, and functional tests of patient EVs on muscle or endothelial cells.
Tissue of origin of the EVs (muscle, platelet, endothelium).

findings.finding: Repeated maximal handgrip testing shows lower strength, faster decline across repetitions and poorer recovery after 60 minutes in ME/CFS, correlating with severity and PEM.
findings.plain: Squeezing a grip meter ten times in a row, twice an hour apart, shows patients' strength fading faster and recovering less than healthy people's. It is cheap and quick.
findings.detail: Jäkel 2021 (105 ME/CFS, 18 cancer-related fatigue, 66 controls; Charité): lower Fmax and Fmean (p<0.0001), higher fatigue ratio, lower recovery ratio (Fmean2/Fmean1); lower grip linked to severity, PEM, muscle pain and post-exertion CK/LDH. Paffrath 2024 (144 women with post-COVID, 78 meeting CCC): grip impaired across post-COVID, but linked to key symptoms only in ME/CFS. Walitt 2024 (NIH) found normal MVC but shorter time to failure at 50% MVC (p=0.0002) and faster decline on repetitive grip, which the authors attributed to 'effort preference', an interpretation that has been disputed. Paul 1999 (10 vs 10) showed slower quadriceps strength recovery up to 24 h. Most data come from one centre; effort and motivation cannot be fully excluded from voluntary tests.

studies.design: repeat maximal HGS (10 pulls x 2, 60 min apart)
studies.result: Lower strength, higher fatigue ratio, lower recovery ratio; correlates with severity and PEM
Impaired HGS in all; associations with PEM, fatigue, cognition only in ME/CFS

studies.design: grip MVC, time to failure, repetitive grip
studies.result: Normal MVC; shorter time to failure; faster decline on repetitive grip

studies.design: quadriceps fatiguing protocol with recovery to 24 h
studies.result: Similar decline during exercise; recovery prolonged in CFS at 200 min and 24 h
reduced fatigability/recovery
reduced grip strength/fatigability

contradicting.result: argues effort/central factors
Grip-strength variability (CV) overlapped heavily between ME/CFS and controls told to give 50% effort; a trajectory metric separated them better, so CV is a poor effort-validity marker

open_questions: Independent validation outside Charité with deconditioned and depressed controls.
Can repeat HGS track PEM day by day or serve as a trial endpoint?
How much reflects central drive versus peripheral muscle fatigue (Walitt found no central or peripheral fatigue markers)?
