findings.test_available: Yes: handgrip dynamometer (cheap; offered by some ME/CFS clinics, e.g. Charité protocol)

findings.finding: Muscle-derived proteins (myoglobin, troponins, CA3 and similar) are lower in ME/CFS blood at rest across three SomaScan cohorts and UK Biobank, not explained by step counts or walking pace.
findings.plain: Proteins that leak from muscle into blood are slightly lower in patients, which suggests less muscle mass or slower muscle turnover rather than ongoing damage.
findings.detail: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: muscle-damage set d -0.50 (95% CI -0.76 to -0.24, q=0.002, I2 0.07) across Hoel (-0.85), Germain (-0.43) and Walitt (-0.34); UK Biobank competitive shift negative; not mediated by walking pace; unrelated to steps, Bell score or illness duration within patients. Lean mass was not available, so reduced muscle mass from inactivity cannot be excluded. Resting CK and myoglobin are expected to be low-normal.

studies.n: Hoel 50/24, Germain 78/51, Walitt 21/21, plus UK Biobank
studies.result: Muscle protein set d -0.50, consistent across cohorts

open_questions: Does the signal survive adjustment for DXA lean mass?
Does it relate to type I fibre atrophy or capillary loss in biopsies from the same people?
findings.test_available: Not clinically meaningful; DXA lean mass is available

findings.finding: Several designs (aerobic-capacity-matched controls, idiopathic-fatigue and MS comparison groups, and a 60-day bed-rest model) indicate that deconditioning alone does not explain the exercise and muscle abnormalities in ME/CFS.
findings.plain: It is often said patients are just unfit from resting. Studies that compared them with equally unfit people or with healthy volunteers kept in bed found differences that inactivity did not produce.
findings.detail: Keller 2024: day-2 declines persisted in 55 pairs matched for peak VO2. van Campen 2021 and Hodges 2018: idiopathic chronic fatigue and MS patients improved on day 2. Lane 1998: biopsy changes were not those of inactivity. Charlton 2026: bed rest caused atrophy with preserved fibre type and capillary-to-fibre ratio; patients showed the opposite pattern; OXPHOS-VO2max coupling present after bed rest but absent in patients. Vermeulen 2014: a high cardiac output/VO2 slope argues against central deconditioning. These are mostly cross-sectional and from enthusiast centres; Mancini 2026 found no day-2 decline at all.

studies.n: 84 ME/CFS vs 71 sedentary controls (55 VO2-matched pairs)
studies.result: ME/CFS failed to reproduce day-1 values: e.g. ~6% fall in peak VO2/kg and 6.7% fall in VO2 at ventilatory threshold in matched pairs; controls stable; both groups met maximal-effort criteria

studies.n: 19-23 ME/CFS, 24-25 long COVID, 29-30 matched controls, 24 healthy people after 60-day bed rest
studies.result: ME/CFS: lower type I fibre proportion and type I-specific atrophy, lower SDH activity, lower OXPHOS capacity, lower capillary-to-fibre ratio; bed rest caused atrophy but no fibre-type shift; OXPHOS tracked VO2max only after bed rest
ICF improved on day 2; ME/CFS declined
Argues cardiac deconditioning is a myth in long COVID PEM

contradicting.result: No day-2 change in peak VO2 (22.3 to 22.5 ml/kg/min) or VO2 at threshold in either group; patients had lower peak HR and higher perceived exertion; authors say 2-day CPET should not be used to define PEM

open_questions: A prospective study following new post-infectious patients from onset, measuring muscle before inactivity accumulates.

findings.finding: People with long COVID have lower peak VO2 than recovered controls on average (about 5 ml/kg/min), with patterns pointing to deconditioning, chronotropic incompetence and impaired peripheral extraction rather than a cardiac or ventilatory limit.
findings.plain: On an exercise bike, people with long COVID reach a lower maximum oxygen use than people who recovered. The heart's pumping is usually normal; the problem looks more like heart-rate control, fitness loss and muscles taking up less oxygen.
findings.detail: Bridges ME/CFS single-CPET findings to LC; selection (hospitalised vs mild, active vs sedentary) explains much of the heterogeneity.

studies.design: systematic review and meta-analysis of CPET
studies.result: peak VO2 -4.9 ml/kg/min (95% CI -6.4 to -3.4); low certainty; deconditioning, dysfunctional breathing, chronotropic incompetence and impaired extraction all reported
lower OUES and anaerobic threshold; lower NIRS-measured muscle oxidative capacity; no macro/microvascular dysfunction
lower peak VO2 and heart-rate reserve; cardiac reserve and resting MSNA normal

contradicting.result: mean exercise capacity normal; distinct subgroups with chronotropic incompetence and dysautonomic breathing
normal cardiopulmonary responses

open_questions: Does peak VO2 in LC with PEM differ from LC without PEM?

findings.finding: Invasive CPET in long COVID with exercise intolerance repeatedly shows low systemic oxygen extraction with normal or high cardiac output, and in a subset reduced biventricular filling (preload failure), mirroring ME/CFS iCPET findings.
findings.plain: When doctors measure oxygen in arteries and veins during exercise, many long COVID patients' muscles take less oxygen out of the blood even though the heart pumps plenty. Some also have too little blood returning to the heart.
findings.detail: Should cross-link to vascular-oxygen-extraction and muscle-exertion-oxygen-extraction.

studies.result: 75% impaired peak O2 extraction with supranormal cardiac output; about 25% had HFpEF or exercise pulmonary hypertension
reduced peak extraction, worse after severe acute infection; metabolomic shifts
low systemic O2 extraction; endotheliopathy proteomic signature
low O2 pulse and blunted heart-rate response
preload insufficiency in a large share
impaired muscle oxygenation, worse on day 2

findings.finding: Long COVID patients show early lactate accumulation and reduced fat oxidation during exercise, with plasma metabolite and lipid shifts consistent with impaired mitochondrial fatty-acid use.
findings.plain: Muscles of long COVID patients switch early to burning sugar and make lactate sooner, and they burn less fat, suggesting the energy factories are not working normally.

studies.cite: de Boer 2022, Am J Respir Crit Care Med (letter)
studies.result: decreased fatty-acid oxidation and early lactate (letter; abstract not available)
altered fatty-acid and energy metabolism in PASC
reduced fat oxidation, higher lactate at given loads
lipid and energy-metabolism shifts

findings.finding: Muscle oxidative capacity measured by 31P-MRS (slower PCr recovery) or NIRS is reduced in long COVID, though the deficit does not consistently correlate with fatigue.
findings.plain: Scans of muscle energy show long COVID muscles take longer to recharge after effort, but how slow they are does not track neatly with how tired people feel.

studies.result: PCr recovery tau 92.5 vs 51.9 s; lower Qmax; not correlated with fatigue
lower muscle oxidative capacity
impaired muscle oxygenation
OXPHOS gene expression down; respiration -11 to -28% (n.s.)

findings.finding: A substantial share of long COVID patients with fatigue have myopathic EMG and/or biopsy abnormalities (mitochondrial changes, fibre atrophy, inflammatory infiltrates, lower capillarisation), but muscle MRI inflammation and neuromuscular-junction jitter are usually normal.
findings.plain: Muscle tests and biopsies often show damage or energy-factory changes in long COVID, though scans for inflammation are usually clear.

studies.result: myopathic EMG 75%; mitochondrial changes 62%; inflammation 62%
myopathic changes in a large share
angulated fibres, fewer myonuclei, lower capillary/fibre ratio
soluble IL-2R in sera impairs myotube mitochondria

contradicting.result: no MRI inflammation
jitter normal

findings.finding: Whether standardised exercise provokes measurable post-exertional symptom worsening in long COVID is contested: a crossover RCT found no greater 48-h fatigue than controls, while symptom-tracking studies find variable PESE peaking within 72 h in subsets.
findings.plain: Trials disagree on whether a single exercise session reliably makes long COVID patients worse in the days after; some patients clearly crash, others do not.
findings.detail: Tryfonos 2024 did not select for PEM; result likely depends on case definition.

studies.result: variable PESE in PASC, peaking within 72 h
PEM-like symptoms common
PEM reported in most

contradicting.result: no greater fatigue at 48 h; more muscle pain after HIIT

hypotheses_notes.for: Lower SDH/OXPHOS and type I atrophy in ME/CFS muscle (Charlton 2026); post-exertion SDH drop in long COVID (Appelman 2024); WASF3 (Wang 2023); 31P-MRS subgroups (Jones 2010/2012); early lactate per watt (Lien 2019); AMPK defect in cultured myotubes (Brown 2015).
hypotheses_notes.against: Ryback 2026 refutes the serum-myoblast respiration effect; blood-cell mitochondrial findings conflict in direction (Tomas vs Missailidis) or are null (Vermeulen 2010, Tomas 2019); OXPHOS does not correlate with VO2max in patients (Charlton 2026), so mitochondria may not be the limiting step; several MRS studies null (Barnes 1993, Godlewska 2025).

hypotheses_notes.for: Lower capillary-to-fibre ratio in ME/CFS muscle not reproduced by bed rest (Charlton 2026); impaired O2 extraction in high-flow iCPET subgroup (Joseph 2021); slower NIRS reoxygenation (McCully 1999).
hypotheses_notes.against: Capillary finding from one lab; long COVID patients in the same study did not show it as strongly; extraction data largely single-centre.

hypotheses_notes.for: Low right atrial pressure during invasive CPET in 160 patients (Joseph 2021); low peak HR across CPET studies.
hypotheses_notes.against: Preload failure explains low peak output but not why muscle pathology worsens a day later or why PEM is delayed.

hypotheses_notes.for: Higher muscle sodium on 23Na-MRI, inversely correlated with grip (Petter 2022); grip fatigability (Jäkel 2021); review by Scheibenbogen & Wirth 2025.
hypotheses_notes.against: Sodium MRI n=6 vs 6, unreplicated; no direct muscle calcium measurement in patients.

hypotheses_notes.for: Fluge 2016 myoblast effect; Mughal 2025 3D muscle force loss (n=4); Prusty 2026 IgG fragments endothelial mitochondria (non-muscle).
hypotheses_notes.against: Ryback 2026 pre-registered replication (67 vs 53) null, excluding the original effect size.

hypotheses_notes.for: Amyloid-containing deposits in long COVID muscle increased after PEM induction (Appelman 2024).
hypotheses_notes.against: Not yet shown in ME/CFS muscle; single lab; the composition of the deposits is not established.

hypotheses_notes.for: T-cell and macrophage infiltration in long COVID muscle after exertion (Appelman 2024); exaggerated innate responses and complement after exercise (Che 2025); complement up in male EVs (Glass 2025).
hypotheses_notes.against: Germain 2025 found suppressed rather than activated lymphocyte signalling in recovery; single-cell RNA after exercise showed minimal immune changes (Vu 2024).

hypotheses_notes.for: Delayed, prolonged PEM (Moore 2023) and recovery-phase molecular changes (Germain 2025) fit a stress response that persists after the stimulus.
hypotheses_notes.against: No study has measured purinergic/cell-danger signalling directly in muscle during PEM.

hypotheses_notes.for: 31% SFN and shunting physiology in iCPET (Joseph 2021); loss of normal pH-efflux coupling linked to autonomic function (Jones 2010); adrenergic receptor mRNA changes after exercise (Light 2012).
hypotheses_notes.against: Denervation severity did not correlate with exertional measures (Joseph 2021).

hypotheses_notes.for: Walitt 2024 framed grip and effort findings as altered effort preference.
hypotheses_notes.against: Effort criteria are met in most CPETs; objective muscle, capillary and post-exertion biopsy changes (Appelman, Charlton) are not explained by behaviour; the effort-preference interpretation has been formally criticised.

hypotheses_notes.for: (New id: exercise and muscle abnormalities are secondary to inactivity.) Low peak VO2 overlaps with sedentary controls; lower muscle proteins in blood could reflect reduced mass; Mancini 2026 found no day-2 decline.
hypotheses_notes.against: VO2-matched pairs still declined on day 2 (Keller 2024); bed rest does not reproduce fibre-type shift, capillary loss or OXPHOS uncoupling (Charlton 2026); disease controls improve on day 2 (van Campen 2021, Hodges 2018).

hypotheses_notes.for: (New id: endoplasmic reticulum stress impairs mitochondrial supercomplexes and energy production.) WASF3 and ER-stress markers raised in ME/CFS muscle (Wang 2023); ER-stress EV proteins track PEM severity (Glass 2025).
hypotheses_notes.against: Both small and unreplicated; no trial of ER-stress modulators.

hypotheses_notes.for: Fluge 2016 amino-acid pattern implies altered fuel handling.
hypotheses_notes.against: Kynurenine pathway metabolites show no patient-specific exercise response in the Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Germain 2022.

hypotheses_notes.for: Enterovirus RNA in muscle in older studies (Bowles 1993).
hypotheses_notes.against: Not reproduced with modern methods; Appelman 2024 did not report persistent virus as the driver of post-exertion pathology.

glossary.plain: A worsening of symptoms after physical, mental or emotional effort, often delayed by hours to a day and lasting days or longer.
Cardiopulmonary exercise test: cycling or treadmill to exhaustion while breathing gases and heart rate are measured.
Two CPETs 24 hours apart, used to see whether performance drops on the second day.
The most oxygen the body can take up and use per minute at maximal effort; the standard measure of aerobic capacity.
The point during exercise when breathing rises faster than oxygen use because muscles lean more on lactate-producing fuel use.
The heart rate fails to rise as much as expected during exercise.
CPET with catheters in the heart and an artery, measuring filling pressures, cardiac output and oxygen extraction directly.
How much oxygen tissues remove from the blood that flows through them.
A magnetic resonance scan that measures phosphorus-containing energy molecules (PCr, ATP) and acidity inside working muscle.
An MRI scan tuned to sodium, used to measure salt content in tissue.
Type I fibres are slow, endurance, mitochondria-rich; type II are faster and more reliant on glycolysis.
A mitochondrial enzyme whose staining is used as a marker of mitochondrial content in muscle sections.
Oxidative phosphorylation: the mitochondrial process that uses oxygen to make most of the cell's ATP.
A plate-based instrument measuring how fast cells use oxygen and make acid, used to estimate mitochondrial function.
The enzyme that lets the product of sugar breakdown enter mitochondria; if blocked, cells make more lactate.
Peripheral blood mononuclear cells: lymphocytes and monocytes isolated from a blood sample.
Small membrane packages released by cells into blood, carrying proteins and RNA.
The fall in grip strength across repeated maximal squeezes, and how well it recovers after rest.
A protein that, when raised, disrupts the assembly of mitochondrial energy-producing complexes.

key_reviews.cite: Scheibenbogen & Wirth 2025, J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle
key_reviews.why: Collects the evidence for skeletal muscle disturbance and the sodium/calcium overload model (advocacy-leaning, from the model's authors).
Opinion piece from the Amsterdam biopsy group on muscle adaptations and PEM in long COVID.
Meta-analysis of 2-day CPET; workload at ventilatory threshold is the most discriminating measure.

key_reviews.cite: Franklin & Graham 2022, Fatigue: Biomed Health Behav
key_reviews.why: Meta-analysis estimating clinically meaningful day-2 drop in work at anaerobic threshold (-21 W).
Methods paper for administering 2-day CPET in ME/CFS.
Recent review of skeletal muscle involvement in ME/CFS (title/abstract seen only).
Within-person re-analysis of Germain 2022 metabolomics; participant-level check of Ryback 2026; muscle-protein meta-analysis.

gaps: No ME/CFS (as opposed to long COVID) study has biopsied muscle before and after induced PEM; the registered Amsterdam study NCT05225688 and Systrom's OMF-funded biopsy study have not yet reported.

No independent replication of 2-day CPET from a group outside the Workwell/Ithaca/van Campen network that also reports test-retest variability in sedentary controls; Mancini 2026 null needs explaining.
Severe and housebound patients are almost absent from exercise, biopsy and MRS studies; a provocation-free design (e.g. orthostatic or small-muscle stressor) is needed.
No study pairs muscle biopsy, 31P-MRS, sodium MRI and invasive CPET in the same people to locate the limiting step in the oxygen cascade.
Serum-transfer studies have not used sera drawn during PEM, fractionation (IgG, complement, EVs), or blinded multi-lab sample exchange.
No pre-registered multi-site PBMC or muscle respirometry study with adequate controls exists.
Lean mass has not been measured alongside the low muscle-protein blood signal.
Handgrip fatigability needs external validation against deconditioned, depressed and other-fatigue controls before use as a trial endpoint.
Whether the amyloid-containing deposits in long COVID muscle also occur in ME/CFS, and what they are made of, is untested.

domains.title: Nervous system and brain
domains.overview: The most consistent nervous-system findings in ME/CFS are physiological rather than anatomical. Brain blood flow drops more than normal when patients are upright, often with over-breathing (low CO2), and resting heart-rate variability is lower; both are seen across several independent labs. Small-fibre nerve loss on skin biopsy is common in referral clinics (roughly 30-55%), but the main controlled NIH study found no difference, and nobody has yet shown that nerve loss explains symptoms. Brain imaging gives many positive but small and mostly unreplicated results: raised ventricular lactate (mostly one group), raised brain temperature (one study), TSPO-PET neuroinflammation (one positive and one negative ME/CFS study), and newer diffusion MRI signals. Structural MRI, routine sleep studies and markers of nerve injury are mostly normal or inconsistent. The NIH 'effort preference' interpretation has been seriously challenged, because patients in that study often could not complete the hard task. Claims about craniocervical instability rest on uncontrolled clinic series and case reports.

findings.finding: Blood flow to the brain falls much more than normal during head-up tilt in ME/CFS (about 26% vs 7% in controls), including in patients whose heart rate and blood pressure stay normal.
findings.plain: When patients are tilted upright, less blood reaches the brain than in healthy people, even if their pulse and blood pressure look normal. That can explain light-headedness and brain fog when standing.
findings.detail: van Campen 2020 measured extracranial carotid plus vertebral flow by Doppler during a 30-min tilt in 429 patients vs 44 controls. End-tilt drop was 7% in controls and 26% in patients overall: 24% with a normal HR/BP response, 28% with delayed orthostatic hypotension and 29% with POTS. About 90% exceeded the control range. Transcranial Doppler studies (Medow 2014; Novak 2026, 88% of 170 ME/CFS) agree. A 2025 systematic review (118 studies) found reduced CBF in 12 of 26 ME/CFS-only studies and a larger fall when ME/CFS and orthostatic intolerance coexist. Caveats: most data come from referral clinics; controls are few; and CBF velocity (transcranial Doppler) is not the same as volume flow.

studies.result: End-tilt CBF -26% vs -7%; ~90% of patients abnormal, incl. normal HR/BP responders
Reduced orthostatic CBF velocity in 88% ME/CFS and 92% long COVID
CBFv fell 22.5% vs 8.7% in controls
CBF reduced in ME/CFS and in OI; larger reduction when both present (4/11 studies)

contradicting.result: No group differences in orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia or tilt-related stopping (CBF not measured)

open_questions: Does the CBF fall cause the cognitive symptoms, or only accompany them?
How much is driven by hypocapnia versus low stroke volume?
Is it specific to ME/CFS versus deconditioning, hEDS or other dysautonomias?
findings.test_available: Tilt with extracranial Doppler (few centres, e.g. Netherlands) or transcranial Doppler in some autonomic labs; mostly research or specialist only

findings.finding: Many patients over-breathe when upright and lower their end-tidal CO2. This drives part of the fall in brain blood flow, and correcting it with phenylephrine restored blood flow and working memory in one small trial.
findings.plain: Standing makes some patients breathe off too much carbon dioxide. Low CO2 narrows brain blood vessels, so less blood reaches the brain. A drug that tightens blood vessels prevented this and improved a memory test in a small study.
findings.detail: Medow 2014: on tilt, ETCO2 was 33.9 vs 42.8 Torr in 15 CFS vs 11 controls. Phenylephrine prevented the hypocapnia, cut the CBFv fall from 22.5% to 8.1%, and returned n-back reaction time to supine levels. Yamazaki 2026: 40.8% of 49 adults met the criteria for postural orthostatic syndrome of hypocapnia (POSH) on a lean test with capnography, more often than POTS. Novak 2026 defines a hypocapnic cerebral hypoperfusion phenotype. In long COVID (O'Brien 2026, n=50), 64% had supine or orthostatic hypocapnia. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: hypocapnia on tilt is reported by 5 groups and the CBF fall by 4. Treatment evidence is still single-group and acute.

studies.result: ETCO2 33.9 vs 42.8 Torr on tilt; phenylephrine normalised CBFv and n-back

studies.design: cross-sectional, lean test with capnography + Daxor blood volume
studies.result: POSH in 40.8%; lean-test abnormalities not related to blood volume

studies.design: clinic cohort, NASA lean test + ETCO2
studies.result: Hypocapnia 64%; POTS 32%; breathing retraining improved symptoms, not ETCO2

studies.cite: Medow & Stewart 2024, Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol
studies.result: Phenylephrine alters CBFv-BP phase synchronisation in ME/CFS with OI

open_questions: Is hypocapnia primary (respiratory/chemoreflex) or compensation for low venous return?
Would capnography-guided treatment (compression, midodrine, breathing retraining) improve function over weeks?
findings.test_available: Capnography during a 10-min stand or lean test: cheap; available in some respiratory/autonomic clinics

findings.finding: POTS occurs in a minority of ME/CFS patients, and published rates vary widely (about 6-43%) with the setting, the age group and the test protocol.
findings.plain: Some, but not most, people with ME/CFS meet the heart-rate criteria for POTS. How many depends a lot on who was tested and how.
findings.detail: van Campen 2020: 120 of 429 tilt-tested patients (28%) had POTS. Novak 2026: POTS in 19% of ME/CFS and 22% of long COVID, but widespread mild autonomic failure in 89-95%. Adolescents (Leone 2026): PoTS in 7/18 ME/CFS vs 0/18 controls on a 10-min stand, although 83% reported OI symptoms. In the NIH cohort (Walitt 2024, n=17), tilt showed no excess tachycardia. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of the literature: POTS prevalence is inconsistent (6-43%) and lists it among the contradictory findings. Orthostatic intolerance symptoms are far more common than POTS defined by heart rate.

studies.result: POTS 28%, delayed OH 14%, normal HR/BP 58%
POTS 19%, neurogenic OH 15%, mild-moderate autonomic failure 89%
PoTS 39% vs 0%; OI history 83% vs 17%
neurally mediated hypotension in most
POTS/orthostatic intolerance common
POTS 32.5%
orthostatic intolerance
Multi-site, 301 ME/CFS vs 141 controls: COMPASS-31 34.1 vs 6.8; orthostatic intolerance 33.9% vs 0.7%; 97% had an autonomic symptom

contradicting.result: No excess orthostatic tachycardia vs controls

open_questions: Do POTS and non-POTS ME/CFS differ in mechanism (e.g. hyperadrenergic vs low-flow)?
How much do medication, test length and time since onset change the rate?
findings.test_available: 10-min active stand or tilt table test: widely available clinically

findings.finding: Resting heart rate is higher and high-frequency heart-rate variability lower in ME/CFS. This fits reduced vagal (parasympathetic) tone.
findings.plain: The 'rest and digest' nerve signal to the heart looks weaker. The heart beats a little faster at rest, and its beat-to-beat variation is reduced.
findings.detail: Nelson 2019 meta-analysis (64 case-control studies): resting HR +4.1 bpm, HR on tilt SMD 0.92, resting LF/HF SMD 0.39 higher, HF-HRV SMD -0.34, and peak HR 13.8 bpm lower. Walitt 2024: 24-h Holter SDNNi, rMSSD and pNN50 were lower, HF and LF power reduced, and Valsalva baroreflex-cardiovagal function was lower. Effects are moderate. They are not specific to ME/CFS, and deconditioning, medications and sleep loss confound them. HRV is not a diagnostic test.

studies.result: RHR +4.1 bpm; HF-HRV SMD -0.34; HRtilt SMD 0.92; HRmax -13.8 bpm
Lower 24-h HRV time and frequency domains; reduced baroreflex-cardiovagal function
reduced HRV
autonomic dysregulation

open_questions: Is low HRV cause, consequence or a marker of deconditioning/sleep disruption?
Can wearable HRV usefully track PEM risk in individuals?
findings.test_available: 24-h Holter HRV (clinical); consumer wearables give rough trends

findings.finding: On the 10-minute NASA lean test, a subgroup of recent-onset patients shows a rising heart rate with an abnormally narrow pulse pressure. Autonomic specialists say the test has not been validated against tilt or active stand.
findings.plain: The lean test (standing against a wall for 10 minutes while pulse and blood pressure are recorded) is a cheap way to see orthostatic problems. It is useful for spotting a pattern, but it is not an approved test for diagnosing POTS.
findings.detail: Lee 2020 (Bateman Horne Center): 150 ME/CFS (75 ill <4 y, 75 ill >10 y) vs 75 controls. At least 5 min was needed to see changes. The <4-y group had higher HR, a narrower pulse pressure and more OI symptoms, interpreted as inadequate ventricular filling. Yamazaki 2026 found lean-test abnormalities (most often hypocapnia) in 55% of 49 patients, unrelated to measured blood volume. Teuschl 2025 (European autonomic experts) argue that NLT criteria were borrowed from 1970s NASA physiology, that the leaning posture mixes active stand and passive tilt, and that the NLT 'may currently not be used as a diagnostic tool'.

studies.result: <4-y patients: higher HR and narrowed pulse pressure vs >10-y and HC
55% had >=1 lean-test abnormality (POSH 41%); not related to blood volume

contradicting.result: No validation vs tilt/active stand; should not be used for autonomic diagnosis

open_questions: Head-to-head diagnostic accuracy of NLT vs tilt in ME/CFS
Does narrow pulse pressure on NLT predict response to volume or compression?
findings.test_available: NASA lean test: any clinic or at home with a BP cuff (for monitoring, not formal diagnosis)

findings.finding: Skin biopsies show reduced small-nerve-fibre density in about 31-53% of ME/CFS patients from specialist referral cohorts, but the controlled NIH study found no difference from healthy volunteers.
findings.plain: In some clinics, a third to a half of patients have lost some of the thinnest nerves in the skin. Those nerves control sweating and blood vessels. But a carefully matched NIH study did not find this, so how common and how important it is remains uncertain.
findings.detail: Joseph 2021 (Systrom/Oaklander, Harvard): 31% of 160 ME/CFS biopsies were consistent with SFN (epidermal innervation <=5th percentile of predicted). Denervation severity did not correlate with exertional measures. Novak 2026 (same network): SFN in 53% of ME/CFS and 67% of long COVID; hEDS had more severe neurodegeneration. Azcue 2025 (30 ME/CFS, 30 long COVID, 30 HC) found corneal fibre tortuosity and heat-detection changes rather than a clear length-dependent pattern. Walitt 2024: no difference in small-fibre density. Major caveats: the positive cohorts were referred for exertional intolerance or dysautonomia; biopsy normative cut-offs and patchy, non-length-dependent SFN make rates sensitive to method; and ME/CFS-specific matched-control biopsy studies are few. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Finnish registry data: an SFN diagnosis is about 8-10 times more common than expected in post-viral fatigue (crude, shared with fibromyalgia).

studies.result: 31% SFN; severity not correlated with exertional limits
SFN 53% ME/CFS, 67% LC

studies.design: case-control, QST, Sudoscan, corneal confocal microscopy
studies.result: Corneal fibre tortuosity higher (AUC 0.72); heat detection impaired

contradicting.result: Small nerve fibre density not different

open_questions: What is the SFN rate in unselected, community ME/CFS with blinded, matched controls?
Does fibre loss explain any symptom (OI, pain, exertional intolerance)?
Is it autoimmune, and does IVIG change it? (no ME/CFS RCT)
findings.test_available: 3 mm skin punch biopsy for IENFD via neurology (clinically available); corneal confocal microscopy in some centres

findings.finding: Long COVID patients referred for neuropathy evaluation often have small-fibre neuropathy on skin biopsy, including loss of autonomic fibres to sweat glands and hair muscles.
findings.plain: Similar nerve damage turns up in long COVID, especially in patients with pain or nerve-type symptoms.
findings.detail: Oaklander 2022 (NIH/MGH): 10 of 16 skin biopsies (63%) in referred long COVID were abnormal; 52% average improvement over 1.4 years, often after immunotherapy (uncontrolled). Falco 2026: piloerector and sweat-gland nerve density reduced in 31 painful long COVID vs 42 controls, even with normal IENFD, but not correlated with COMPASS-31 symptom scores. These are selected samples with neuropathic complaints, so the results do not give a general prevalence.

studies.result: 63% of biopsies confirm SFN
Autonomic fibre density reduced; no correlation with symptoms
IVIG response in SFN

open_questions: Prevalence in unselected long COVID
Does SFN predict who develops ME/CFS after COVID?
findings.test_available: Skin biopsy (IENFD, sweat-gland nerve density in specialist labs)

findings.finding: Conventional structural MRI (grey matter volume, routine clinical reads) shows no consistent abnormality in ME/CFS. Reported regional volume differences rarely replicate across groups.
findings.plain: Standard brain scans usually look normal. Studies that report bigger or smaller brain regions mostly disagree with each other.
findings.detail: Shan 2020 systematic review (63 imaging studies to 2018): the only findings reported by multiple teams were extra brain-area recruitment during cognitive tasks (11 studies), brainstem abnormalities (9), sluggish BOLD responses, reduced serotonin transporter and regional hypometabolism. Volumetric findings were inconsistent. Lee 2023 meta-analysis (65 studies, 1529 patients) reported insular and thalamic hypoactivity but noted poor inter-rater reliability. Walitt 2024: brain MRI unremarkable. Kimura 2026 (38 ME/CFS, 27 LC, 47 HC): amygdala subfield differences did not survive correction. For contrast, the UK Biobank pre/post scans (Douaud 2022) show that SARS-CoV-2 infection itself produces small grey-matter changes, although that sample was not long COVID or ME/CFS.

studies.result: Few consistent findings; brainstem and task recruitment most repeated
Insula and thalamus hypoactivity; frontal cortex most often reported
reduced grey matter, reversed after CBT

contradicting.result: Brain imaging unremarkable
No amygdala subfield difference after correction

open_questions: Large, multi-site, pre-registered MRI with harmonised protocols has not been done
Do subtle changes track severity or duration longitudinally?
findings.test_available: Clinical MRI (useful only to exclude other diagnoses)

findings.finding: Advanced diffusion MRI models report widespread white-matter differences in ME/CFS that conventional DTI misses, and the pattern may differ between post-infectious and gradual-onset cases.
findings.plain: Newer scan analyses suggest subtle changes in the brain's wiring, possibly swelling or inflammation. Standard analyses of the same scans find little.
findings.detail: Yu 2026 (Shan group, 67 vs 67 matched): a neuroinflammation-imaging (NII) model gave lower hindered and restricted water fractions and higher fibre fraction across association, commissural and projection tracts. The authors read this as oedema, cellular infiltration and axonal reorganisation, while conventional DTI showed minimal differences. Yu 2025 (same group): post-infectious cases had higher axial diffusivity, while gradual-onset cases had lower AD in the corpus callosum. Singh 2026 (Griffith, 37 ME/CFS, 19 LC, 27 HC) found DTI/DKI alterations in the cingulum, SMA and corpus callosum. The model-based metrics are not validated against histology in ME/CFS, the analyses carry many degrees of freedom, and independent replication is missing.

studies.result: Widespread NII differences; conventional DTI minimal

studies.n: PI and GO subgroups vs sedentary HC
studies.result: Opposite axial diffusivity patterns by onset type
Microstructural changes in cingulum, SMA, corpus callosum
right arcuate FA increased

contradicting.result: No reported imaging abnormality

open_questions: Independent replication with shared analysis code
Correlation with TSPO-PET or MRS markers in the same people

findings.finding: Brainstem differences (volume larger or smaller, altered signal or connectivity) are among the more often repeated imaging findings in ME/CFS, though the methods differ between studies.
findings.plain: The brainstem controls breathing, heart rate and arousal. Several groups using different scans have reported differences there.
findings.detail: Shan 2020 counted brainstem abnormalities in 9 studies from different teams and modalities. Bader 2026 (preprint, 26 vs 27): brainstem volume 1.46 vs 1.55% of eTIV (FDR p=0.039), with deep grey matter and whole-brain volume unchanged. Inderyas 2026 (7T fMRI, 32 ME/CFS): altered cuneiform-nucleus to medulla connectivity during Stroop. The Griffith (Barnden/Thapaliya) group produced several of the brainstem reports, so the evidence is not fully independent. This imaging work does not support the mechanical 'craniocervical compression' model, which is a separate claim (see neuro-cci).

studies.design: case-control volumetry + ASL + MRS under hypoxia
studies.result: Brainstem volume reduced
Altered brainstem functional connectivity during cognitive fatigue
Brainstem abnormalities repeatedly reported

contradicting.result: larger brainstem volumes (direction conflicts with atlas wording)

open_questions: Which brainstem nuclei, and do they map onto autonomic or respiratory findings (hypocapnia, low HRV)?

findings.finding: After a single 30-minute exercise bout, women with ME/CFS performed worse on a demanding cognitive task and recruited more parietal and cingulate cortex. Controls improved.
findings.plain: Exercise made patients' thinking worse the next day, and their brains had to work harder at the same task. This is one of the few direct brain measurements of post-exertional malaise.
findings.detail: Cook 2017: 15 vs 15 women, scanned 1 week before and 24 h after 30 min of cycling at 70% peak HR. Group x time interactions showed worse PASAT performance in patients and increased activation in bilateral inferior/superior parietal and cingulate cortex, correlated with symptom change. Finger tapping did not differ. Patients cycled at lower watts, so absolute workload differed. Related work: Schönberg 2024 (34 vs 34) found that BOLD signals in ME/CFS did not adapt across repeated task blocks as they did in controls, and Shan 2020 counted extra task recruitment as a finding repeated by several teams. A direct replication of the exercise-provocation design has not been published.

studies.result: Post-exercise cognitive decline and increased parietal/cingulate activation in patients

studies.cite: Schönberg 2024, J Cereb Blood Flow Metab
studies.result: Absent BOLD adaptation across repeated SDMT blocks

open_questions: Replication with workload matched relative to individual capacity
Time course over 24-72 h of PEM

findings.finding: During a sustained grip task, ME/CFS patients fatigue earlier while their brain motor-network activity fails to ramp up as it does in controls (NIH; reduced temporoparietal-junction activation).
findings.plain: When squeezing repeatedly, patients tire sooner. Their brains do not step up the drive to the muscle the way healthy brains do.
findings.detail: Walitt 2024 reported decreased right temporoparietal junction activation during repeated 50% MVC grip in fMRI and a faster decline in force. The authors linked it to 'effort preference', which is disputed. Bedard 2026 (NIH, 15 vs 19, EEG+EMG+fMRI) found that maximum force was equal, but patients reached fatigue much earlier and showed minimal change in brain and muscle activity across blocks. Healthy controls increased activity until fatigue. Interpretation: a central contribution to fatigability. Both studies come from the same NIH programme and have small samples.

studies.result: Reduced TPJ activation; earlier force decline
Earlier fatigue; brain output did not increase to drive muscle

open_questions: Is the lack of central ramp-up primary or protective (driven by peripheral afferent feedback)?
Independent replication outside NIH

findings.finding: Brain lactate measured by MR spectroscopy is raised in ME/CFS: ventricular CSF lactate in three cohorts from one group, and thalamic or regional lactate in two other groups. It is also raised in depression, so it is not specific.
findings.plain: Brain scans that measure chemicals show more lactate, a by-product of energy production without enough oxygen, in patients' brains. The same change appears in depression.
findings.detail: Mathew 2009: ventricular lactate +348% vs healthy and +297% vs anxiety disorder (16 vs 15 vs 14). Shungu 2012 (third cohort, 15 vs 13): raised lactate and lower cortical glutathione, not different from major depression. Natelson 2017 replicated higher lactate, lower GSH and lower CBF in pooled CFS. Mueller 2020 (Younger group, whole-brain EPSI, 15 vs 15): raised LAC/CR in some regions, overlapping with raised temperature. Bader 2026 (Vienna, 26 vs 27, preprint): thalamic Lac/tCr 0.171 vs 0.135 at normoxia, with no further rise under hypoxia, unlike controls. Bradley 2016 found raised ventricular lactate in adolescent depression. Small samples, MRS quantification at 3T near detection limits, and the lack of specificity limit interpretation.

studies.result: Ventricular lactate +348% vs HC
Raised lactate, lower GSH, lower rCBF; CFS ~ MDD
Replicated raised lactate, lower GSH and CBF; 13/26 had >=2 abnormal brain measures
Thalamic lactate raised at rest, no rise with hypoxia

contradicting.result: Raised ventricular lactate in adolescent depression (shows non-specificity)

open_questions: Does brain lactate rise further after exertion (PEM)?
Is it from hypoperfusion, mitochondrial limitation or glial activation?

findings.finding: MRS thermometry found raised temperature in several brain regions (insula, putamen, frontal cortex, thalamus, cerebellum) in women with ME/CFS, not explained by body temperature.
findings.plain: One study found parts of the brain running slightly warmer in patients, which could signal low-grade inflammation. It has not been repeated.
findings.detail: Mueller 2020: 15 vs 15 women, whole-brain echo-planar spectroscopic imaging. Temperature was raised in the right insula, putamen, frontal cortex, thalamus and cerebellum (p<0.05, many regions tested), along with raised choline/creatine in the left anterior cingulate. The method responded to an experimental inflammatory challenge (typhoid vaccine) in 44 of 47 regions, but whole-brain temperature did not change (Plank 2022), so its sensitivity is modest. No independent ME/CFS replication was found.

studies.result: Raised regional brain temperature; raised CHO/CR

contradicting.result: Regional but not whole-brain temperature rose (method validity context)

open_questions: Independent replication
Correlation with TSPO-PET in the same people

findings.finding: TSPO-PET evidence of microglial activation in ME/CFS is contested: one Japanese study found 45-199% higher binding in limbic and brainstem regions, and a Dutch study using the same tracer found none.
findings.plain: A special scan for brain immune cells showed inflammation in one small study and none in another of the same size. The question is open.
findings.detail: Nakatomi 2014: [11C]-(R)-PK11195, 9 vs 10. BPND was higher in the cingulate, hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, midbrain and pons, and correlated with cognitive impairment and pain. Raijmakers 2021: same tracer, 9 CFS, 10 Q-fever fatigue and 9 matched women, stricter exclusion. No difference, and a negative correlation with severity in CFS. Both used the cerebellum as reference region, which can bias results if the reference is also affected. PK11195 has a low signal-to-noise ratio, and second-generation tracers need TSPO genotyping. Stanford DPA-713 data exist only as a conference abstract (not verified). A Belgian [18F]DPA714 study is in protocol (Dooms 2026).

studies.result: BPND +45-199% in limbic/brainstem regions

contradicting.result: No difference in BPND

open_questions: Adequately powered study with a second- or third-generation tracer, arterial input and genotyping
Does TSPO signal change during PEM?

findings.finding: In long COVID, one [11C]PBR28 PET study found widespread raised TSPO signal that correlated with vascular markers, and a [11C]PK11195 study found no group difference.
findings.plain: Long COVID brain-inflammation scans also disagree. One found widespread signal and another found none.
findings.detail: VanElzakker 2024: 12 PASC vs 43 normative controls. Raised PBR28 in the mid and anterior cingulate, corpus callosum, thalamus, basal ganglia and periventricular regions, correlated with plasma vascular-dysfunction analytes. The comparison against a pooled normative control set and the small n are limits. Tuomaala 2026: 14 LC vs 11 HC vs 13 MS. TSPO DVR was not raised in LC, though higher in people imaged within 16 months, and limbic DVR correlated with depression and anxiety. An earlier Braga 2023 report in long COVID with depression/cognitive symptoms was not verified this session.

studies.result: Widespread raised PBR28; correlates with vascular markers

contradicting.result: No TSPO elevation vs HC; time-since-infection effect

open_questions: Does neuroinflammation fade with time since infection?
Is it seen in long COVID that meets ME/CFS criteria specifically?

findings.finding: Resting (supine) cerebral blood flow by ASL or SPECT is reported as lower in some ME/CFS studies, but the results are inconsistent and often confounded by unmeasured orthostatic intolerance.
findings.plain: Lying-down brain blood flow is sometimes lower, but not consistently. The clearest effect appears when patients are upright.
findings.detail: Shungu 2012 (ASL) found lower rCBF in the left anterior cingulate and right lingual gyrus vs controls, but not vs depression. Natelson 2017 pooled CFS had lower CBF. Christopoulos 2025 review: only 12 of 26 ME/CFS-only studies found reduced CBF, and most did not record OI status. Bader 2026: whole-brain CBF responses to hypoxia were similar in mean but far more variable in patients (variance ratio up to 6.9).

studies.result: Lower regional CBF in 2 regions
12/26 reduced
reduced CBF

contradicting.result: No mean group difference; higher variability in patients

open_questions: Resting CBF stratified by OI and hypocapnia status

findings.finding: In the NIH cohort, CSF levels of the catechol metabolites DOPA, DOPAC and DHPG were lower in post-infectious ME/CFS. Noradrenaline and dopamine did not differ.
findings.plain: Spinal fluid showed lower breakdown products of dopamine and noradrenaline, which hints at reduced activity of these brain chemical systems. It comes from one small study.
findings.detail: Walitt 2024: CSF DOPA, DOPAC and DHPG were reduced; noradrenaline, cys-DOPA and dopamine were unchanged. Excluding participants on central-acting drugs did not change the result. Catechols correlated with perceived symptoms and, in patients, with only one cognitive test (WCST). CSF metabolomics also showed lower glutamate, tryptophan, spermidine and citrate. n was about 17 vs 21, with many outcomes and no correction across domains. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: plasma VMA showed nothing, which fits a central rather than peripheral signal but is weak support.

studies.result: Lower DOPA, DOPAC, DHPG
CSF noradrenaline-pathway markers lower in post-infectious ME/CFS and PASC than healthy volunteers, as in Parkinson disease (same NIH cohort as earlier work)

open_questions: Replication in an independent CSF cohort
Relation to orthostatic phenotype and HRV
findings.test_available: research only (lumbar puncture with catechol panel)

findings.finding: CSF cytokine and proteome studies report differences (e.g. raised eotaxin/CCL11, distinct immunotypes), but no CSF protein signature has replicated, and ME/CFS and fibromyalgia CSF proteomes were indistinguishable.
findings.plain: Spinal-fluid tests have hinted at immune changes, but different studies point in different directions, and none gives a reliable marker.
findings.detail: Baraniuk 2005: pooled and individual CSF proteomics (about 10-20 per group) gave a 5-protein set with 80% concordance; pilot only. Hornig 2016 (online 2015): 32 cases vs 40 MS vs 19 controls, 51-plex. CCL11 was raised and the IL-1 network disturbed, with interpretation hindered by the small control group. Schutzer 2023: 2083 proteins quantified; no protein differed between ME/CFS with and without fibromyalgia. Bastos 2025 (40 cases, CSF in cases only) found two MMP-defined clusters. Bragée 2026 (31 cases, no CSF controls) found complement/coagulation pathways associated with severity and POTS. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: the Walitt CSF SomaScan set gives 0 FDR hits, and CSF neuronal markers do not replicate.

studies.result: CCL11 up; IL-1 network disturbance
5-protein set, 80% concordance
Two MMP-based CSF immunotypes
Complement/coagulation pathways linked to severity; neutrophil degranulation with POTS
CSF abnormalities in subset

contradicting.result: No proteins differed: indistinguishable

contradicting.cite: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis (Walitt 2024 CSF SomaScan, GEO GSE251790)
contradicting.result: 0 FDR hits; no case-control leak-score difference

open_questions: A CSF study with adequate healthy controls (n>50) and pre-registered analysis
Paired pre/post-exertion CSF

findings.finding: Targeted CSF metabolomics found raised serine and phospholipids and reduced 5-methyltetrahydrofolate in ME/CFS, with different metabolite responses to exercise than in controls.
findings.plain: Spinal fluid chemistry suggests changes in a vitamin/amino-acid pathway (folate and serine), possibly affecting brain fats. These are single-group results.
findings.detail: Baraniuk 2025 (Sci Rep; separate non-exercise and post-exercise LP cohorts): ME/CFS showed raised serine, sarcosine, creatine, purines and sphingomyelins and lower 5MTHF, dimethylglycine and choline. After exercise, metabolites were consumed in ME/CFS but generated in controls. The design is cross-sectional with separate cohorts per condition, not paired. Earlier Baraniuk 2021 work found little non-exercise ME/CFS vs GWI difference. NIH found lower CSF glutamate, tryptophan and spermidine (Walitt 2024), so the two sets point in different directions.

studies.n: ME/CFS vs sedentary controls, rest and post-exercise cohorts
studies.result: Serine up, 5MTHF down; divergent exercise response

contradicting.result: Different pattern: lower glutamate, tryptophan, spermidine, citrate

open_questions: Replication; paired pre/post-exercise sampling in the same people

findings.finding: Markers of neuronal or glial injury (NfL, GFAP, tau, UCH-L1) are not raised in ME/CFS blood or CSF.
findings.plain: Blood and spinal-fluid tests that pick up nerve-cell damage in diseases like MS or dementia are normal in ME/CFS. That argues against ongoing destruction of brain tissue.
findings.detail: Walitt 2024 measured Simoa Neurology 4-Plex (NfL, tau, GFAP, UCH-L1) in plasma and CSF: no group difference. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of SomaScan/Olink proteomics across about 150 patients: NEFL and GFAP flat or inconsistent (neuronal_glial set -0.25, p=0.07). Long COVID TSPO-PET (Tuomaala 2026) also measured serum NfL/GFAP, without a clear LC effect. A normal result does not exclude functional or neuroinflammatory changes without cell death.

studies.result: No difference in plasma or CSF NfL/GFAP/tau/UCH-L1
NEFL/GFAP not different

contradicting.result: NfL higher in ME/CFS

open_questions: Do levels rise transiently during PEM or in severe/bedbound patients?
findings.test_available: Serum NfL/GFAP increasingly available clinically (mainly to exclude other disease)

findings.finding: Uncontrolled clinic series report high rates of craniocervical 'obstruction', low-lying tonsils and signs of raised intracranial pressure in severe ME/CFS, and surgical case reports describe improvement. There are no controlled imaging studies or trials.
findings.plain: Some clinics report that many severe patients have crowding where the skull meets the neck, or high spinal-fluid pressure, and a few patients improved after neck surgery. Without comparison groups or controlled trials, it is unknown whether these findings are more common than in healthy people or whether surgery helps.
findings.detail: Bragée 2020 (Swedish referral clinic, 229 CCC patients, retrospective): hypermobility 50%, enlarged optic-nerve-sheath ratio 55%, possible IH signs 83%, tonsils below McRae line 56%, and cervical 'craniocervical obstructions' 80% of 125 scanned. No controls; MRI reads were not blinded and the radiological thresholds are not validated. Jolley 2026 (34 cases, no controls): LP opening pressure >=20 cmH2O in 38%; that group reported more relief after LP (80% vs 19%, unblinded). Rowe/Edwards case reports (3+1 patients) describe improvement after cervical decompression. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Finnish registry data: CSF-leak codes are not specific (36% of LPs in ME/CFS vs 32% in fibromyalgia, 45% in hypermobility). Neurosurgical series (Ruhoy 2025, n=717) are in connective-tissue-disorder cohorts, not ME/CFS. The evidence quality is low, and surgery carries serious risk.

studies.result: 80% craniocervical obstruction; 83% possible IH signs; 56% low tonsils
38% opening pressure >=20 cmH2O; more post-LP relief in high-OP group
Symptoms returned with recurrent stenosis and improved after re-operation

contradicting.result: CSF-leak codes equally common in fibromyalgia/hypermobility; not ME/CFS-specific

open_questions: Blinded, controlled upright/dynamic MRI comparing ME/CFS, hypermobile and healthy controls
Any randomised or sham-controlled evaluation of surgery or CSF drainage
findings.test_available: Clinical cervical MRI is available; upright/flexion MRI and CCI surgery are offered privately with no controlled evidence

findings.finding: The NIH claim that altered 'effort preference' defines post-infectious ME/CFS rests on the EEfRT (OR 1.65 for choosing hard tasks). Patients completed only 65% of the hard tasks they chose vs 96% for controls, which confounds preference with ability.
findings.plain: The NIH team said patients chose the harder button-pressing task less often and called this 'effort preference'. Critics showed that many patients could not physically finish the hard task, so the choice more likely reflects ability than wanting to avoid effort.
findings.detail: Walitt 2024: 15 PI-ME/CFS vs 16 HV on EEfRT. Controls were 1.65x more likely to choose hard (95% CI 1.03-2.65, p=0.04), and no group difference in task-related fatigue response was reported. Kirvin-Quamme 2025 re-analysed mapMECFS data. Hard-task completion was 65% (SD 37) in patients vs 96% (SD 8) in controls; 7/15 patients completed fewer hard tasks than any control. Choice correlated with completion (rs 0.38). This fails the EEfRT's own ability check (Treadway 2009). Davenport 2025 (Nat Commun Matters Arising) also criticised the single-day CPET, matching for deconditioning and generalisation from n=17. The NIH reply defended single CPET on safety grounds. The effort result also sits on p=0.04 with no multiplicity correction.

studies.result: OR 1.65 for hard-task choice in controls
Defends single CPET and interpretation

contradicting.result: Hard-task completion 65% vs 96%; choice confounded with ability
Single CPET cannot assess PEM; deconditioning/effort conclusions not supported

open_questions: An effort-based decision task calibrated to each participant's ability
Relation of motor fatigability to peripheral muscle findings

findings.finding: Meta-analysis shows moderate-to-large deficits in information-processing speed, attention, working memory and reaction time in ME/CFS, with intact vocabulary and reasoning. Performance worsens with upright posture and after exertion.
findings.plain: 'Brain fog' shows up on tests as slower processing and difficulty holding information, especially over sustained effort, rather than loss of intelligence or knowledge.
findings.detail: Cockshell & Mathias 2010: 50 studies, deficits mainly in attention, memory and reaction time, with fine motor speed, vocabulary and reasoning spared. On tilt, n-back reaction time rose from 96 to 148 ms in CFS but not controls (Medow 2014). Post-exercise, PASAT performance fell (Cook 2017). The NIH study found no differences on any of 15 neuropsychological tests despite large subjective complaints (n=17), which shows that small samples and unprovoked testing can miss deficits. Reaction-time variability and sustained-attention tasks are more sensitive than standard batteries.

studies.result: Moderate-large deficits in processing speed, attention, memory, RT
Orthostatic worsening of n-back; reversed by phenylephrine

contradicting.result: No group differences in objective performance

open_questions: A standard provocation protocol (upright, post-exertion) for clinical cognitive testing
Contribution of sleep, medication and orthostatic hypoperfusion
findings.test_available: Clinical neuropsychology; computerised reaction-time tests; tests done upright or after exertion are research only

findings.finding: Objective sleep in adult ME/CFS shows modestly longer sleep latency, more wake after sleep onset and lower sleep efficiency. Standard polysomnography usually finds no clinical disorder that explains non-restorative sleep.
findings.plain: Sleep studies show patients take longer to fall asleep and wake more, but the differences are small. They do not explain why sleep feels so unrefreshing.
findings.detail: Mohamed 2023 meta-analysis: 20 adult studies (426 vs 375) showed more time in bed, longer SOL and WASO, lower efficiency, less N2, more N3 and longer REM latency. In 4 adolescent studies (242 vs 235), total sleep was longer. Heterogeneity was high, and the stage-level findings are inconsistent with older reviews (Jackson & Bruck 2012: few PSG differences; microstructure, such as instability and alpha intrusion, more promising). Walitt 2024: PSG without clinically relevant findings. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Finnish registries: hypersomnia codes are enriched about 20-50x and sleep apnoea precedes diagnosis (HR 15), probably reflecting diagnostic work-up as well as biology. Primary sleep disorders still need excluding clinically.

studies.result: Lower efficiency, longer SOL/WASO in adults

studies.cite: Jackson & Bruck 2012, J Clin Sleep Med
studies.result: Few PSG differences; microstructure/HRV in sleep promising
reduced glymphatic index
Wrist actigraphy, 38 vs 38: more time in bed, lower sleep efficiency and more night-to-night variability; total sleep time unchanged

contradicting.result: No clinically relevant findings

open_questions: What makes sleep non-restorative: autonomic arousal, microstructure, or glymphatic function?
No ME/CFS trials of orexin antagonists or low-dose sedating agents
findings.test_available: Clinical polysomnography (to exclude apnoea, PLMs, narcolepsy)

findings.finding: Self-reported light and sound sensitivity is common in ME/CFS. One ERP study found normal early sensory gating (P50) but a reduced P300, pointing to higher-order processing rather than early filtering.
findings.plain: Many patients find light and noise hard to tolerate. The single brain-wave study suggests that the basic filtering of sounds is normal and that later attention steps are affected.
findings.detail: Kumar 2026: 31 vs 30, auditory paired-click and oddball paradigms. Patients reported more sensory problems; the P50 suppression index did not differ, while P300 amplitude was reduced. Severe and very severe patients report extreme sensitivity (Vink 2026 review), but they are largely absent from laboratory studies. There are no controlled studies of photophobia thresholds, hyperacusis audiometry or migraine-type central sensitisation specific to ME/CFS. The genetic overlap with chronic pain and migraine (Solving ME/CFS genetics re-analysis) is consistent with shared central sensitisation.

studies.result: Normal P50 gating; reduced P300
Extreme light/sound sensitivity described in severe ME

open_questions: Quantitative sensory thresholds in severe patients (home-based measurement)
Overlap with migraine and fibromyalgia central sensitisation

findings.finding: Blood-brain barrier disruption (DCE-MRI leakage, serum markers) is reported in long COVID with brain fog; no ME/CFS data exist.
findings.plain: Brain scans suggest the protective barrier around the brain is leakier in long COVID patients with brain fog. It has not been tested in ME/CFS.

studies.n: LC with brain fog vs controls
studies.result: BBB disruption in brain fog; serum S100B/TGF-beta changes
BBB permeability changes
BBB water permeability (WEPCAST MRI) higher in 97 LC vs 31 recovered; no difference in cerebral blood flow or brain volume; linked only to motor scores

open_questions: Is BBB leakage present in ME/CFS of non-COVID onset?

findings.finding: Long COVID shows structural differences in thalamus, basal ganglia and choroid plexus (enlarged) on MRI relative to recovered controls.
findings.plain: MRI studies find changes in deep brain structures and an enlarged fluid-producing tissue (choroid plexus) in long COVID.

studies.result: thalamus and basal ganglia changes associated with fatigue
subcortical microstructural changes
choroid plexus enlarged

findings.plain: Brain sugar-use scans in long COVID give conflicting results.

findings.finding: Quantitative EEG shows group differences in spectral power and connectivity in ME/CFS (and LC), with classification accuracy reported in single centres, but methods are heterogeneous.
findings.plain: Brain-wave recordings differ on average in ME/CFS, but studies use different methods and are not yet a test.

studies.result: coherence factors distinguished CFS from controls and depression
altered connectivity/power
inconsistent but frequent spectral differences; low quality
Lower posterior resting alpha EEG sources in post-COVID patients without cognitive or psychiatric disorder, strongest in those with fatigue

findings.plain: Brain scans at rest find differences in how brain regions communicate, but different studies find different networks.

hypotheses_notes.for: Reduced vagal HRV (meta-analysis), orthostatic CBF fall and hypocapnia across labs, SFN in 31-53% of referral cohorts, autonomic-fibre loss in long COVID, POTS in a minority.
hypotheses_notes.against: SFN not found in the controlled NIH cohort; SFN severity does not correlate with exertional limits or symptom scores; HRV changes are non-specific and confounded by deconditioning.

hypotheses_notes.for: Orthostatic CBF fall even without tachycardia; narrow pulse pressure on lean test in recent-onset patients; preload failure in 92% of iCPET-tested ME/CFS (Novak 2026).
hypotheses_notes.against: Yamazaki 2026: measured total and red-cell volume did not predict lean-test abnormalities; hypocapnia, not volume, was the most common abnormality.

hypotheses_notes.for: Nakatomi TSPO-PET; MRS raised lactate, choline and brain temperature; diffusion NII signals; VanElzakker PBR28 in long COVID; CSF cytokine changes (Hornig).
hypotheses_notes.against: Raijmakers TSPO-PET null; Tuomaala long COVID TSPO null; NfL/GFAP normal; CSF proteomes indistinguishable from fibromyalgia and no replicated CSF signature.

hypotheses_notes.for: Brainstem imaging differences repeatedly reported (volume, connectivity); uncontrolled series with high rates of craniocervical findings and raised opening pressure in a subset.
hypotheses_notes.against: No controlled or blinded imaging of craniocervical anatomy; no trials of surgery; CSF-leak codes not specific to ME/CFS in registry data; imaging brainstem changes need not be mechanical.

hypotheses_notes.for: Central fatigability (brain fails to ramp up motor drive), lower CSF catechol metabolites, altered task activation after exertion: consistent with a brain-level 'sickness' state.
hypotheses_notes.against: The 'effort preference' reading is confounded by inability to complete hard tasks; central changes could equally be downstream of peripheral pathology.

hypotheses_notes.for: Raised brain lactate at rest and failure to raise it further under hypoxia (Bader 2026); lower cortical glutathione; post-exertion cognitive decline.
hypotheses_notes.against: Brain lactate also raised in depression; no 31P-MRS energetics replicated; samples small.

hypotheses_notes.for: Hypermobility in 50% of a severe-clinic series; hEDS cohorts show more severe neurodegeneration and share the autonomic phenotype.
hypotheses_notes.against: Clinic series are uncontrolled; overlap may reflect referral patterns.

hypotheses_notes.for: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: DecodeME heritability enriched in brain tissues and neurons, with shared architecture with chronic pain and migraine.
hypotheses_notes.against: Structural MRI largely normal; no neuronal injury markers; no locus is an autonomic gene.

glossary.plain: Symptoms (dizziness, fog, fatigue, nausea) that come on when upright and ease when lying down.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome: heart rate rises by 30+ bpm (40+ in teenagers) within 10 minutes of standing, without a big blood-pressure drop, plus symptoms.
Low carbon dioxide from over-breathing. POSH means CO2 drops when upright; low CO2 narrows brain blood vessels.
Beat-to-beat variation in heart rhythm; higher high-frequency HRV reflects stronger vagal (calming) nerve activity.
10 minutes leaning with shoulders on a wall while pulse and blood pressure are taken each minute. Cheap, but not validated for formal diagnosis.
Loss of the thinnest nerves in skin and organs, which carry pain/temperature and control sweating and blood vessels; diagnosed by counting fibres in a 3 mm skin biopsy (IENFD).
An MRI method that measures chemicals such as lactate, choline and glutathione in brain tissue, and can estimate tissue temperature.
A PET scan using a tracer that binds a protein raised in activated microglia and astrocytes, used as a marker of brain inflammation.
MRI that tracks water movement along nerve fibres to infer white-matter structure.
Cerebrospinal fluid, which bathes the brain and spinal cord; sampled by lumbar puncture.
Proteins released when neurons (NfL) or astrocytes (GFAP) are damaged; raised in MS, stroke and dementia.
Effort-Expenditure for Rewards Task: repeated choices between an easy and a hard button-pressing task for money; used by NIH to define 'effort preference'.
Proposed abnormal movement at the skull-neck junction that compresses the brainstem; mainly discussed in hypermobile patients.

gaps: No adequately powered (n>50 per group), multi-site TSPO-PET study in ME/CFS using a modern tracer and arterial input.
No blinded, controlled imaging study of craniocervical anatomy in ME/CFS vs hypermobile and healthy controls, and no controlled trial of CCI surgery or CSF drainage.
No skin-biopsy SFN prevalence study in unselected community ME/CFS with matched controls and blinded reading.
Brain measures before and after exertion (MRS lactate, fMRI, CSF) in the same people across the 24-72 h PEM window are almost absent; Cook 2017 has not been directly replicated.
No CSF study with a large healthy-control group and a pre-registered analysis; most recent CSF cohorts lack controls.
No trial of treatments that target orthostatic hypocapnia or cerebral hypoperfusion (capnography-guided breathing, midodrine, compression) measuring function over weeks.
Severe and very severe patients are largely excluded from imaging, CSF and sensory studies.
Few studies stratify by orthostatic phenotype (POTS vs hypocapnia vs normal HR/BP), which may explain much of the inconsistency in perfusion and imaging results.
No effort-based decision study in ME/CFS that calibrates task difficulty to each person's ability.

domains.title: Immune system
domains.overview: Immunology is the oldest and most heavily worked area of ME/CFS research, and the one with the widest gap between positive reports and independent replication. Reduced natural-killer-cell killing is the most repeated finding (meta-analytic Hedges g about 0.96 across 28 papers), yet the largest standardised multi-site attempt (MCAM, 174 vs 86) and two careful phenotyping studies found nothing, so the honest grade is 'contested and not usable as a test'. Several newer cell-level findings are more consistent in direction than in detail: CD8 T-cell exhaustion programmes, shifts in B-cell maturation (more naive, fewer switched-memory), monocyte dysregulation, and an exaggerated innate response to microbial stimulation that worsens after exercise. Cytokines look disturbed in aggregate (TNF, IL-2, IL-4, TGF-beta, CRP in meta-analysis) but no single cytokine survives as a marker, TGF-beta turned out to be largely a blood-handling artefact, and the clearest pattern is that abnormalities depend on illness duration (Hornig 2015) and severity (Montoya 2017) rather than on diagnosis alone. The autoimmunity strand has had the clearest negative resolution: GPCR autoantibodies against beta2/M3/M4 receptors are not reproduced by unbiased antigen profiling, removing them by immunoadsorption fails against sham, rituximab failed in a 151-patient RCT, and BC007's larger trial failed; what survives is narrower and interesting - patient IgG does things to endothelial mitochondria and, in long COVID, transfers pain and fatigue-like phenotypes to mice, and plasma-cell depletion with daratumumab produced striking but uncontrolled responses in 6 of 10 patients. Common-variant genetics (DecodeME) shows no enrichment in any blood immune cell type, which pushes most of these immune findings toward being consequences or state markers rather than inherited causes.

findings.finding: Natural-killer-cell cytotoxicity is reduced in ME/CFS in meta-analysis of the older literature (Hedges g ~0.96), but the largest standardised multi-site study and two deep-phenotyping studies found no difference.
findings.plain: The most-repeated immune finding in ME/CFS is that one type of white blood cell kills target cells less well. When labs tried to turn it into a standardised test, the difference disappeared.
findings.detail: Baraniuk, Eaton-Fitch and Marshall-Gradisnik 2024 pooled 28 papers and 55 effector:target data points: cytotoxicity about half of control levels, overall Hedges g 0.96 (0.75-1.18), heterogeneity high and explained by E:T ratio and method. Against this: the CDC Multi-Site Clinical Assessment (MCAM) sub-study used an assay validated for overnight-shipped blood in 174 ME/CFS vs 86 healthy controls and found 34.1% vs 33.6% cytotoxicity (p=0.79), with no association with symptom domains; Theorell 2017 found no reproducible difference in two cohorts (48 patients) across granule content, exocytosis, killing or adrenaline sensitivity; Cliff 2019 found no difference in NK numbers, subsets or in vitro responsiveness in 251 patients (54 severe) vs 107 controls. The assay requires fresh blood and is highly method-sensitive, so publication-era and logistics effects are plausible explanations for the discrepancy. Treat reduced NK function as a real signal in some cohorts with some assays, not as a disease marker.

findings.finding: Reduced TRPM3 ion-channel current and calcium influx in patients' NK cells has been reported repeatedly, including a two-site study (36 vs 42), but only ever by one research group.
findings.plain: One Australian group finds that a calcium channel on immune cells works poorly in patients, which they argue explains weak NK killing. No other lab has tested it.
findings.detail: Sasso 2026 (Front Med) ran whole-cell patch-clamp on isolated NK cells at two laboratory sites with independent investigators: 36 CCC-defined ME/CFS vs 42 healthy controls, significant reduction in all TRPM3 parameters with no site effect. Earlier work in the same programme: Eaton-Fitch 2022 (impaired TRPM3-dependent calcium influx, restored in vitro by naltrexone), Eaton-Fitch 2021 (TRPM3/PIP2 co-localisation), Magawa 2026 (deficient TRPM3-linked mitochondrial calcium influx), plus a post-COVID extension (Magawa 2026, Eur J Immunol) and LDN restoration in long COVID NK cells (Sasso 2025). The 'two sites' are both within the same group's network, so this is internal consistency rather than independent replication; patch-clamp of isolated NK cells is a demanding, low-throughput method available in very few labs. Against it indirectly: DecodeME common-variant genetics shows no enrichment in any blood immune cell type, and the low-dose naltrexone RCT in post-COVID ME/CFS (n=137) was negative, which weakens the therapeutic corollary.

studies.result: Significant reduction in all TRPM3 current parameters; no effect of laboratory site
Impaired TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ influx; restored in vitro by naltrexone

studies.result: Deficient TRPM3-linked mitochondrial Ca2+ influx

contradicting.result: No immune-cell subtype, gene or methylation site separates cases from controls reproducibly; nothing passed FDR in more than one dataset
No enrichment in any of 29 immune cell types; signal is brain/neuronal

Is reduced TRPM3 current a cause of poor cytotoxicity or a downstream consequence of cell state/handling?

findings.finding: CD8+ effector-memory T cells in ME/CFS show transcriptional and chromatin features of exhaustion, with supporting flow cytometry and an independent cell-free RNA signature.
findings.plain: Killer T cells in patients look 'worn out', like cells that have been fighting an infection for a long time.
findings.detail: Iu 2024 (PNAS) integrated scRNA-seq, bulk RNA-seq and ATAC-seq across sorted T-cell subsets (336,269 T-lineage cells from 28 patients and 30 sedentary controls at baseline and after symptom provocation), finding upregulated exhaustion transcription factors, altered chromatin accessibility and metabolic reprogramming most marked in CD8+ effector-memory and innate-like T cells, validated by flow cytometry in an extended cohort (15 patients, 11 controls, female, age/BMI matched). Gardella 2025 independently found T-cell-exhaustion and cytokine-signalling signatures in plasma cell-free RNA (93 vs 75). Supporting but not identical: Mandarano 2020 found reduced CD8+ mitochondrial membrane potential and reduced glycolysis at rest in 53 vs 45. The main caveat is that the Cornell scRNA cohorts are not independent of each other and a re-analysis of the same public scRNA data found no exhausted-CD8 composition difference once cell typing was redone, so the effect may live in gene programmes rather than cell counts.

studies.result: Exhaustion TFs up in CD8+ Tem, altered chromatin and metabolism; higher frequency of exhaustion markers by flow
Cytokine-signalling and T-cell-exhaustion network signatures; classifier AUC 0.81
Reduced CD8+ mitochondrial membrane potential; reduced resting glycolysis in CD4+ and CD8+
Exhausted SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells, systemic inflammation, uncoordinated T/B responses

contradicting.result: Exhausted-CD8 gating null; 0 genes at q<0.05 at baseline in all 15 cell types

open_questions: Is the exhaustion programme driven by a persisting antigen, and if so which?
Does checkpoint blockade or metabolic rescue change anything in vivo (never tried)?
Why do composition-level and programme-level analyses of the same data disagree?

findings.finding: T-cell abnormalities differ by severity: mild/moderate patients show cytotoxic/immunosenescence features, severe patients show activated lymphocytes and higher stimulated pro-inflammatory cytokines.
findings.plain: Mildly and severely affected patients show different immune pictures, which may mean different disease mechanisms rather than one disease of different intensity.
findings.detail: Lee, Cliff and colleagues (UK ME/CFS Biobank; medRxiv 2025, J Transl Med Dec 2025) compared 43 mild/moderate with 53 severe patients by flow cytometry. Mild/moderate: increased cytotoxic effector molecules and more CD28-CD57- early-immunosenescent cells, a pattern associated with persistent viral infection. Severe: more CD69+ and CD38+ activated circulating lymphocytes and more IFN-gamma, TNF and IL-17 after in vitro stimulation, consistent with non-specific ongoing inflammation. Changes spanned CD8+ T cells, MAIT cells and NK cells. This is a within-patient-group comparison without a healthy-control contrast for the severity axis, and severe patients differ in sampling conditions (home visits, deconditioning, medication), so confounding by illness state is not excluded.

studies.cite: Lee JS 2025, J Transl Med (also medRxiv 2025.01.02.24319359)
studies.design: case-case flow cytometry, UK ME/CFS Biobank
studies.result: Immunosenescence/cytotoxic markers in mild-moderate; activation (CD69+, CD38+) and higher stimulated IFN-gamma/TNF/IL-17 in severe
T-cell severity association (check not already cited)

open_questions: Do these two patterns define stable subgroups or stages of one illness?
Does the severe-patient activation pattern reflect being bedbound rather than disease mechanism?

findings.finding: Increased mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cell proportions and a shift in CD8+ memory subsets were found in the largest single ME/CFS flow-cytometry cohort, but the finding has not been reproduced in independent data.
findings.plain: One large study found more of a gut-associated T-cell type in patients, especially severe ones. Re-analyses of other datasets do not show it.
findings.detail: Cliff 2019 (251 patients incl. 54 severe, 107 controls, 46 MS) reported increased effector-memory CD8+ and decreased terminally differentiated effector CD8+ T cells, plus a significantly increased proportion of MAIT cells, most marked in severe patients, with no differences in herpesvirus seroprevalence. Iu 2024 also flagged 'certain innate T cells' as among the most dysregulated. Against: a re-analysis across five cohorts and three data types (scRNA of 503,739 PBMCs, four methylation cohorts, B- and T-cell repertoires) found MAIT, gamma-delta T, Th17 and exhausted-CD8 gating all null, and blood RNA cohorts do not show reduced Th17 (meta p=0.39).

studies.result: MAIT proportion increased (most in severe); CD8+ Tem up, TEMRA down

contradicting.result: MAIT, gamma-delta, Th17, ABC B cells and pDC interferon all null; Th17 meta p=0.39

open_questions: Is the MAIT signal a gut-mucosa readout, and does it track gut findings in the same people?

findings.finding: T-cell receptor repertoires do not distinguish ME/CFS from controls, arguing against a dominant shared antigen-driven clonal expansion.
findings.plain: If one infection or self-target were driving the disease, you would expect to see armies of identical T cells. Sequencing says they are not there.
findings.detail: Dibble 2024 (BMC Research Notes) sequenced alpha/delta, beta and gamma TCR loci in 40 samples each from severe ME, mild/moderate ME, MS disease controls and healthy controls, and applied P-SVM classification: the method worked on simulated data but could not partition the real samples significantly. A re-analysis of UK ME/CFS Biobank T-cell repertoires (304 samples) likewise found nothing passing FDR in more than one dataset, with only exploratory herpesvirus-related trends (higher share of EBV-specific TCR-beta in severe patients' CD8, 0.88% vs 0.45%, p=0.06). A near-genome-wide candidate, the TRA locus (Ueland 2022), has not replicated either.

studies.design: bulk TCR repertoire sequencing + machine learning
studies.result: No statistically significant partitioning; 'findings do not support altered T-cell receptor diversity'
Nothing reproducible; EBV-specific TCR-beta share higher in severe CD8 at p=0.06 only

open_questions: Would antigen-specific sorting (rather than bulk repertoire) reveal expansions invisible in bulk?
Could tissue (muscle, gut, brainstem) repertoires differ while blood looks normal?

findings.finding: The NIH deep-phenotyping study found more naive and fewer switched-memory B cells in post-infectious ME/CFS, consistent with chronic antigenic stimulation; supporting signals exist but are weak.
findings.plain: Patients seem to have more 'untrained' B cells and fewer that have already matured, as if the immune system keeps being prodded by something.
findings.detail: Walitt 2024 (Nat Commun) did intensive inpatient phenotyping of a small, rigorously selected post-infectious ME/CFS cohort (17 PI-ME/CFS vs 21 healthy volunteers for immune measures) and reported increased naive and decreased switched-memory B cells, interpreted as chronic antigenic stimulation and linked to STAT4-TLR9 B-cell pathway signals; PBMC gene-expression and metabolic differences were sex-dependent. A Solving ME/CFS re-analysis found plasma-cell/immunoglobulin transcripts lower in 2 of 4 blood RNA cohorts (meta d -0.42, p=0.06), which points the same way without reaching significance. Earlier B-cell phenotype work (Mensah 2016, 2018) found no reproducible subset differences but raised CD24 expression on naive and memory B cells. The cohort is tiny and much of Walitt 2024's framing (effort preference) is contested, so this should be read as a lead, not an established feature.

studies.n: 17 PI-ME/CFS vs 21 HV (immune measures; 16 vs 20 for switched memory)
studies.result: Naive B cells increased, switched-memory B cells decreased; interpreted as chronic antigenic stimulation
Plasma-cell/immunoglobulin transcripts lower in 2 of 4 cohorts, meta d -0.42, p=0.06
No reproducible subset differences; higher CD24 expression within naive and memory B cells

contradicting.result: No B-cell composition difference survived; ABC B-cell call lower only at p=0.03, not replicated

open_questions: Does the naive/switched-memory shift replicate in a larger, less selected cohort?
Is it explained by medication, inactivity or infection history?
findings.test_available: Lymphocyte subset flow cytometry is widely available, but the naive/memory B-cell split is not a validated marker

findings.finding: Reported skewing of the B-cell receptor repertoire (IGHV3-30/3-33 overuse) partially replicates in mild/moderate patients but shows no clonality, somatic-hypermutation or autoimmunity signature.
