findings.test_available: Yes: 9am serum cortisol, salivary awakening cortisol, short Synacthen test (mainly to exclude true adrenal insufficiency)

findings.finding: Challenge tests show a blunted cortisol response to ACTH and exaggerated cortisol suppression after a glucocorticoid dose, consistent with enhanced negative feedback.
findings.plain: When the stress-hormone system is pushed or braked in a test, it responds less to the push and more to the brake than in healthy people.
findings.detail: Woo 2026 included 12 pharmacological challenge studies: impaired cortisol release after ACTH stimulation and greater suppression after dexamethasone or hydrocortisone. The pattern resembles the 'hypocortisolism with enhanced feedback' described in PTSD, fibromyalgia and atypical depression, so it is not specific to ME/CFS. Insulin stress tests in the Cleare 1999 trial showed the adrenal glands were not suppressed by low-dose hydrocortisone. POTS patients showed normal adrenal responses to ACTH (Laurin 2023, n=8 vs 5).

studies.result: Impaired ACTH-stimulated cortisol; exaggerated glucocorticoid suppression

contradicting.result: Normal aldosterone and cortisol responses in POTS

open_questions: Is the feedback change central (hypothalamus/pituitary) or adrenal?
Does it differ between infection-onset and gradual-onset cases?
findings.test_available: Research only (dexamethasone suppression or CRH tests); short Synacthen test is clinical

findings.finding: Lower cortisol in long COVID, reported in a 2023 Nature cohort, has not held up in later clinic and cohort studies that controlled for sampling time.
findings.plain: One high-profile study found low cortisol in long COVID. Later studies that timed the blood draws carefully mostly found normal levels.
findings.detail: Klein 2023 (n=275) reported lower cortisol in long COVID among other immune features. Dalhuisen 2024 (UCSF, n=200, banked 8am–12pm samples) found no overall difference (median 8.9 vs 8.8 µg/dL). Its sub-hour analyses were inconsistent: lower at 8–9am but higher at 9–10am in the ME/CFS-like group. Quach 2025 (Stanford clinic, n=86, 5–10am) found only 1 low value; 36% were above range. Camici 2026 (Rome, n=96) found normal blood cortisol but flattened salivary rhythms. Post-COVID controls without symptoms showed the same salivary pattern, so the change may follow infection rather than long COVID itself.

studies.result: Cortisol lower in long COVID
Reduced morning salivary cortisol, flattened rhythm; blood cortisol not different; ACTH higher

contradicting.result: No overall difference in morning cortisol
Low morning cortisol in 1.2%; 36% elevated

open_questions: Do serial or salivary measurements in long COVID with PEM reproduce the ME/CFS pattern?
Is the change post-infectious and non-specific?
findings.test_available: Yes: timed morning cortisol; salivary diurnal profile (private labs)

findings.finding: Low-dose hydrocortisone produced at most small, short-term fatigue benefits in two RCTs, at the cost of adrenal suppression and bone loss at higher doses.
findings.plain: Replacing some cortisol was tried in the 1990s. The effect was small, side effects were real, and it is not recommended.
findings.detail: McKenzie 1998 (JAMA, n=70, 25–35 mg/day for 12 weeks): global wellness responders 66.7% vs 54.3% (p=0.31). A secondary 5-point improvement was 53% vs 29% (p=0.04), but cosyntropin tests showed adrenal suppression. A sub-study (n=23) found lumbar spine bone density fell 2.0% on hydrocortisone. Cleare 1999 (Lancet, n=32 crossover, 5–10 mg for 1 month) found fatigue fell 4.5 points more than on placebo; 28% vs 9% reached normal-range fatigue. The trial was short, strictly selected (no psychiatric comorbidity) and never replicated. Blockmans 2003 (n=100 crossover, hydrocortisone 5 mg plus fludrocortisone 50 µg for 3 months) was null.

studies.result: Fatigue reduced vs placebo (paired difference 4.5 points, p=0.009)
Primary outcome ns (p=0.31); adrenal suppression
Lateral spine BMD −2.0% on hydrocortisone

contradicting.result: No difference in fatigue or well-being

open_questions: Would a subgroup with objectively low cortisol or blunted Synacthen response benefit?
No modern trial has used PEM-based criteria.
findings.test_available: Not applicable (treatment); not recommended outside proven adrenal insufficiency

findings.finding: Fludrocortisone, a synthetic salt-retaining steroid, did not improve CFS with neurally mediated hypotension in a 100-person RCT, and failed again in combination with hydrocortisone.
findings.plain: A drug that makes the kidneys hold salt and water was expected to help low blood pressure on standing. In proper trials it did not help overall.
findings.detail: Rowe 2001 (JAMA, n=100, tilt-positive neurally mediated hypotension, 0.1 mg/day for 9 weeks): ≥15-point wellness improvement in 14% vs 10% (p=0.76). Blockmans 2003 (n=100) found no effect of hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone. Small open series in POTS still report individual responders, and the trials did not select for measured hypovolaemia or low aldosterone.

studies.result: No benefit (14% vs 10% responders)

open_questions: Would patients selected for low aldosterone or measured low plasma volume respond?

findings.finding: Diagnosed adrenal insufficiency and hypopituitarism are 7 to 13 times more common than expected among Finnish patients coded with postviral fatigue syndrome.
findings.plain: A small minority of people labelled ME/CFS may have a real, treatable gland failure. That makes basic hormone screening worthwhile.
findings.detail: In Finnish registry data (FinRegistry about 1,622 G93.3 cases, FinnGen 348), the crude observed/expected ratio is 9.5–13 for adrenal insufficiency and 6.7–7.6 for hypopituitarism. Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone prescriptions are enriched 11–62x (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Risteys). These figures are not adjusted for age or sex and are inflated by healthcare use. They may reflect misdiagnosis, a true subgroup, or steroid treatment causing adrenal suppression. Case reports describe isolated ACTH and GH deficiency first labelled as CFS, which improved with hydrocortisone (Tokumasu 2021).

studies.result: Adrenal insufficiency O/E 9.5–13; hypopituitarism 6.7–7.6
Idiopathic ACTH + GH deficiency mimicking CFS

open_questions: What fraction of a well-phenotyped ME/CFS cohort fails a Synacthen test?
Is this misdiagnosis, a subgroup, or a treatment effect?
findings.test_available: Yes: 9am cortisol, ACTH, short Synacthen test; pituitary panel if indicated

findings.finding: After overnight fluid deprivation, plasma vasopressin was undetectable in 82% of 111 Swedish ME/CFS patients despite high plasma osmolality in 57%, suggesting partial central diabetes insipidus-like physiology.
findings.plain: Vasopressin (ADH) is the hormone that tells the kidneys to keep water. Some patients appear to make too little of it even when their blood is concentrated, which could worsen low blood volume.
findings.detail: Huhmar 2025 was a consecutive, uncontrolled clinic series (n=124). Urine osmolality was below 750 mOsm/kg in 66%. In the 13 patients tested with copeptin, which is a more stable marker of vasopressin secretion, all values were within the reference range, though at the low end. Brain MRI showed no hypothalamic or pituitary lesions. Miwa 2016 (18 vs 15) found ADH 2.2 vs 3.3 pg/mL (p=0.02) alongside lower aldosterone and small hearts. In open label use, desmopressin improved orthostatic symptoms in 5 of 10 patients. Vasopressin immunoassays are unreliable, and the normal copeptin results argue for caution.

studies.result: Vasopressin undetectable in 82%; copeptin normal-low
Lower ADH (p=0.02) and aldosterone (p=0.004)

contradicting.result: All copeptin values within reference range

open_questions: Does a controlled water-deprivation or hypertonic saline copeptin test confirm low vasopressin?
Does low vasopressin predict desmopressin response?
Is it central (hypothalamic) or due to altered osmoreceptor input?
findings.test_available: Yes: copeptin with paired plasma and urine osmolality (fasting); formal water deprivation or hypertonic saline test via endocrinology

findings.finding: Patients with POTS and with ME/CFS show normal or low renin and low aldosterone despite reduced blood volume (the 'renin-aldosterone paradox').
findings.plain: When blood volume is low, the kidneys should release renin and the adrenals aldosterone to retain salt. In POTS and ME/CFS this response seems muted.
findings.detail: Raj 2005 (POTS 15 vs 14, iodine-131 albumin) found a plasma volume deficit of 334 vs 10 mL with unchanged renin activity and aldosterone of 190 vs 380 pmol/L (p=0.017). Miwa 2016 (ME 18 vs 15) found aldosterone 104 vs 157 pg/mL (p=0.004) and renin activity 1.6 vs 2.5 (p=0.06). The adrenal glands respond normally to ACTH in POTS (Laurin 2023), so the defect is upstream of the adrenal. In SomaScan and Olink proteomics, renin, ACE and BNP show no group difference (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis), but those assays measure protein abundance, not posture-stimulated activity.

studies.result: Low aldosterone, unchanged renin despite hypovolaemia
Lower aldosterone and borderline lower renin

contradicting.result: Renin, ACE, BNP, EPO, hepcidin not different at rest
Angiotensin II slightly higher in paediatric POTS

open_questions: Are supine/upright renin and aldosterone low in PEM-defined ME/CFS with measured blood volume?
Is the defect renal, sympathetic or central?
findings.test_available: Yes: supine and upright renin and aldosterone; blood volume (Daxor or CO-rebreathing) in specialist centres

findings.finding: In one Dutch case-control study, CFS patients had normal TSH but lower total T3, T4 and free T3, with a higher reverse-T3 fraction ('low T3 syndrome' pattern in 16% vs 7%).
findings.plain: The thyroid itself looks normal by standard tests, but the active thyroid hormone (T3) runs slightly lower, as seen in many long-term illnesses.
findings.detail: Ruiz-Núñez 2018 (98 vs 99, age/sex matched): TT3 −12.5%, TT4 −11.9%, deiodinase activity −14.4%, rT3 fraction +13.3%. FT3 below range in 16/98 vs 7/99 (OR 2.56, 95% CI 1.00–6.54). The median difference in free T3 was tiny (0.1%), and thyroid values correlated with hsCRP. This pattern ('non-thyroidal illness') appears in many chronic and inflammatory states and is usually adaptive. It has not been independently replicated in ME/CFS. There is no trial of T3 treatment in ME/CFS.

studies.result: Lower TT3/TT4/FT3, higher %rT3, normal TSH; low-T3 OR 2.56

open_questions: Does it replicate in a PEM-defined cohort?
Is it a sign of reduced metabolic rate (hypometabolism) or just non-specific illness?
findings.test_available: Yes: TSH, free T4, free T3; reverse T3 (some labs)

findings.finding: Reports of low IGF-1 and reduced growth hormone responses in CFS conflict, and the largest controlled study found an intact GH/IGF system.
findings.plain: Growth hormone helps with repair and energy. Early small studies hinted it was low, but a larger careful study found it normal.
findings.detail: Allain 1997 found lower IGF-I (214 vs 263 µg/L) and IGF-II and a reduced GH response to hypoglycaemia. Berwaerts 1998 (20 vs 20) found IGF-I SDS −0.39 vs +0.33 (p=0.02) and a trend to lower nocturnal GH (p=0.06), but normal stimulated GH peaks. Cleare 2000 (37 vs 37, medication-free) found no difference in IGF-I/IGFBPs, urinary GH or GHRH and insulin-stress responses. In a GH treatment RCT (Moorkens 1998, n=20) IGF-1 rose but quality of life did not improve.

studies.result: Lower IGF-I/IGF-II; blunted GH response
Lower IGF-I SDS; normal stimulated GH

contradicting.design: case-control with GHRH and insulin tests
contradicting.result: No GH deficiency; IGF system intact
IGF-1 rose; quality of life not improved

open_questions: Is nocturnal GH reduced as a consequence of non-restorative sleep?
findings.test_available: Yes: IGF-1 (stimulation tests only if pituitary disease suspected)

findings.finding: ME/CFS and long COVID are more common in women (ME/CFS prevalence about 1.4% vs 0.9%; DecodeME 82% female), but genetic risk variants are not sex-specific.
findings.plain: More women than men get ME/CFS and long COVID. Inherited risk looks the same in both sexes, so the difference probably lies in hormones, immunity or exposure, not in different genes.
findings.detail: Lim 2020 meta-analysis: pooled prevalence 1.36% in women vs 0.86% in men. Clinic cohorts are typically 75–85% female. In RECOVER-Adult (n=12,276), female sex raised long COVID risk (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.06–1.62), but not at age 18–39 (RR 1.04). At age 40–54 the RR was similar for menopausal (1.42) and non-menopausal (1.45) women. DecodeME: 12,833 female and 2,746 male cases, no sex-biased loci, and two female-discovered signals replicate in males. The mostly male Million Veteran Program replicates the polygenic signal (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

studies.result: Women 1.36% vs men 0.86%
Female RR 1.31 for long COVID; age- and pregnancy-dependent
No sex-biased loci; male replication of 2 signals

open_questions: Which biological factor (sex hormones, X-linked immune genes, autoimmunity propensity) drives the excess?
Why is the excess absent in young adults in RECOVER?

findings.finding: Women with CFS report more endometriosis, heavy bleeding, pelvic pain, hysterectomy and earlier menopause than controls in US population-based case-control studies.
findings.plain: Gynaecological problems and early menopause are more common in women with ME/CFS. We do not know which comes first or why.
findings.detail: Boneva 2015 (Georgia, 84 cases vs 73 controls) reported earlier menopause (37.6 vs 48.6 years; adjusted OR 1.22 per year), endometriosis 29.8% vs 12.3% (aOR 3.67), hysterectomy 54.8% vs 19.2% (aOR 3.23) and non-menstrual pelvic pain (aOR 12.0). The Wichita sample (36 vs 48) showed similar but mostly non-significant patterns. Surgical menopause after hysterectomy or oophorectomy confounds the 'early menopause' result, and recall bias is possible. 2026 survey work (Habermann-Horstmeier) describes different symptom structures by sex and a menopausal-status proxy, but it is cross-sectional and self-reported.

studies.result: Earlier menopause, more endometriosis and hysterectomy
More pelvic pain and endometriosis; menopause about 4 years earlier (ns)
Immune/GI symptom architecture differs by sex and menopausal proxy

open_questions: Does onset cluster at perimenopause after adjusting for age?
Does HRT change ME/CFS course? No trial exists.
Do symptoms vary with menstrual cycle in a measurable way?
findings.test_available: Clinical gynaecological assessment; no ME/CFS-specific hormone test

findings.finding: Lower plasma androgenic steroids in ME/CFS (Cornell metabolomics) is mostly an age and sex artefact and does not replicate in BioMapAI.
findings.plain: An earlier claim that patients have low 'male-type' steroid hormones mostly disappears once age and sex are accounted for.
findings.detail: Across the two Cornell cohorts the androgenic steroid class was −0.42 SD, but in Germain 2022 the effect shrinks after age/sex/BMI adjustment. BioMapAI (n=236) shows −0.01 (p=0.90) and Che testosterone −0.18 (p=0.22) (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). Cleare 2004 measured DHEA/DHEA-S and their response to CRH as a separate question.

studies.result: Androgen deficit not replicated after adjustment

open_questions: Are sex steroids altered within defined subgroups (e.g. men, post-menopausal women)?
findings.test_available: Yes: testosterone, SHBG, DHEA-S (not diagnostic for ME/CFS)

findings.finding: Melatonin may help the subgroup with delayed melatonin onset, and melatonin plus zinc modestly reduced physical fatigue in one small RCT.
findings.plain: Melatonin is the night-time hormone. A small trial and an open study suggest it can help some patients, especially those whose body clock runs late.
findings.detail: van Heukelom 2006 (open-label, n=29 with DLMO after 21:30; 5 mg 5 h before DLMO for 3 months) improved fatigue, concentration and activity, more when DLMO was after 22:00. Fatigue normalised in 8/27. Castro-Marrero 2021 (RCT, n=50, melatonin 1 mg plus zinc 10 mg for 16 weeks) reduced physical fatigue at the last visit and improved SF-36 physical summary. Multiple outcomes were tested and the trial was not replicated.

studies.result: Reduced physical fatigue vs placebo (p<0.05)
Fatigue improved, mainly if DLMO >22:00

open_questions: What proportion of patients have delayed DLMO?
Does timed low-dose melatonin help in a blinded DLMO-selected trial?
findings.test_available: Research/private: salivary dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO); actigraphy

findings.finding: ME/CFS genetic risk is enriched in brain tissues and the pituitary, but genetically predicted morning cortisol does not change risk.
findings.plain: Genes linked to ME/CFS are especially active in the brain and the pituitary, the master hormone gland. Genetically high or low cortisol does not seem to cause ME/CFS.
findings.detail: In a DecodeME + Million Veteran Program meta-analysis (Maccallini 2026 preprint, 19,470 cases), tissue enrichment implicated multiple brain regions and the pituitary, with no peripheral tissue. MR using a single morning-cortisol instrument gave OR 1.04 (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis), which is underpowered. The pituitary result could reflect neural gene expression shared with brain rather than endocrine function.

studies.result: Brain regions and pituitary enriched
Morning cortisol (1 SNP) OR 1.04, null

open_questions: Do pituitary-specific eQTLs colocalise with ME/CFS loci?
Can a multi-SNP cortisol instrument test causality properly?

hypotheses_notes.for: A meta-analysis of 46 studies shows mildly low free cortisol and enhanced feedback. The genetic signal is enriched in the pituitary. Adrenal/pituitary diagnoses are enriched in Finnish registries.
hypotheses_notes.against: The effects are small and overlap normal ranges. A similar pattern appears in other fatigue and pain conditions. Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone trials were weak or null. Cortisol MR is null. In long COVID, low cortisol did not replicate in timed samples.

hypotheses_notes.for: One large uncontrolled series found undetectable vasopressin despite high osmolality. Miwa found low ADH and partial response to desmopressin.
hypotheses_notes.against: Copeptin, the more reliable marker, was normal or low-normal. There is no controlled water-deprivation study and no pituitary lesions on MRI.

hypotheses_notes.for: The renin-aldosterone paradox in POTS and ME, plus low ADH, would explain failure to restore low plasma volume.
hypotheses_notes.against: Resting proteomic renin, ACE and BNP are normal. Fludrocortisone, which replaces aldosterone action, failed in RCTs.

hypotheses_notes.for: Hypocortisolism with enhanced feedback fits a chronic post-infectious or inflammatory state.
hypotheses_notes.against: This cannot be separated from deconditioning or sleep effects in cross-sectional data.

glossary.plain: The hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal chain that controls cortisol release.
The normal rise in cortisol in the 30–45 minutes after waking, measured in saliva.
An injection of synthetic ACTH, with cortisol measured afterwards, to check whether the adrenal glands work.
A dose of a strong steroid to see how much the body's own cortisol is switched off (feedback sensitivity).
The pituitary hormone that makes the kidneys keep water.
A stable fragment released with vasopressin. It is easier to measure accurately than vasopressin itself.
Kidney and adrenal hormones that make the body hold salt and water when blood volume is low.
Low active thyroid hormone with normal TSH, often seen in chronic illness rather than thyroid disease.
A blood marker of growth hormone activity.
Dim-light melatonin onset, the evening time melatonin starts rising. It is a marker of body-clock timing.

key_reviews.why: Most comprehensive meta-analysis of HPA findings (46 studies, all sample types and challenge tests).
Review of HPA changes and HPA-targeted treatments in CFS.
Hypothesis review of why vasopressin and RAAS fail to correct hypovolaemia (not peer reviewed).
Clinical update on small heart, orthostatic intolerance and down-regulated volume hormones.

gaps: No controlled copeptin study with a standard stimulus (water deprivation, hypertonic saline or arginine) in PEM-defined ME/CFS.
No study pairs measured blood volume with supine/upright renin, aldosterone and copeptin in the same patients.
No longitudinal study shows whether low cortisol precedes illness, as it could in post-infection cohorts.
No modern RCT of any hormone therapy using PEM-based criteria or biomarker selection, for example hydrocortisone only in Synacthen low-responders, or desmopressin with copeptin stratification.
There are no trials of HRT or menstrual-cycle-linked interventions, and no prospective data on onset around perimenopause.
Low T3 has not been replicated and never tested as a treatment target.
Prevalence of true adrenal insufficiency or hypopituitarism among clinic ME/CFS patients is unknown.

domains.title: Gut and microbiome
domains.overview: Gut bacteria differ between people with ME/CFS and healthy controls more consistently than almost any blood measure. Fewer butyrate-producing species (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Coprococcus, Anaerostipes, Eubacterium rectale) and more Ruminococcus gnavus-type species appear in at least four independent cohorts across three labs, including a pre-specified test in the NIH cohort. The same pattern appears in long COVID. Blood levels of a gut-made metabolite, indole-3-propionate (IPA), are lower in four of four plasma cohorts, and re-analysis traces this to the R. gnavus-type overgrowth. What is not established is whether any of this causes symptoms. Dysbiosis is milder in long-standing illness, does not track severity reliably, and genetically predicted gut metabolite levels do not change ME/CFS risk. Markers of a 'leaky gut' (LPS, sCD14) come from a handful of studies, and the only randomised faecal transplant trial (n=11) was negative. Larger trials are under way.

findings.finding: Stool from ME/CFS patients has fewer butyrate-producing bacteria (notably Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale, Roseburia, Coprococcus) and reduced microbial capacity to make butyrate.
findings.plain: Some 'good' gut bacteria that feed the gut lining by making butyrate are consistently scarcer in ME/CFS.
findings.detail: Guo 2023 (106 vs 91, shotgun metagenomics, qPCR and stool SCFA) found lower F. prausnitzii and E. rectale and lower butyrate synthesis capacity. Its classifier was robust across US sites and to a validation cohort. Xiong 2023 (75 short-term, 79 long-term vs 79) found reduced butyrate biosynthesis genes and lower plasma butyrate, mostly in short-term patients. Giloteaux 2016 (16S, 48 vs 39) found lower diversity and fewer Firmicutes. Nagy-Szakal 2017 (50 vs 50) found lower Faecalibacterium in the IBS subgroup. In the NIH Walitt cohort (15 vs 17), a pre-specified 14-species signature built on other cohorts separated patients with AUC 0.87; all butyrate producers combined were −0.87 SD (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). The NIH authors' own per-species tests did not pass FDR (min q 0.088).

studies.result: Reduced F. prausnitzii, E. rectale and butyrate synthesis capacity
Reduced butyrate biosynthesis; dysbiosis strongest in short-term illness
Lower diversity, fewer Firmicutes
Dysbiosis, with distinct taxa depending on IBS status

studies.cite: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Walitt 2024 NIH stool
studies.result: AUC 0.87; butyrate producers −0.87 SD (p=0.015)
microbiome shift

contradicting.result: No species significant after FDR
Effect sizes agree NIH vs Columbia (rho 0.57) but not NIH vs Netherlands (rho 0.07)

open_questions: Is the change a cause, or a consequence of diet, inactivity, medication or IBS?
Does it appear before or at onset in prospective post-infection cohorts?
findings.test_available: Private shotgun stool metagenomics only; no validated clinical test or reference range

findings.finding: Ruminococcus gnavus, Flavonifractor plautii, Ruthenibacterium lactatiformans and Enterocloster species are increased in ME/CFS, consistently across BioMapAI, Guo 2023 and NIH cohorts and in long COVID.
findings.plain: Alongside the loss of 'good' species, a group of bacteria often linked to gut inflammation is overgrown.
findings.detail: In BioMapAI/JAX data (143 vs 88 people), R. lactatiformans (β +0.69), R. gnavus (+0.68) and F. plautii (+0.60) were raised (all q<1e-3). Guo 2023 agreed in direction for 14/17 shared species (binomial p=0.013; Solving ME/CFS re-analysis), but Guo listed only nominally significant species. In the NIH cohort, R. gnavus was +0.80 SD (p=0.014), E. bolteae +0.91 and C. symbiosum +0.77. Long COVID shows the same direction: Liu 2022 (106 patients followed 6 months) found higher R. gnavus and lower F. prausnitzii in post-acute COVID syndrome.

studies.result: R. gnavus, F. plautii, R. lactatiformans raised
PACS linked to higher R. gnavus, lower F. prausnitzii

open_questions: Does R. gnavus produce inflammatory polysaccharides or interfere with tryptophan metabolism in these patients?
Is the bloom driven by antibiotics, diet or low gut transit?

findings.finding: Plasma indole-3-propionate (IPA), a gut-bacteria product of tryptophan, is lower in ME/CFS in 4 of 4 plasma cohorts (pooled −0.33 SD), and the deficit is fully explained by stool composition, mainly the R. gnavus-type overgrowth.
findings.plain: A protective molecule that only gut bacteria make is slightly low in patients' blood. The overgrown bacteria seem to crowd out the microbes that make it.
findings.detail: Pooled across Germain 2020, Germain 2022, Che 2022 and BioMapAI: −0.33 SD (95% CI −0.49 to −0.16), p=0.0001. As a test it is weak (AUC 0.57–0.60). In 231 people with paired stool and plasma, a stool model predicted plasma IPA (CV Spearman 0.44), and adjusting for it removed the patient-control gap (−0.36 → −0.06). R. gnavus, F. plautii and R. lactatiformans were each inversely related to IPA. The IPA-producing C. sporogenes guild was not reduced. Fruit intake tracks IPA. No severity association survived FDR (all Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

studies.result: IPA −0.33 SD; gap explained by stool composition
Altered microbiome-tryptophan-metabolite links

contradicting.result: Genetically higher IPA does not lower ME/CFS risk (OR 1.19, 0.93–1.53)

open_questions: Does raising IPA (diet, fibre, polyphenols) change any symptom?
Does low IPA replicate with paired stool in a second cohort?

findings.finding: The replicated deficit of aromatic lactates (indolelactate, phenyllactate, 4-hydroxyphenyllactate) in ME/CFS blood is not predicted by stool bacteria or bacterial genes, so it is probably host-side or due to absorption, not dysbiosis.
findings.plain: Another set of low blood molecules looks like gut products, but the gut bacteria data do not explain them, so probiotics aimed at them are unlikely to help.
findings.detail: Aromatic-lactate score −0.55 SD (p 6.5e-6) in BioMapAI, and −0.53 SD across 5 cohorts. Stool species and gene models predict it at zero (CV Spearman 0.01). 0/4,429 KEGG genes and 0/1,696 taxa associate with it, and Bifidobacterium plus Lactobacillus abundance is uncorrelated (rho −0.01). Adjusting for diet, medications, IBS and kidney function makes the deficit larger, not smaller. In Esteban 2026, stool aromatic metabolites were higher in patients, which hints at reduced absorption (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

studies.result: No gut predictor of the lactate deficit

studies.design: case-control, targeted stool metabolomics + AHR assay
studies.result: Nine tryptophan metabolites elevated in stool; AHR activation not different

open_questions: Is it host transamination/LDH handling, small-intestine microbes (not sampled by stool) or uptake?
D- vs L-phenyllactate would distinguish bacterial from human origin.

findings.finding: Gut dysbiosis is strongest in the first years of illness and largely resolves in patients ill for more than 10 years, while their metabolic and clinical abnormalities persist.
findings.plain: Gut differences are clearest early in the illness and fade later, even though patients stay ill. This argues against gut bacteria alone keeping the illness going.
findings.detail: Xiong 2023: short-term (<4 years, n=75) patients showed significant microbial dysbiosis, while long-term (>10 years, n=79) patients had largely resolved dysbiosis but more severe metabolic and clinical aberrations. This comes from one cross-sectional comparison of two cohorts, not follow-up of the same people. The NIH cohort, which is mostly under 5 years ill, still shows the signature (AUC 0.87).

studies.result: Dysbiosis mainly in short-term illness

open_questions: Do the same patients' microbiomes normalise over time?
Is early dysbiosis a consequence of the triggering infection or antibiotics?

findings.finding: Links between specific gut bacteria and symptom severity are inconsistent: F. prausnitzii tracked fatigue in one cohort, but nothing survived correction for multiple testing in a 143-patient re-analysis.
findings.plain: It is not yet clear that people with more abnormal gut bacteria are sicker.
findings.detail: Guo 2023 found F. prausnitzii abundance inversely associated with fatigue severity. Nagy-Szakal 2017 reported correlations between distinct taxa and pain, fatigue and motivation within subgroups. In BioMapAI (143 patients), no taxon or metabolite module associated with severity, orthostatic intolerance or duration at FDR. The best nominal result was lower IPA with worse GI symptoms (p=0.005, q=0.41) (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

studies.result: F. prausnitzii inversely associated with fatigue

contradicting.result: No severity, OI or duration association at FDR

open_questions: Do within-person changes in microbiome track PEM episodes?

findings.finding: IBS is about seven times more common in ME/CFS (pooled OR 7.20; prevalence about 37%), and IBS status drives much of the measured microbiome difference.
findings.plain: Many people with ME/CFS also have irritable bowel syndrome. Studies need to separate the two, because IBS changes gut bacteria by itself.
findings.detail: Rajabi 2026 meta-analysis: 22 studies, 18 pooled. OR 7.20 (2.77–18.76), I² 72%; pooled IBS prevalence 37% (23–54%), varying by ME/CFS criteria. Brown 2026 (116 vs 80): 53% vs 8% prior IBS diagnosis, with GI symptom burden tracking fatigue, cognitive, pain and flu-like symptoms. In Nagy-Szakal 2017, IBS co-morbidity was the strongest factor separating microbiome networks, and the top marker taxa differed between IBS and non-IBS subgroups. Genetically, ME/CFS correlates with IBS (rg 0.57) and its heritability is enriched in enteric neurons (Lee 2026 medRxiv; from Solving ME/CFS genetics summary).

studies.result: OR 7.20 for IBS; prevalence 37%
IBS 53% vs 8%; GI burden correlates with CRP and core symptoms
IBS status strongest driver of microbiome separation

open_questions: Is ME/CFS dysbiosis independent of IBS in properly stratified analyses?
Are enteric-neuron genetics a shared gut-brain mechanism?
findings.test_available: Clinical: Rome IV IBS criteria; faecal calprotectin to exclude IBD

findings.finding: Blood markers of bacterial translocation (LPS, LPS-binding protein, sCD14, IgA/IgM to enterobacterial LPS) are raised in several small ME/CFS studies, but standardised replication is lacking.
findings.plain: Some studies suggest bits of gut bacteria leak into the blood ('leaky gut') and trigger inflammation. The evidence is small, uses different tests, and comes mostly from a few labs.
findings.detail: Giloteaux 2016 (48 vs 39) found LPS, LBP and sCD14 elevated and correlated with each other. I-FABP (gut-cell damage) was also measured. Maes 2007 reported higher serum IgA and IgM against LPS of gram-negative enterobacteria, correlated with severity and IBS symptoms. De Meirleir 2018 (140 vs 140, retrospective) found sCD14 among the most discriminating serum markers. In the Solving ME/CFS tally, 5 groups report raised LPS/sCD14 and 2 do not. Brown 2026 found higher IgM to LPS only in the subgroup with more flu-like symptoms. Endotoxin assays are contamination-prone, sCD14 is a general monocyte activation marker, and no study has used a direct permeability test (lactulose/mannitol). Maes' 'leaky gut diet' studies were uncontrolled.

studies.result: Raised LPS, LBP, sCD14
Raised IgA/IgM to enterobacterial LPS
sCD14 among best discriminating markers
post-exercise bacterial translocation
translocation markers
barrier markers

contradicting.result: Claimed improvement with 'leaky gut' supplements; no control group
Reduced, not increased, serum IgG reactivity to stool microbes

open_questions: Does a direct permeability test (sugar absorption, zonulin is unreliable) show a difference?
Do translocation markers rise after exertion (PEM)?
findings.test_available: Research only (LPS, LBP, sCD14); commercial 'leaky gut' panels are not validated

findings.finding: Quadram Institute studies of severe ME/CFS with household-matched controls report altered gut phage communities and reduced serum IgG reactivity to gut microbes, in very small samples.
findings.plain: A Norwich team is studying the viruses that infect gut bacteria, and the immune response to gut microbes, comparing patients with people in the same household. Their samples are tiny so far.
findings.detail: Hsieh 2023 combined virus-like-particle and whole-metagenome sequencing in a small severe-ME/CFS cohort. It defined a core of tailed Caudoviricetes phages and predicted ME/CFS-specific virus-host links involving Anaerotruncus. Seton 2023 (5 pairs with same-household controls) found reduced serum IgG capacity and reactivity to stool microbes. In a twin pair discordant for ME/CFS, Giloteaux 2016 reported lower diversity and expanded Caudovirales phages in the ill twin. The virome of the Norwegian Comeback FMT trial (Quadram/UEA thesis 2024) and a RESTORE-ME trial virome analysis are in progress, and no results are published.

studies.result: Core phage virome; predicted disease-associated virus-host interactions
Reduced serum IgG reactivity to gut microbes
Ill twin: lower diversity, Caudovirales expansion

open_questions: Do phage shifts replicate in a powered cohort?
Does reduced anti-microbial IgG reflect immune exhaustion or sampling noise?

findings.finding: The only published randomised faecal microbiota transplant trial in CFS (n=11) found no benefit, and a larger Norwegian RCT (n=80) has not yet reported.
findings.plain: Transferring stool from a healthy donor has been tried once in a proper small trial and did not help. A bigger trial is under way.
findings.detail: Salonen 2023 (Finland, donor FMT n=5 vs autologous n=6 by colonoscopy) found no change in VAS, MFIS, 15D or EQ-5D at 1 or 6 months, and no adverse events. It was underpowered. Kenyon 2019 reported improvement in a retrospective non-randomised series. The Comeback Study (NCT03691987, Harstad; 80 participants randomised 1:1:2 to two donors or autologous placebo, primary outcome FSS at 3 months) published its protocol in 2024. As of October 2026 no results have been reported.

studies.result: No improvement in fatigue or HRQOL
Results pending

contradicting.result: Reported improvement with FMT

open_questions: Will the Comeback RCT show benefit?
Should FMT target patients with the butyrate-loss / R. gnavus signature?

findings.finding: Probiotic trials in CFS are small; one 39-person RCT of Lactobacillus casei Shirota reduced anxiety but did not target fatigue.
findings.plain: No probiotic has been shown to improve ME/CFS itself.
findings.detail: Rao 2009 (n=39, 24 billion CFU daily for 2 months) raised stool Lactobacillus and Bifidobacteria and reduced Beck anxiety scores (p=0.01). Fatigue was not the primary outcome. Venturini 2019 was an uncontrolled pilot. Re-analysis argues against Bifidobacterium/Lactobacillus products for the indolelactate deficit, because their abundance does not track it. Fibre and polyphenols have a better mechanistic case for IPA, but there are no trials (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

studies.result: Reduced anxiety; stool lactobacilli up
Changes in immune/oxidative markers

open_questions: Would a butyrate-producer consortium or fibre intervention shift symptoms in signature-positive patients?

findings.finding: ME/CFS genetic risk overlaps with IBS and is enriched in enteric neurons, but genetically predicted gut-derived metabolites (IPA, indolelactate, kynurenine, bile acids) do not change ME/CFS risk.
findings.plain: The genes involved overlap with those for irritable bowel syndrome and gut nerves. But inheriting higher or lower levels of gut metabolites does not change ME/CFS risk, so those metabolites are probably effects, not causes.
findings.detail: Solving ME/CFS MR (DecodeME discovery, MVP replication): IPA OR 1.19 (0.93–1.53), indolelactate 0.99, kynurenine 1.01, glycocholate 1.02, all null. Lee 2026 (medRxiv, from Solving ME/CFS genetics summary): rg with IBS 0.57 and heritability enrichment in enteric neurons (FDR 0.004). Wielscher 2026 (preprint): 'barrier-microbiome' traits show among the strongest genetic overlap, with IBS contributing most pleiotropy. OLFM4, a DecodeME locus, is highly expressed in ileal stem cells and neutrophils.

studies.result: All gut-metabolite exposures null
Barrier-microbiome traits and IBS share pleiotropy with ME/CFS

open_questions: Is the shared IBS genetics neuronal (enteric nervous system) rather than microbial?

findings.finding: In long COVID, the gut microbiome at hospital admission predicted persistent symptoms, and at 6 months patients had more R. gnavus and fewer butyrate producers, mirroring ME/CFS.
findings.plain: Long COVID shows a gut pattern similar to ME/CFS, and in one study the gut profile early in COVID predicted who stayed ill.
findings.detail: Liu 2022 (Hong Kong, 106 patients, 258 serial stool samples; 68 controls) reported that admission microbiota composition was associated with PACS. Patients who recovered had normalised microbiomes, while PACS showed higher R. gnavus and B. vulgatus and lower F. prausnitzii. Butyrate producers (B. pseudocatenulatum, F. prausnitzii) showed the largest inverse correlation with PACS. Antibiotic use and hospital care in severe COVID are confounders.

studies.result: Admission microbiome associated with PACS; R. gnavus up, F. prausnitzii down
Gut microbiota differed in POTS (27) and, less so, post-acute COVID (32) vs controls; symptoms correlated with diversity

open_questions: Does pre-infection microbiome predict long COVID in community (non-hospitalised) cohorts?

findings.finding: Microbiome-based machine-learning classifiers distinguish ME/CFS from controls in held-out and external cohorts (BioMapAI, Guo 2023), but they are research tools with modest real-world specificity.
findings.plain: Computer models can tell patient and control stool apart better than chance, but this is not a diagnostic test yet.
findings.detail: BioMapAI (Xiong 2025, Nat Med; 249 participants over 4 years) integrated metagenomics, plasma metabolomics, immune profiling and labs to predict severity. It classified held-out and external cohorts and linked SCFA, BCAA, tryptophan and benzoate metabolism to MAIT/γδT inflammation. Guo 2023's classifier generalised across US sites. Classifiers have not been tested against disease controls (IBS, depression, MS, fibromyalgia), so specificity is unknown. Within-cohort cross-validation in the plasma metabolome transferred poorly (AUC 0.56; Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

studies.result: Classifies ME/CFS in held-out and external cohorts
Robust to geography; generalised to validation cohort

open_questions: How do classifiers perform against IBS and other fatigue conditions?

hypotheses_notes.for: Loss of butyrate producers and an R. gnavus-type bloom are seen in at least 4 cohorts and 3 labs, and a pre-specified NIH test gave AUC 0.87. Low IPA in 4/4 cohorts is explained by stool composition. The same pattern occurs in long COVID, where the admission microbiome predicted persistence. There is a genetic overlap with IBS and enteric neurons.
hypotheses_notes.against: Dysbiosis fades in long-standing illness while symptoms persist and does not track severity at FDR. MR shows gut metabolites are not causal. IBS confounds the comparison. The only FMT RCT was null (n=11). The translocation markers are small, lab-specific and use contamination-prone assays.

hypotheses_notes.for: Raised LPS/LBP/sCD14 in some studies. In BioMapAI, the microbiome links to MAIT/γδT inflammatory cells.
hypotheses_notes.against: Re-analysis found 0/622 immune-module associations at q<0.1. The Quadram feasibility study found reduced anti-microbial IgG.

hypotheses_notes.for: Heritability is enriched in enteric neurons and the genetic correlation with IBS is about 0.57, suggesting a gut-brain neural link.
hypotheses_notes.against: These are preprints, and the NOS1 region shared with IBS does not colocalise.

glossary.plain: The community of bacteria, viruses and fungi living in the gut.
An imbalance in the gut microbial community compared with healthy people.
A short-chain fatty acid made by some gut bacteria from fibre. It fuels the cells lining the colon and dampens inflammation.
Sequencing all DNA in stool to identify species and their genes, more detailed than 16S sequencing.
A cheaper method that identifies bacteria by one marker gene, usually only to genus level.
A protective tryptophan breakdown product made only by certain gut bacteria.
LPS is a component of bacterial walls. sCD14 and LBP are proteins the body makes in response to it, used as markers of bacteria leaking into blood.
The viruses in the gut, most of which infect bacteria (bacteriophages).
Faecal microbiota transplantation: transferring stool from a healthy donor to a patient.
Irritable bowel syndrome, a disorder of gut-brain interaction causing pain and altered bowel habit.

key_reviews.why: Broad review of microbiome hypotheses (dysbiosis, permeability, SCFA, D-lactate, tryptophan) and interventions.
Recent overview of gut microbiome mechanisms in ME/CFS.
First meta-analysis quantifying IBS overlap.
Argues that mucosal viruses are an under-studied piece.

gaps: No prospective study samples stool before or at the triggering infection and follows people into ME/CFS, outside the hospitalised COVID cohort of Liu 2022.
No microbiome study of ME/CFS uses disease controls (IBS without ME/CFS, depression, MS, deconditioned controls) to test specificity.
No direct intestinal permeability measurement (lactulose/mannitol or similar) in a powered ME/CFS cohort; no study of translocation markers before and after exertion.
Results of the 80-person Comeback FMT RCT and the RESTORE-ME virome work are not yet published.
No intervention trial selects patients by microbiome signature (e.g. butyrate-producer loss) or tests fibre/polyphenols to raise IPA.
Small-intestinal microbiota (which stool does not sample) has not been studied, though it could explain the aromatic-lactate deficit.
Within-person longitudinal sampling is needed to test whether microbiome shifts track PEM or relapses.

domains.title: Genetics
domains.overview: ME/CFS runs in families, and twin, genealogy and three-generation cohort studies put familial or heritable risk at roughly 20 to 50%. In 2025 DecodeME (15,579 cases) found the first eight robust genome-wide loci, with SNP heritability of about 8 to 10%. Each variant shifts risk only slightly (odds ratios 1.07 to 1.10), so no gene test can diagnose or predict ME/CFS. The overall genetic signal replicates in independent biobanks (MVP, FinnGen, UK Biobank), but the individual loci mostly do not yet, partly because those biobanks use loose case definitions. Across several analyses the signal points to neurons in the brain (and possibly the pituitary), not blood immune cells. It overlaps strongly with chronic pain, fibromyalgia, IBS and migraine, and partly with depression, though the specific ME/CFS loci do not share causal variants with depression. Earlier small candidate-gene and HLA findings mostly failed to replicate. Several 2025–2026 follow-ups (Mendelian randomisation, rare variants, a UK Biobank/All of Us GWAS) are preprints that still need confirmation.

findings.finding: ME/CFS aggregates in families: relatives of cases have about 2-3x the risk, MZ twins are more concordant than DZ twins, and familiality in a 153,803-person Dutch cohort was 42%.
findings.plain: Having a close relative with ME/CFS raises your own risk, which means genes (and perhaps shared environment) play a part.
findings.detail: In the Utah Population Database (Albright 2011), relative risk was 2.70 (1.56–4.66) for first-degree relatives, 2.34 for second-degree and 1.93 for third-degree, with excess distant relatedness (p=0.010). Buchwald 2001 (146 female twin pairs) found 55% MZ vs 19% DZ concordance for idiopathic chronic fatigue and estimated heritability up to 51%. Its confidence intervals are wide, and it measured chronic fatigue, not strict ME/CFS. Bos 2025 (Lifelines, 153,803 people, 90,397 with a first-degree relative) found recurrence risk ratio 1.45–2.23 within disorders and familiality 42% (33–50) for ME/CFS. Familial correlations were 0.97 with fibromyalgia and 0.83 with depression. Familiality includes shared household environment.

studies.result: First-degree RR 2.70; third-degree RR 1.93
MZ 55% vs DZ 19% concordance; h² up to 51%
Familiality 42% for ME/CFS; rf 0.97 with fibromyalgia, 0.83 with MDD

open_questions: How much of familiality is genetic vs shared environment or infection exposure?
Does the familial risk differ between infection-onset and gradual-onset cases?

findings.finding: DecodeME (15,579 PEM-defined cases vs 259,909 controls) identified 8 genome-wide significant loci, each with a small effect (OR about 1.07-1.10), and SNP heritability of about 8-10%.
findings.plain: The largest DNA study of ME/CFS found eight regions of the genome linked to the illness. Each nudges risk only a tiny amount.
findings.detail: Lead genes as assigned: RABGAP1L, BTN2A2/TRIM38, FBXL4, SUDS3, OLFM4, CCPG1, CA10, ARFGEF2/CSE1L/ZNFX1 (the chr20 signal p=1e-11). Four loci (RABGAP1L, FBXL4, OLFM4, CA10) were nominally associated (p<0.05) with PEM-plus-fatigue cases in UK Biobank and Lifelines, but none passed multiple-testing correction in external sets. There was no sex-biased locus, and ARFGEF2 and CA10 replicated in males. The CA10 signal colocalises with multisite chronic pain. As of October 2026 this is still a medRxiv preprint, with no peer-reviewed version. Gene assignments are weak at some loci: the 6q16 lead is about 890 kb from FBXL4, and the chr1 lead sits inside DARS2 (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). An absolute-risk calculation shows one risk copy moves baseline risk from about 0.9% to about 0.97–0.99%.

studies.result: 8 loci; no colocalisation with depression/anxiety

contradicting.cite: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis (MVP-only and FinnGen replication)
contradicting.result: Lead loci 5/8 same direction in MVP (p=0.13), 4/8 in FinnGen; BTN2A2, OLFM4, CA10 wrong way in MVP

open_questions: Which genes are causal at each locus (fine-mapping, functional work)?
Will loci replicate in a cohort with PEM-based phenotyping?
findings.test_available: Not useful individually (no clinical genetic test)

findings.finding: The genome-wide DecodeME signal replicates in independent cohorts: genetic correlation 0.65-0.73 with the Million Veteran Program CFS GWAS and 0.80-0.90 with UK Biobank CFS, plus concordant directions for sub-threshold SNPs in FinnGen.
findings.plain: Even though single hits do not yet repeat everywhere, the overall genetic fingerprint of ME/CFS shows up again in other large populations, including mostly male US veterans.
findings.detail: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis derived MVP-only statistics (3,891 independent cases) from the public DecodeME+MVP meta. rg 0.73 ± 0.16. DecodeME SNPs at p<1e-5 were concordant 42/63 in MVP (p=0.006) and 41/61 in FinnGen postviral fatigue (p=0.005). Pan-UKB self-report CFS gave rg 0.90, but it shares controls. An independent GitHub re-analysis (trafalmadorian97) reported rg 0.65 with MVP and 0.80 with Neale UKB. The MVP cohort is mostly male, so polygenic risk applies across sexes.

studies.result: rg 0.73; concordance p=0.006 (MVP), 0.005 (FinnGen)
5 loci incl. new TSHZ3 region; brain and pituitary enrichment
UK Biobank: 295 CFS had lower movement and wrist-temperature amplitude; of 30 published CFS variants, 1 associated with fatigue and 1 with actigraphy in the general population

open_questions: How much does loose biobank phenotyping (billing codes, self-report) dilute single-locus replication?

findings.finding: Genome-wide ME/CFS heritability is enriched in brain tissues and neurons (including glutamatergic synapse genes and subcortical/cerebellar neuron types), with no enrichment in blood immune cells.
findings.plain: The genes involved are mainly active in nerve cells in the brain, not in blood immune cells. This suggests the brain is central to inherited risk.
findings.detail: DecodeME: MAGMA gene-property enrichment in all 13 GTEx brain tissues and no others. Independent S-LDSC re-analysis (trafalmadorian97 GitHub): CNS tissues and chromatin only. ImmGen and blood-cell ATAC-seq were null, and medium spiny neuron clusters were implicated. Maccallini 2026 (DecodeME+MVP): brain regions and pituitary, glutamatergic synapse gene sets, with 7/12 gene sets replicating in rare-variant genes from HEAL2. Lee 2026 (medRxiv): inhibitory neurons (p=1.2e-7) and enteric neurons. Immune abnormalities may still be downstream of illness. A locus-level permutation with only 8 loci could not place any tissue (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

studies.result: All 13 brain tissues enriched; no others
Glutamatergic synapse; subcortical and cerebellar neurons; pituitary

contradicting.result: No tissue survives FDR at locus level (expected with 8 loci)

open_questions: Which brain circuits (basal ganglia, cerebellum, claustrum) matter, and do imaging studies of genetic-risk extremes show differences?

findings.finding: ME/CFS genetics overlaps most with chronic pain, fibromyalgia, IBS and migraine, and substantially with depression, but none of the 8 DecodeME loci share a causal variant with depression.
findings.plain: Genes that raise ME/CFS risk also raise risk of chronic pain and gut-brain conditions. This is shared biology, not evidence that ME/CFS is depression.
findings.detail: The CA10 locus colocalises with multisite chronic pain (PPH4 92.8%). Re-analyses report the highest rg with fibromyalgia, then multisite pain, as well as syncope, migraine and asthma. Lee 2026 medRxiv: rg with major depression 0.60 and with IBS 0.57. MR in Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: depression OR 1.82 (MVP 1.36) and multisite pain OR 3.3, but reverse MR is also positive (ME/CFS → depression OR 1.15) and heterogeneity is high, which indicates shared liability rather than one-way causation. A UK Biobank MR (Song 2025) found no causal effect of depression on ME/CFS.

studies.result: CA10 shares causal variant with chronic pain; no colocalisation with depression/anxiety
Depression, pain, insomnia associated both ways; shared liability

contradicting.result: No causal effect of MDD on ME/CFS

open_questions: Which part of ME/CFS genetics is specific after subtracting pain genetics? A re-analysis suggests the chr6 BTN region and one striatal neuron cluster.

findings.finding: Three DecodeME loci lie near infection-response genes (OLFM4, RABGAP1L, BTN2A2/TRIM38), and the OLFM4 effect is larger in infection-onset cases, but infection- and non-infection-onset cases are genetically highly correlated.
findings.plain: Some risk genes help the body respond to infections, which fits the common post-viral onset. But people whose illness began without an obvious infection carry similar overall genetic risk.
findings.detail: Infection-onset GWAS (9,738 cases): 3 loci (6p22.2, 20q13.13, OLFM4). The OLFM4 beta was 0.095±0.017 with infection onset vs 0.034±0.022 without. The no-infection GWAS (5,841) found nothing, which is a power issue. Independent re-analysis finds high rg between onset subgroups. OLFM4 is a neutrophil and ileal stem-cell protein. ZNFX1 (a dsRNA sensor) and CSE1L (needed for STAT1 import) sit at the chr20 locus. Genetically higher EBV DNA load gave OR 1.13 (ns) in DecodeME and 1.59 (p=0.012) in MVP (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). MHC-based negative controls (VZV, HHV-6B) also aligned, so the result is not EBV-specific. The long COVID FOXP4 variant is not associated with ME/CFS (p=0.59).

studies.result: OLFM4 effect larger with infection onset
liability to chronic fatigue OR 1.59

contradicting.result: FOXP4 lead variant; no association with ME/CFS in DecodeME

open_questions: Do OLFM4 risk-genotype carriers show different neutrophil or gut responses (recall-by-genotype)?
Is self-reported onset type too noisy to stratify on?

findings.finding: Reported HLA associations are inconsistent: Lande 2020's HLA-C*07:04 and DQB1*03:03 risk alleles are not among DecodeME's hits, and DecodeME's protective HLA-DQA1*05:01 signal is barely visible at SNP level.
findings.plain: HLA genes shape immune responses and are linked to autoimmune diseases. Claims of specific HLA types in ME/CFS have not held up consistently.
findings.detail: Lande 2020 (426 Norwegian CCC cases vs 4,511 controls) reported HLA-C*07:04 (OR 2.1) and DQB1*03:03 (OR 1.5); carriers of either were 19.2% vs 12.2%. DecodeME reported DQA1*05:01 as protective (p=1.4e-10; 21.7% vs 23.2%), with no DRB1*03:01 or DQB1*02:01 signal. In Solving ME/CFS re-analysis, the best DQ2.5 tag SNP was OR 0.96 (p=0.025). That gap suggests the imputed-allele p-value is inflated, possibly because HLA was imputed separately for cases and controls, a problem the authors flagged. MHC z-scores correlate only 0.21 between DecodeME and MVP. A purely in-silico 2025 study modelled Lande alleles binding herpes peptides, with no patient data.

studies.result: DQA1*05:01 protective p=1.4e-10

contradicting.result: Best DQ2.5 tag OR 0.96; DecodeME-MVP MHC z correlation 0.21

open_questions: Will joint HLA imputation of cases and controls confirm any allele?
findings.test_available: HLA typing is available but not useful for ME/CFS

findings.finding: Specific inhibitory KIR alleles (e.g. KIR3DL1*020, KIR3DL2*009) were more or less common in 418 Norwegian patients than 473 controls, though KIR gene content did not differ.
findings.plain: Variants in genes for natural killer cell 'brake' receptors may differ slightly in ME/CFS. This has not been checked in another cohort.
findings.detail: Ramadan 2025 used high-resolution KIR sequencing with HLA ligand annotation. Patient-enriched alleles were KIR3DL3*002 (OR 1.43), KIR3DL1*020 (OR 2.20) and KIR3DL2*009 (OR 1.56); reduced alleles were KIR3DL3*013 (OR 0.60) and KIR3DL2*010 (OR 0.46, p=0.0005). There was no association with gene content or copy number. Nominal p-values without a replication cohort; KIR is poorly captured by GWAS arrays, so DecodeME cannot test it.

studies.result: Several inhibitory KIR alleles associated (nominal p 0.0005–0.01)

open_questions: Replication in UK or US cohorts; link to NK cytotoxicity measures.

findings.finding: Before DecodeME, small GWAS and candidate-gene studies (GRIK2, NPAS2, TPPP, TRA locus and many others) produced no association that replicated in UK Biobank or later cohorts.
findings.plain: Older genetic studies were too small. Their 'hits' did not hold up when tested in larger groups.
findings.detail: Smith 2011 (40 vs 40, 116k SNPs plus expression) flagged GRIK2 and NPAS2. Hajdarevic 2022 (Norwegian 427 discovery, Danish 460, UKB 2,105) found no genome-wide significant loci; the best signal was TPPP (p=8.5e-7) and the top SNP did not replicate. Dibble 2020 concluded that most candidate gene associations are not replicated by the UK Biobank CFS cohort. Ueland 2022's T-cell receptor alpha signal did not replicate (from Solving ME/CFS genetics summary).

studies.result: No genome-wide significant loci; TPPP not replicated
Most candidate gene associations not replicated
GRIK2, NPAS2 nominal

findings.test_available: No: commercial 'ME/CFS gene panels' are not supported

findings.finding: A 2026 UK Biobank GWAS with stricter, multi-source case definitions (1,268 cases) reports 7 loci that replicate in disjoint UK Biobank or All of Us cohorts (near BICD1, GRIN2A, CSMD1, RORA, CLYBL), though none replicate in all three.
findings.plain: A new study using carefully confirmed cases in two biobanks found seven genetic regions that repeated in a second group. It is a preprint and the groups are small.
findings.detail: Slaughter 2026 (medRxiv) used TarGene with electronic health records plus survey data to confirm case and control status. 176 variants passed FDR<5% in discovery, and replication cohorts had 319 (UKB) and 371 (All of Us) cases. Fine-mapping at one locus colocalised with reduced CLYBL expression in putamen, but the CLYBL stop-gain variant was not associated. No gene-by-sex or gene-by-deprivation interactions survived correction. FDR-based discovery in a small sample and no overlap with DecodeME's 8 loci call for caution. GRIN2A (an NMDA receptor subunit) fits the glutamatergic signal.

studies.result: 7 replicated loci, none in all three cohorts

open_questions: Do these loci show any signal in DecodeME summary statistics?

findings.finding: Proteome-wide cis-MR finds genetically higher plasma EPHB1 (a pain-sensitisation receptor) and CLEC3B (tetranectin) associated with ME/CFS risk in DecodeME, replicating in the independent MVP cohort.
findings.plain: Using genes as a natural experiment, two blood proteins look like they may influence ME/CFS risk. One of them is involved in how the nervous system amplifies pain.
findings.detail: Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of about 1,950 UKB-PPP and 1,690 deCODE plasma proteins (Wald ratio). EPHB1: OR 1.18/SD (p=2e-4), MVP 1.29 (p=0.0016), combined FDR 0.002; its pQTL is in LD with the regional DecodeME peak (r² 0.84). CLEC3B: OR 1.21, MVP 1.44 (p=0.0008), but not in LD with the regional peak. PRDX6 (1q25) was protective (0.75; MVP 0.70, p=0.037), and dermatopontin was nominal on both platforms. Only 4/93 nominal hits replicated, versus about 2.3 expected by chance, so these are leads. There was no formal colocalisation because full pQTL statistics need a login, and there are no usable drugs.

studies.result: EPHB1 and CLEC3B replicate; PRDX6 nominal

open_questions: Full colocalisation with deCODE/UKB-PPP region data; CSF/brain pQTLs for EPHB1.

findings.finding: MR of DecodeME suggests higher mitochondrial DNA copy number is protective and higher GlycA and mean platelet volume raise risk, while genetically predicted metabolite leads (IPA, kynurenine, ketones, carnitine, bile acids) and vitamin D, BMI and blood pressure are null or unreplicated.
findings.plain: Genetic natural experiments hint that inflammation and blood platelets may contribute to risk. Many blood molecules that are low in patients look like effects of being ill, not causes.
findings.detail: Wielscher 2026 (Research Square, not peer reviewed) reported mtDNA copy number as protective and GlycA and MPV as risk-raising. It also found the strongest genetic overlap in barrier-microbiome, neurovascular and energetics traits. Solving ME/CFS MR found indolelactate OR 0.99, kynurenine 1.01 and 3-hydroxybutyrate 0.99, all null. Palmitoylcarnitine 0.88 did not replicate. Vitamin D OR 0.88 (p=0.03) was not replicated and had a pleiotropic Egger intercept. Many published two-sample MR papers on CFS use small UK Biobank self-report GWAS; one was retracted in 2025.

studies.result: mtDNA copy number protective; GlycA, MPV risk
Metabolite and risk-factor exposures null or unreplicated
Mendelian randomisation (UK Biobank, 2,076 cases): higher CXCL5 and CCL20 linked to higher ME/CFS risk, higher TNF to lower risk; small-effect instruments

contradicting.result: Example of low-quality MR in CFS literature

open_questions: Replicate GlycA/MPV/mtDNA MR in MVP; test platelet activation in patients.

findings.finding: Whole-genome sequencing of 464 cases and 611 controls with a deep-learning rare-variant model (HEAL2) proposes 115 loss-of-function-intolerant risk genes, partly overlapping the common-variant synaptic signal.
findings.plain: Looking at rare DNA changes, one study suggests a set of genes, many active in nerves and immune cells. The method is new and the sample is small.
findings.detail: Zhang 2025 (medRxiv) reports that a genetic score from personal rare variants tracked PEM, unrefreshing sleep, brain fog and muscle pain. Patient multi-omics showed reduced expression of the risk genes, including in cytotoxic CD4 T cells. Maccallini 2026 found 7 of 12 common-variant gene sets replicate among HEAL2 genes. Deep-learning gene prioritisation in about 1,000 genomes has high overfitting risk, and there has been no independent sequencing replication. No single rare variant has been shown to cause ME/CFS. A verified, specific rare-variant 'Mendelian ME/CFS' report does not exist to my knowledge.

studies.result: 115 risk genes; symptom links

open_questions: Independent WGS replication; burden tests in DecodeME exomes when available.
findings.test_available: Research only; clinical exome only for red-flag mimics (mitochondrial, HLH, immunodeficiency)

findings.finding: Proprietary combinatorial SNP analyses (PrecisionLife) report thousands of multi-SNP signatures in UK Biobank and DecodeME, with top vs bottom decile of signature count giving OR 1.64.
findings.plain: A company's method finds combinations of DNA variants linked to ME/CFS, but the method is closed and hard for others to check.
findings.detail: Das 2022 (2,382 UKB cases) mapped 84 SNP combinations to 14 genes, including CLOCK, SLC15A4, INSR and KCNB1. Sardell 2026 (J Transl Med, DecodeME vs UKB controls) reported 22,411 signatures from 7,555 SNPs in 2,311 genes, reproducible across three disjoint DecodeME case sets (p=4e-21 for count), 259 core genes, and 76/180 long-COVID genes overlapping. 'Reproducible' here means within related cohorts sharing UK Biobank controls; the method is proprietary and the gene list is very broad.

studies.result: OR 1.64 top vs bottom decile of signature count
14 genes; 5 SNPs replicated in a UKB CFS set

open_questions: Do signatures replicate in an external cohort with different controls (MVP, FinnGen, All of Us)?

findings.finding: TRPM3 ion channel dysfunction in NK cells and TRPM3 SNPs are reported repeatedly by one research group, but the SNP studies are tiny and no TRPM3 association appears in GWAS.
findings.plain: A calcium channel called TRPM3 is reported to work poorly in immune cells of ME/CFS patients. Nearly all of this comes from one team, and large DNA studies do not point to the TRPM3 gene.
findings.detail: Marshall-Gradisnik 2016 genotyped B cells from 11 patients vs 11 controls and reported SNPs/genotypes in TRPM3 and acetylcholine receptor genes. Functional work: Sasso 2026 used patch-clamp at two sites run by the same consortium (36 vs 42) and found reduced TRPM3-like currents in NK cells. Independent-lab replication and blinding details are lacking, and TRPM3 is not among DecodeME, MVP or Slaughter 2026 loci. Functional changes could be acquired rather than inherited.

studies.result: Reduced TRPM3 function in NK cells
TRPM3 and AChR gene SNPs reported

contradicting.result: No TRPM3 locus among genome-wide hits

open_questions: Will an independent lab, blinded to case status, reproduce reduced TRPM3 currents?
Is TRPM3 gene-level association present in DecodeME MAGMA results?

findings.finding: Joint hypermobility and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are over-represented in ME/CFS (Beighton ≥4 in 60% of children with CFS vs 24% of controls; 50% in a Swedish severe cohort; EDS about 100x expected in Finnish registries).
findings.plain: People with very flexible joints, or hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, seem more likely to have ME/CFS or long COVID with PEM. No gene test exists for the hypermobile type.
findings.detail: Barron 2002 (58 incident paediatric CFS vs 58 controls): median Beighton 4 vs 1, OR 3.5 (1.6–7.5). Bragée 2020 (229 severe CCC patients, no controls): 50% hypermobile, with high rates of possible intracranial hypertension and craniocervical findings on MRI. Finnish FinnGen/FinRegistry postviral fatigue shows EDS O/E 106–153, which is crude and inflated by healthcare use (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). Lubell 2026 (online survey, 1,816 people after COVID) found extreme hypermobility OR 3.15 for long COVID with high post-exertional symptom exacerbation, rising to OR 9.46 with a pre-COVID orthostatic/neurocognitive profile. Hypermobile EDS has no known causal gene, and connective-tissue genes are not among GWAS hits. Collagen breakdown markers are raised in 4/4 Metabolon cohorts (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

studies.result: Hypermobility 60% vs 24%; OR 3.5
50% hypermobile
Extreme hypermobility OR 3.15 for long COVID with high PESE

open_questions: Prevalence in population-based ME/CFS cohorts with blinded Beighton scoring?
Does hypermobility define a subgroup with distinct orthostatic or craniocervical features?
findings.test_available: Yes: Beighton score and 2017 hEDS criteria (clinical); genetic testing only for other EDS types

findings.finding: Mitochondrial DNA haplogroups and common mtDNA SNPs are not associated with ME/CFS status, though some variants were associated with particular symptoms.
findings.plain: Inherited types of mitochondrial DNA do not differ between patients and controls.
findings.detail: Billing-Ross 2016 (Cornell cohorts) found no haplogroup or SNP association with disease status but reported variant links to symptom severity. Hanson 2016 is the authors' reply clarifying this. MR suggesting higher mtDNA copy number is protective (Wielscher 2026) concerns copy number, not haplogroup. The chr1 DecodeME lead lies in DARS2, a mitochondrial tRNA synthetase, which is a weak hint.

studies.cite: Hanson 2016, J Transl Med (reply on Billing-Ross 2016)
studies.result: No association with disease status; symptom associations

open_questions: Heteroplasmy and somatic mtDNA changes in muscle have not been studied at scale.

hypotheses_notes.for: Brain-only tissue enrichment (DecodeME and independent re-analyses), glutamatergic synapse and specific neuron types (Maccallini 2026), CA10 shared with chronic pain, EPHB1 MR, and GRIN2A in Slaughter 2026.
hypotheses_notes.against: Most results are preprints. Individual loci do not yet replicate. Neuronal enrichment is common to many brain-related traits, and the overlap with pain and depression may reflect shared symptom liability.

hypotheses_notes.for: Infection-response genes at 3 loci, a larger OLFM4 effect in infection onset, and suggestive EBV-load MR (MVP p=0.012).
hypotheses_notes.against: Infection and non-infection onset are genetically similar, EBV MR control viruses align too, and immune cell types are not enriched.

hypotheses_notes.for: HLA associations reported in Norway (Lande 2020) and DQA1*05:01 in DecodeME.
hypotheses_notes.against: The HLA findings disagree with each other and the DecodeME signal is weak at SNP level. Common-variant genetics shows no immune-cell enrichment.

hypotheses_notes.for: Hypermobility and EDS are enriched clinically and in registries, collagen breakdown markers are raised, and hypermobility is a risk factor for long COVID with PEM.
hypotheses_notes.against: No connective-tissue genes appear among GWAS loci, the hEDS gene is unknown, and the studies are mostly clinic- or survey-based with selection bias.

hypotheses_notes.for: MR suggests mtDNA copy number is protective, and the DARS2 gene sits at the chr1 lead.
hypotheses_notes.against: There is no muscle tissue enrichment, mtDNA haplogroups are not associated, and the FBXL4 assignment is distant.

glossary.plain: Genome-wide association study: compares millions of DNA letters between cases and controls to find regions linked to a disease.
A region of the genome. A GWAS 'hit' is a locus, not necessarily a known gene.
How much one copy of a variant changes the odds of disease. 1.08 means 8% higher odds, which is a very small effect.
The share of variation in risk explained by common DNA variants measured on chips.
How much the genetic risk for two traits overlaps (from −1 to 1).
Using inherited variants as a natural experiment to test whether a factor (such as a protein level) causes a disease.
A test of whether two genetic signals in the same region share the same causal variant.
Immune genes that present fragments of microbes to T cells; often linked to autoimmune disease.
A 9-point bedside test of joint flexibility; 4 or more (adults often 5) suggests generalised hypermobility.
Risk spread across thousands of variants, each with a tiny effect.

key_reviews.why: Critical review of pre-DecodeME genetics showing candidate genes do not replicate.
Primary report of the 8 loci, HLA, sex and onset analyses; summary statistics public on OSF.
DecodeME+MVP meta-analysis with tissue, cell-type and rare-variant cross-replication.

gaps: DecodeME is still a preprint; peer review and independent locus-level replication in a PEM-phenotyped cohort are needed.
No GWAS of PEM severity or of illness course; DecodeME questionnaires would allow one.
No recall-by-genotype studies (e.g. OLFM4 or CA10 risk homozygotes) to link variants to measurable biology.
Non-European ancestry is almost absent from ME/CFS genetics.
HLA needs joint imputation or sequencing of cases and controls; KIR findings need replication.
No independent, blinded replication of TRPM3 functional or SNP findings outside the originating consortium.
Hypermobility prevalence in population-based ME/CFS with blinded assessment is unknown, and genetic studies of hypermobility-ME/CFS overlap have not been done.
Rare-variant evidence rests on one deep-learning study of about 1,000 genomes; larger sequencing studies are needed.

domains.title: Treatment trials and natural history
domains.overview: No treatment has replicated, placebo-controlled evidence of benefit in ME/CFS or post-COVID ME/CFS. Since 2019 the large, well-controlled trials have been negative: rituximab, Paxlovid (three trials), immunoadsorption against sham (two trials), ivabradine for long-COVID POTS, temelimab, and low-dose naltrexone for fatigue. The positive signals (daratumumab, cyclophosphamide, low-dose rapamycin, low-dose aripiprazole, single-dose pyridostigmine, 40-session HBOT) come from small, open-label or single-centre studies, and they need to be read against placebo response rates of 35-40% or more. Graded exercise is no longer recommended in England (NICE 2021), and patient surveys and a German rehab study report frequent worsening, while pacing and volume/compression measures are the most highly rated but untested by trials. Natural history data show low full recovery in adults (median ~5%), prevalence of ~0.2-1%, a female excess of 3-4:1, no clear rise in all-cause mortality, and a marked rise in suicide.

findings.finding: B-cell depletion with rituximab did not improve fatigue or function versus placebo in a 151-person phase III trial (RituxME).
findings.plain: A drug that removes antibody-making B cells looked promising in small Norwegian studies, but a large placebo-controlled trial found it worked no better than a dummy infusion.
findings.detail: RituxME (Fluge 2019): 77 rituximab vs 74 placebo over 24 months; overall response 26.0% vs 35.1% (difference 9.2 points favouring placebo, 95% CI -5.5 to 23.3, p=0.22); no difference on any secondary endpoint; serious adverse events 26% vs 19%. Six-year follow-up (Rekeland 2024): SF-36 physical function 32.9 to 45.5 on rituximab vs 32.3 to 43.1 on placebo. The earlier positive phase II results (Fluge 2011, 2015) were small and partly open-label; the phase III result is the standard example of how large the placebo/natural-course improvement can be in ME/CFS trials.

studies.design: phase III double-blind RCT, 5 Norwegian centres
studies.result: Response 26.0% rituximab vs 35.1% placebo, p=0.22; no secondary benefit
SF-36 PF at 6 yr 45.5 rituximab vs 43.1 placebo; SF-36 PF >=70 in 27.6% vs 20.4%

contradicting.result: 18/29 reported clinically significant responses (not controlled)

open_questions: Is there a B-cell-dependent subgroup that a whole-population trial would dilute?
Why did both arms improve by ~10 SF-36 points over 18 months?

findings.finding: In an open-label phase II study, 55% of 40 patients responded to six IV cyclophosphamide infusions, and many responders stayed improved at 6 years, but there was no control arm.
findings.plain: A chemotherapy drug that suppresses the immune system was followed by improvement in about half of a small Norwegian group, but without a comparison group the effect cannot be separated from natural improvement or placebo.
findings.detail: CycloME (Rekeland 2020): 600-700 mg/m2 every 4 weeks x6; 22/40 (55%) responders; SF-36 PF 35.4 to 54.4 at 18 months and 56.7 at 6 years; 44.1% had SF-36 PF >=70 at 6 years versus 20.4% of RituxME placebo patients (different trial, not randomised). Nausea in ~90%; 11 serious adverse events in 8 patients. Response was higher in carriers of HLA-DQB1*03:03 and/or HLA-C*07:04 (83% vs 43%), an unreplicated post hoc finding. The authors themselves advise against use outside trials because of toxicity (infertility, bladder and cancer risk).

studies.result: 55% responders; 68% of responders still improved at 3-4 years
SF-36 PF 56.7 at 6 yr; 17.6% at >=90 (normal range)

open_questions: Would a randomised trial against an active-placebo reproduce the effect?
Does the HLA association replicate (HLA-C*07:04 also appears in other ME/CFS genetic reports)?

findings.finding: In an open-label pilot, 6 of 10 women with moderate-to-severe ME/CFS improved markedly after the anti-CD38 antibody daratumumab, and low baseline NK-cell count predicted non-response.
findings.plain: A drug that removes long-lived antibody-producing plasma cells was followed by large, lasting improvements in six of ten patients. This is the most striking recent signal, but it is ten people with no placebo group.
findings.detail: Fluge 2025: 4-7 subcutaneous injections after a 12-week run-in. Mean SF-36 PF 25.9 to 55.0 at 8-9 months (p=0.002); in the 6 responders 32.2 to 78.3; 5 sustained improvement (SF-36 PF ~88) with step counts above 10,000/day for weeks. Mean steps 3,359 to 5,862. IgG fell 54% in responders vs 40% in non-responders. Low baseline NK-cell counts associated with no response. No serious adverse events. A randomised trial is planned in Norway; Charité is pursuing a related approach with inebilizumab. Given RituxME's ~35% placebo response, n=10 open-label cannot establish efficacy.

studies.result: 6/10 marked improvement; SF-36 PF 25.9 to 55.0 (p=0.002)
Fluge reported 5 of 6 responders still in remission at 2-3 years

open_questions: Does the response survive randomisation and blinding?
Is NK-cell count a genuine predictor or a chance correlation in n=10?
Which antibodies, if any, are being removed?

findings.finding: Removing antibodies by immunoadsorption was no better than a sham procedure in two controlled trials (IAMPOCO, n=40; IA-PACS-CFS, n=65), although open-label series had reported 50-70% responders.
findings.plain: Filtering antibodies out of the blood seemed to help in uncontrolled studies. When patients were compared with others who had a fake procedure, both groups improved similarly.
findings.detail: Stein 2025 (open-label, post-COVID ME/CFS with raised beta2-adrenergic receptor antibodies, n=20): 70% 'responders', SF-36 PF +17.75 at 4 weeks; antibody fall did not distinguish responders. IAMPOCO (Mainz, tryptophan adsorbers, patient-blinded sham crossover, n=40): no difference on the Post-COVID Functional Scale (OR 1.17, p=0.771) or fatigue, cognition, grip strength; 24 vs 10 adverse events. IA-PACS-CFS (Charité, 44 IA vs 21 sham, 5 sessions): 'no statistically or clinically significant differences' on Chalder fatigue at day 60 (preliminary, conference). Critics note IA-PACS-CFS did not select for autoantibody-positive patients; IAMPOCO removed GPCR antibodies and still showed no benefit. A 2025 antigen-profiling study found no elevated GPCR autoantibodies in ME/CFS at all.

studies.design: prospective open-label cohort (repeat IA, beta2-AR antibody positive)
studies.result: 70% responders at 4 weeks; no control

studies.cite: Stortz/Kraus et al. 2026, IAMPOCO (Mainz repository; Lancet Reg Health Eur correspondence)
studies.result: No difference: PCFS OR 1.17, p=0.771; no secondary benefit
Failed primary endpoint (Chalder fatigue, day 60)

contradicting.result: 7/15 responded
Reports changes in autoantibodies and performance after 5 sessions

open_questions: Does an autoantibody-selected subgroup benefit in a sham-controlled design?
Are the measured GPCR antibodies meaningful at all, given negative antigen-profiling data?
findings.test_available: Not recommended outside trials; GPCR antibody tests (CellTrend) are commercial but of unproven meaning

findings.finding: The aptamer BC007 (rovunaptabin) failed to beat placebo in the company's 114-person long-COVID trial; a 30-person investigator-led trial reported secondary-endpoint gains.
findings.plain: A drug designed to neutralise antibodies against blood-vessel and heart receptors was tested twice in long COVID. The larger trial found no benefit; a smaller exploratory one reported improvements on fatigue scales.
findings.detail: reCOVer (Erlangen, Hohberger 2025): n=30 with GPCR autoantibodies, primary endpoint safety (9 vs 5 adverse events, NS); secondary endpoints improved (FACIT fatigue p=0.038, Bell score p=0.0004, FSS p=0.009) in an exploratory crossover analysis. BLOC (Berlin Cures, NCT05911009, ~114 participants, 19 sites): topline November 2024 showed no difference from placebo; data unpublished; the company stopped operating. The negative result is larger but unpublished; the positive one is small, exploratory and multiplicity-prone. Combined with the immunoadsorption sham trials and the negative antigen-profiling study, the GPCR-autoantibody route has weakened.

studies.design: phase IIa double-blind placebo-controlled crossover RCT
studies.result: Safety primary met; secondary fatigue/QoL improvements

contradicting.result: No significant effect vs placebo (company announcement; unpublished)

open_questions: Will the BLOC data be published?
Is there any validated assay for functional GPCR antibodies?

findings.finding: IVIG has no consistent controlled evidence: 1990s ME/CFS RCTs conflicted, and a 30-person trial in autoimmune POTS found no difference from albumin.
findings.plain: Infusions of pooled antibodies from donors are sometimes used for severe patients. Old trials gave mixed answers and the most recent small trial in POTS found the same improvement with a volume-matched control infusion.
findings.detail: iSTAND (Vernino 2024): 16 IVIG vs 14 albumin, 0.4 g/kg x8 over 12 weeks; COMPASS-31 change -5.5 vs -10.6 (p=0.63); responders 46.7% vs 38.5% (NS). Albumin also expands volume, so the comparator may have masked or matched a volume effect. 1990s ME/CFS RCTs: Lloyd 1990 (n=49) positive, Peterson 1990 (n=30) negative, Vollmer-Conna 1997 (n=99) negative. In the Eckey/Xiao 2025 patient survey IVIG was rated among the most helpful in the severe multisystemic cluster (self-report, selected users). The RECOVER-AUTONOMIC IVIG arm in long-COVID POTS has not yet reported (as of Oct 2026).
